Q. Define community. [CU-12Ju,11J]
Q. What are the characteristics of a community?

Answer
Community: The following definition of ‘community’ is accepted by ‘WHO Expert Committee’.
CA community is a social group determined by geographical boundaries and/or common values and
interests
[Ref- Park /24" / 708]
Or,

Community can be defined as ‘a collection of a group of persons in social interaction in a geographical
area and sharing a common social and cultural life’.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5™ / 468]
racteristics of community:

1) The community is a contiguous geographical area.
2), Itis composed of people living together.

3) People co-operate to satisfy their basic needs.
4) ‘There are common emanations ee eeke ganizations, e.g. markets, schools, stores, banks, hospitals.
5) Economic status.
6) Specitic functions or occupations or pursuits as a whole for the community.
7) AA group dependanoror bones pendence or belongingness.
8) An interdependent behaviour.
[Ref- Park / 24" /725 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 468]

History of Community Medicine

History of development of community medicine:
“> Medicine in antiquity:

> Primitive medicine: The concept of disease in which the ancient man believed is known as the
“supernatural theory of disease”.

Indian medicine: The medical systems that are truly Indian in origin and development are the
Ayurveda and the Siddha systems.

Chinese medicine: The Chinese were early pioneers of immunization.

Egyptian medicine: Castor oil, tannic acid, opium, turpentine, gentian, senna, minerals and
root drugs were all used by the Egyptian physicians.

| Mesopotamian medicine: Mesopotamia often called the "Cradle of Civilization". Babylonian
Code of Hammurabi, the very first codification of medical practice.

Greek medicine: Hippocrates, the greatest Greek physician is often called the ‘Father of
Medicine’. He at first distinguished between diseases which were epidemic and those which

| were endemic.

Roman medicine: Public health was born in Rome with the development of baths, sewers and
aqueducts.

Chapter-01: Introduction to the Community medicine SS

Middle ages medicine (500-1500 AD): It was called ‘Dark Ages of Medicine’. But the Arabs
orrowing largely from the Greeks and Romans, they developed their own system of medicine
known as the Unani system of medicine.

* Dawn of scientific medicine;

> Revival of medicine (1453-1600 AD): Fracastorius gave “Theory of Contagion”. He
envisaged the transfer of infection via minute visible particles and explained the cause of
epidemics.

> Sanitary awakening: Great sanitary awakening is a historic - milestone in the evolution of
medicine which took place in England in the mid-nineteenth century and gradually spread to
other countries. .

> Rise of public health: Cholera is called the “father of public health”.

> Germ theory of disease: In 1860, Louis Pasteur demonstrated the presence of bacteria in the
air and in 1877, Robert Koch showed that anthrax was caused by a bacteria. These two
discoveries confirmed the “Germ theory of disease” and it was the golden age of bacteriology.

> Birth of preventive medicine: After the discovery of causative agents of disease and the
establishment of the Germ theory of disease the preventive medicine got a firm foundation.

+ Modern medicine:
> Curative medicine.
> Preventive medicine: The eradication of small pox (the last case of small pox occurred in
Somalia in 1977) is one of the greatest triumphs of preventive medicine in recent times.
> Social medicine.

> Changing concepts in public health,

“ Medical revolution:
> State of the art.
> Failure of medicine.
> Social control of medicine.
> Family and community medicine.

“ Health care revolution:
> Health for All: In May 1977, member countries of WHO at the 30" World Health Assembly
defined Health for All as: ‘Attainment by all the peoples of the world, by the year 2000
AD, of a level of health that will permit them to lead a socially & economically productive
life’. The goal of Health for All has two perspectives:
1) The realization of the WHO’s objective of “attainment by all peoples of the highest
possible level of health”.
2) Asaminimum, all people in all countries should have at least such a level of health
that they are capable of working productively and of participating actively in the social.
life of the community in which they live.

Primary health care.

Deprofessionalization of medicine.
The Millennium Development Goals: In September 2000, representatives from 189 countries

met at the Millennium summit in New York to adopt the United Nations Millennium
Declaration. The leaders made specific commitments in seven areas: peace, security and
disarmament; development and poverty eradication; protecting our common environment,
human rights, democracy and good governance; protecting the vulnerable; meeting the special
needs of Africa; and strengthening the United Nations. The Road Map established goals and
targets to be reached by year 2015 in each of seven areas. The goals in the area of development
and poverty eradication are now widely referred to as ‘Millennium Development Goals’.

Public Health

Q. De’ fvivus health. [CU-13J, RU-12J]
Ansyér
Public health:

The WHO expert committee on public health administration adapting the definition of public health by
C.E.A. Winslow (in 1920), has defined public health as —

“The science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health and efficiency
through organized community efforts for the sanitation of the environment, the control of communicable .
infections, the education of the individual in personal hygiene, the organization of medical and nursing services
for early diagnosis and preventive treatment of disease, and the development of social machinery to ensure for
every individual a standard of living adequate for the maintenance of health, so organizing these benefits as to
enable every citizen to realize his birthright of health and longevity.”

[Ref- Park / 24" /51 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5™ /24]

For Viva
* Aims of public health:
1) Promotion of health.
2) Restoration of distorted health.
3) Prevention of disease.
4) Prolongation of life expectancy.

“ Objectives of public health:

1) Control of physical environment

2) Control of communicable infection.

3) Prevention, treatment and rehabilitation of chronic-diseases and behavioral disorder.

4) To improve the efficacy and health care delivery system.

5) To make maximum utilization of available resources to ensure health for all, by 2005AD.

Q. Why cholera is called the father of public health?
Answer
Cholera is called the father of public health. Because -

An English epidemiologist John Snow studied the epidemiology of cholera in. London from 1848-
1854 and established the role of polluted drinking water in the spread of cholera.

The demand from people for clean water came after the study. For this reason cholera is called the
father of public health as the principal activities of public health are improvement of sanitation & to provide
safe drinking water.

Q. “Great sanitary awakening is a historic milestone in the evolution of medicine”- discuss.
Answer

"Great sanitary awakening is a historic milestone in the evolution of medicine" which took place in
England in the mid-nineteenth century and gradually spread to other countries. It had a tremendous impact in
modifying the behaviour of people and ushering an era of public health. The industrial revolution of the 18th
century sparked off numerous problems —
Creation of slums.
Overcrowding with all its ill effects.
Accumulation of filth in cities & towns.
High sickness & death rates especially among women & children.
Infectious diseases like TB,
Industrial & social problems.

NNN SN

These deteriorate the health of people to the lowest ebb. The mean age at death in London was reported
to be 44 years for the gentry and professionals and 22 years for working class in 1842. Add to this, the frequent
visitations of cholera compounded the misery of the people.

Chapter-01: Introduction to the Community medi¢ine <2 $$ $ a  — 3

f the i The great cholera epidemic of 1882 led Edwin Chadwick, a lawyer in England to’investigate the health
of the inhabitants of the large towns with a view to improve the conditions under they lived.

Chadwick's report on "The Sanitary Conditions of the labouring population" in Great Britain, a
landmark in the history of public health, set London & other cities slowly to improve housing and working
conditions. His report focused the attention of the people and government on the urgent need to improve public
health. Filth was recognized as man's great enemy and this began an anti-filth crusade, “great sanitary
awakening” which led to the enactment of the Public health.

Q. Write short note on: Public health emergency.
Answer

Public health emergency:

Any incidence which causes break down of public health by any means is called public health
emergency. Public health emergency varies from country to country according to the socio-economic
conditions of that country. As for example, if a single case of cholera is found in USA that is the public health

emergency for USA but not for Bangladesh.

Examples of Public health emergency:
> Any epidemic outbreak.

> Natural calamities, i.e. cyclone, flood ete.
> Accidents e.g. serious road transport accident.

Changing concepts of health: A brief account of the changing concepts of health is given below —

1) Biomedical concept: A person was considered as healthy if he was free from disease or absence of
disease. This concept is known as the biomedical concept.
> This concept is based on germ theory of disease.
> Criticism: Role of environmental, social, psychological and cultural determinants of health
are ignored.

2) Ecological concept: The ecologists viewed health as a dynamic equilibrium between man & his
environment and disease a maladjustment of the human organism to environment. The ecological
concept raises two issues:

| > Imperfect man.
> Imperfect environment.

3) Psychosocial concept: Health is not only a biomedical phenomenon, but one which is influenced

by social, psychological, cultural, economic & political factors of the people concerned.
Social factor:

husbandry, food, industry, education, housing, public works, communication and other sectors).

Q. Discuss the most acceptable concept of health with justification. [SUST-13J]
Answer
Most acceptable concept of health: Holistic concept is the most acceptable concept of health.

“> Justification:

The holistic model is a synthesis of all the previous concepts of health, All the previous
concepts e.g. biomedical concept, ecological concept & psychosocial concept have some deficiency.
But the holistic concept is described as a unified or multidimensional process involving the well-being
of the whole person in the context of his environment.

The holistic approach implies that all sectors of society have an effect on health (in particular
agriculture, animal husbandry, food, industry, education, housing, public works, communication and
other sectors). The emphasis is on the promotion and protection of health.

J A‘) Infant mortality.
12) Life expectancy at age one.

Chapter-02: Concept of health & disease ————————

Calculation: For each component, the performance of individual countries is placed on a scale of 0 to 100. ‘0’
represents an absolutely defined ‘worst’ performance and ‘100’ represents an absolutely defined ‘best’
performance. The composite index is calculated by averaging the 3 indicators, giving equal weight to each of
them. The resulting PQLI thus is scaled 0 to 100.

Example: In Bangladesh

a) “> Infant mortality : 57/ 1000/ year
> Life expectancy at age one : 60 years
> Literacy 43%

So, PQLI of Bangladesh is = (57 + 60 + 43) /3 = 53.3

a

Human development index / HDI

Q. What is human development index (HDI)?
Answer
Human development index (HDI):
HDI is defined as “a composite index combining indicators representing three dimensions — longevity
(life expectancy at birth), knowledge (adult literacy rate and mean years of schooling) and income (real G'
per capita in purchasing power parity in US dollars).”
HDI value ranges from 0 to 1.

[Ref- Park / 24" /17]

Health is not static. It is a dynamic phenomenon — explain. [RU-14J]
Q. Write short note on: Health and disease spectrum. [RU-10Ju]
’ Answer
Spectrum of health / health-sickness spectrum:

The spectral concept of health denotes that the health of an individual is not static. It fluctuates within a
range varying from optimum wellbeing to various levels of dysfunction including the state of total dysfunction
(death).

The transition from good health to ill health is often a gradual one and where one step ends and the
other begin as matter of judgment.

The systematic representation of these different levels of health constitutes the health-sickness

spectrum.
‘a

~

Positive health. °
Better health.
Freedom from sickness.

Unrecognized sickness.
Mild sickness.

Severe sickness,

Death.

+ The lowest point on the health-disease spectrum is death and the highest point corresponds to the WHO
definition of positive health.

inants of health:

Explanation of determinants of health:

some types of diabetes, etc.

The way people live.
Cultural pattern.

Ecology of Health
a

Q. Define ecology. [RU-16N, CU-12J]
Answer
Ecology:

Ecology is defined as “‘the science of mutual relationship between living organisms and their
environments.”

; Human ecology is a subject of more general science of ecology.

A full understanding of health requires that humanity be seen as part of an ecosystem. The human
ecosystem includes in addition to the natural environment all the dimensions of the man-made environment -
physical, chemical, biological, psychological: in short, our culture and all its products. Disease is embedded in
the ecosystem of man. Health according to ecological concepts is visualized as a state of dynamic equilibrium

between man and his environment.
[Ref- Park / 24/21]

Q. What is the main distinction between epidemiology and ecology?
Answer
The main distinction between epidemiology and ecology:

Epidemiology is the study of the relationship between variations in man’s environment and his state of
health (or disease), while ecology embraces the interrelationship of all living things. In this regards,
epidemiology constitutes a special application of human ecology or that part of ecology relating to the state of
human health.

[Ref- Park /24"/21]

Viva Q. What is “right to health”?
Answer

Right to health;

= Everyone has the Tight to a standard of living adequate for the health and wellbeing of himself and his
‘amily,

The concept of “right to health” has generated so many questions, e.g. right to medicat care, right to
responsibility for health, right to a healthy environment, right to food, right to procreate, right not to procreate
(family Planning, Sterilization, legal abortion), rights of the diseased persons and the right to die (suicide,
hunger Strike) etc.

Q. De ine health indicator, [CU-18N,16M/J]
we the characteristics / criteria of health indicators.
\ nswer

Health indicators: Health indicators are the tools with which we measure the health status of a community.

Characteristics / criteria of health indicators: Ideal indicators —
1) Should be valid i.e. they should actually measure what they are supposed to measure.
2) Should be reliable & objective, i.e. the answers should be the same if measured by different people
in similar circumstances,
3) Should be sensitive, i.e. they should be sensitive to changes in the situation concerned.
4) Should be specific, i.e. they should reflect changes only in the situation concemed.

Q. How socio-economic indicators reflect healthcare of a community?
Q. How socio-economic indicators are related to positive health of a country? |
Answer
Role of socio-economic indicators in health of a community:
These indicators do not directly measure health. Nevertheless, they are of great importance in the
interpretation of the indicators of health care.

Mortality & Morbidity indicators
Q. Define morbidity [RU-15J] & mortality.

Answer
Morbidity: (from Latin morbidus, meaning “sick, unhealthy”)
Morbidity is a diseased state, disability, or poor health due to any cause,

Mortality: (the opposite of immortality)
Mortality is the state of being mortal, or susceptible to death.

Q. Describe mortality and morbidity indicators.
es Write down 5 (five) examples of mortality [SUST-13J] / morbidity [SUST-11J] indicators.
nswer
Mortality indicators: They are —
1) Crude death rate: It is defined as the number of deaths per thousand per year in a given
community. CDR in BD = 4.8/ 1000/year.
2) Expectation of life: The average number of years that will be lived by those born alive into a
population if the current age specific mortality rate persists. In BD = 61 years.
3) Infant mortality rate: Number of infant deaths per 1000 live birth in one year. In BD IMR = 57/
1000/year.
4) Child mortality rate: Number of deaths at ages 1- 4 years in a given year 1000 children in that age
group at the midpoint of the year concerned.
5) Under 5 proportionate mortality rate.
6) Maternal mortality rate: Number of maternal death per 1000 living birth. In BD MMR =
3/1000/year.
7) Disease specific mortality: Deaths from specific diseases like cancer, cardiovascular diseases,
communicable diseases, accidents, diabetes etc.

8) Proportional mortality rate

Morbidity /aiestoes: To asses ill health of a community the following morbidity rates are useful —
1) Incidence and prevalence rates.

2) Notification rates.
3) Attendance rates at outpatient department, health centers etc.

4) Admission, readmission, and discharge rate.
5) Duration of stay in hospital and
6) Spells of sickness or absence from work or school.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 24, 25]

Q. Justify mortality indicators are fair & good indicators of health. ’
Answer

Mortality indicators are fair & good indicators of health, because —
1) Crude death rate is very important to determine health status of the people. A decrease in death

rate provides a good tool for assessing the overall health improvement in a population.
2) An increase in the expectation of life is regarded, inferentially, as an improvement in health status. .
3) Infant mortality rate is one of the universally accepted indicators of health status not only of
infants, but also of whole population and of the socioeconomic conditions under which they live.
It is a sensitive indicator of the availability, utilization and effectiveness of health care, particularly
perinatal care.

Utilization rates

Q. How the utilization rate influence the health status of a community.

Q. ‘Utilization of healthcare sender reflects people’s health status’-justify it in context of
Bangladesh.

Answer

Utilization of healthcare sender reflects people’s health status:

In order to obtain additional information on health status, the extent of use of health services is often
investigated. Utilization of services or actual coverage is expressed as the proportion of people in need of a
service who actually receive it in a given period, usually a year.

It is argued that utilization rate gives some indication of the care needed by a population, and therefore,
the health status of the population. In other words, a relationship exists between utilization of healthcare
services and health needs and status.

Healthcare utilization is also affected by factors such as availability and accessibility of health services
and attitude of an individual towards his health and healthcare system. A few examples of utilization rates are
given below in context of Bangladesh —

1) Proportion of infants who are "fully immunized” against the 6 EPI diseases (at present 8 EPI
diseases in Bangladesh).

2) Proportion of pregnant woman who receive antenatal care or have their deliveries supervised by
a trained birth attendant.

HFA by 2000 AD:

Health Care of the Community

Q. Define health care.
Q. Mention the characteristics of ideal health care. [DU-15Ju,12Ju, RU-15J]
Answer

Health care: It may be defined as-
“A multitude of services rendered to individuals, families or communities by the agents of the health

services or professions, for the purpose of promoting, maintaining, monitoring or restoring health”.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 33]

Characteristics of ideal health care: . ; ; ;
1) Appropriateness (relevance), i.e. whether the service is needed at all in relation to essential

human needs, priorities and policies. ;
2) Comprehensiveness, i.e. whether there is an optimum mixture of preventive, curative and

promotional services. ;
3) Adequacy, i.e. if the service is proportionate to requirement. ; 7
4) Availability, i.e. ratio between the population of an administrative unit and the health facility (e.g.

population per center, doctor-population ratio). ; _
5) Accessibility, i.e. this may be geographic accessibility, economic accessibility or cultural

accessibility. ; a
6) Affordability, i.c. the cost of health care should be within the means of the individual and the state.

7) Feasibility, i.e. operational efficiency of certain procedures, logistic support, manpower and

material resources.
[Park / 24/33]

Q. Write short note on: Referral system.
Answer

Referral system:
A fundamental and necessary function of health care system is to provide a sound referral system. It

must be a two-way exchange of information and returning patients to those who referred them for follow up
care. It will ensure continuity of care and inspire confidence of the consumer in the system.

A systematic referral system is given below:

1) Primary health care: At village, community clinic, union and Upazilla levels.

2) Secondary health care: District hospitals.
3) Tertiary health care: Regional teaching hospitals, e.g. medical college hospitals.

4) Super-specialized care: National specialized institution e.g. BIRDEM (Bangladesh institute of
research and rehabilitation in diabetes, endocrine and metabolic disorders), NICVD (National
institute of cardiovascular disease), NIKDU (National institute of kidney disease and urology) etc.

Importance of referral system;

1) It is a fundamental and necessary function of health care system.
2) It will ensure continuity of care and inspire confidence of the consumer in this system.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 36]

Comprehensive health care

Q. Define comprehensive health care. [DU-16M,14Ju, CU-13J,12J, SUST-16J, 1 5Ju/J,12Ju,11J]

Q. Discuss comprehensive health care. [SUST-16N]

Q. Explain characteristics [SUST-15Ju] / components [SUST-12Ju] of comprehensive health care.
Q. Explain comprehensive health care with characteristics & examples [SUST-17M]

Q. Write short note on: Comprehensive health care, [SUST-13Ju]

Answer

Comprehensive health care:
The term “comprehensive health care” was first used by the Bhore Committee in 1946. shes
yaw

Comprehensive health care may be defined as {the provision of integrated preventive, curative,
ive and rehabilitative health care from the womb to the tomb to every individual residing in a
defined geographic area.)

Criteria of comprehensive health care: The Bhore committee defined comprehensive health care as having

the following criteria —
Oy Provide adequate preventive, curative and promotive health services.
2) Beas close to the beneficiaries as possible.
3) Has the widest co-operation between the people, the service and the profession.
4) Available to all irrespective of their ability to pay.
5) Look after specifically the vulnerable and weaker sections of the community.
6) Create and maintain a healthy environment both in homes as well as working places.

Objectives of comprehensive health care:
1) Reduction of premature death.
2) Reduction of disease.
3) Reduction of discomfort.
4) Reduction of delinquency.
5) Reduction of disruption.

Requirements of comprehensive health care:

1) Maximum utilization of all available skills in order to ensure the most economic provision of health
services.

2) Co-operation and active involvement of the community with the staff of medical institutions
providing the services.

3) A change in traditional pattern of living and availability of basic sanitary amenities.

4) The available doctors should be concerned not only with the illness of the individual but also with
the factors, which govern the well-being of the whole community.

5) Awareness & acceptance of modem concepts in health and sickness.

Examples of each, components of comprehensive health care:
1) Preventive health services: Prevention of diseases by vaccines, e.g. prevention of poliomyelitis.
2) Curative health services: Treatment of diseases, e.g. anti-tubercular drugs therapy for
tuberculosis.
3) Promotional health services: e.g. health promotion by environmental and personal sanitation.
4) Rehabilitative health care:
> Medical rehabilitation: Restoration of function.
> Social rehabilitation: Restoration of family and social relationships.
> Vocational rehabilitation: Restoration of the capacity to earn a livelihood.
> Psychological rehabilitation: Restoration of personal dignity and confidence.

[Ref- Park /24" /928 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 25]

Primary health care (PHC)

Q. Elaborate Alma-Ata declaration.
Answer

Primary health care (PHC): 8 following an international conference in

The concept of primary health care came into limelight in 197:
Alma-Ata (former USSR). It has been defined as —

“Essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable heer and
technology made universally accessibte to individuals and families in the community through their ie ;
Participation and at a cost that the community and the country can afford to maintain at every stage of their
development in the spirit of self-determination”. [Ref- Park /24" /34]

Q. State the components / elements of primary health care (PHC). [DU-17M,16M, 15Ju,11J,10J,
CU-10J, SUST-15Ju, 14Ju/J,13Ju, 12Ju,1 [Ju]
Q. Enumerate five elements of PHC, [DU-14J]
Answer
Components / elements of PHC: The declaration of Alma-Ata stated that PHC includes at least:
1) Education about prevailing health problems and methods of preventing & controlling them.
2) Promotion of food supply & proper nutrition.
3) An adequate supply of safe water and basic sanitation.
4) Maternal & child health care, including family planning.
5) Immunization against infectious diseases.
6) Prevention & control of locally endemic diseases.
7) Appropriate treatment of common diseases & injuries

8) Provision of essential drugs.
[Ref- Park / 24" /34]

Easy to Remember: Elements of PHC —

E = Education about health problems and their control.

L = Local disease control.

E = EPI (Expanded Program on immunization).

M = Maternal and child health care including family planning.
E = Essential drugs provision.

N = Promotion of food supply and proper nutrition.

T = Treatment of common diseases and injuries.

S = An adequate supply of safe water and basic sanitation.

Viva Q. Mention the background of primary health care.
Answer

Background of primary health care:

The concept of primary health care came into limelight in 1978 following an intentional conference in
Alma-Ata (former USSR). It is accepted by the member countries of WHO as the key to achieving the goal of
health for all by the year 2000 AD.

Before Alma Ata, primary health care was regarded as synonymous with “basic health service”, “first
contact care”, “easily accessible care”, “services provided by generalists” etc. it was the Alma Ata conference
that broadened the earlier restrictive concept and provided it a political dimension and declared the strategy for
achieving the goal of HFA by 2000 AD through the key approach of primary health care.

Explanation of the principles:

~ Equitable distribution: Health services must be shared equally by all people irrespective of their

should be given according to priority of needs i.e. the needy and vulnerable groups of population in

to contribute to their and the community’s development’.

4) Services can be provided at a lower rate.
5) Participation has an intrinsic value for the participants.
6) Itisa catalyst for further development effort.

 Multisectoral approach / intersectoral coordination: The component of PHC cannot be provided by

Bhore committee

Q. Write short note on: Bhore Committee.
Answer
Bhore Committee:
“It was the “Health survey and Development Committee” appointed by the Government of the India in
1943 under the chairmanship of Sir Joseph Bhore. The members of the committee met regularly for 2
years and submitted in 1946 its famous report which runs into 4 volumes.

+ The committee observed, "If the health of the nation is to be built, the health program should be
developed on a foundation of preventive health work and such activities should proceed side by side
with those concerned with treatment of patients."

“> Some of the recommendations of the committee were:
1) Integration of preventive and curative services at all administrative levels.
2) Development of primary health centres in two stages:
> Asa short-term measure: each primary health centre in the rural areas cater to a
population of 40,0000 with secondary health center to serve as a supervisory, co-
ordinating and referral institution.
> Long term programme: Setting up primary health units with 75 bedded hospitals for
each 10,000-20,000 population and secondary units with 650 bedded hospitals, again
regionalized around district hospitals with 2500 beds.
3) Three months training in preventive and social medicine for medical students to prepare ‘social
physicians’.
[Ref- Park / 24/910]

Q. Describe modern concepts of disease causation.

Q. State multifactorial causation of disease. [DU-13Ju]

Q. Describe in brief ‘web of causation’, [RU-12Ju] — .

Q. ‘Disease is the outcome of interaction of multiple factors’- explain it in line with web of

causation. [RU-14Ju]
Answer

Modern theories of disease causation: ‘
** Germ theory of disease: This concept is generally referred to as a one to one relationship between

causal agents and disease. The disease model accordingly is: Disease agent > Man —> Disease.
* Epidemiological triad: Please see below.

* Multifactorial causation: This concept states that multiple factors are responsible for a disease process
to before and de - emphasize the concept of disease agent causation i.e. Germ theory. As for example
lung cancer, coronary heart disease, chronic bronchitis etc, Tuberculosis is not merely due to tubercle
bacilli; factor such as Poverty, over-crowding and malnutrition contribute to its occurrence.

* Web of causation: This is ideally suited in the study of chronic disease. Where the disease agent is
often not known but is the outcome of interaction of multiple factors. E.g. myocardial infraction is web
causation disease. The web of causation does not imply that the disease cannot be controlled unless all

the multiple cause or chairs of causation or at least a number of them are appropriately controlled or
removed,

* The epidemiological wheel Concept: This is another approach to depict man-environment. The host is
surrounded by environment .The size of the different component of wheel depends upon specific
disease entities. The genetic disease the core will be very large.

[Ref- Park / 24" /37, 38]

Q. What is self-care? [DU-13Ju]
Answer
Self-care:
Self-care refers to actions and attitudes which contribute to the maintenance of well-being and
Personal health and promote human development.
In terms of health maintenance, self-care is any activity of an individual, family or community, with the

intention of improving or restoring health, or treating or preventing disease. A holistic health approach is
common in self-care.

Q. Define host. [SUST-17M]

Q. Write short note on: Host.
Answer

Host:

. A person or other animal including birds and arthropods that afford subsistence or lodgment to an
infectious agent under natural conditions,

Classification of host:

1) Obligate host: means the only host, e.g. man in measles and typhoid fever. .
2) Primary or definitive host: Host-in which the parasite attains maturity or passes its sexual stage.

3) Secondary or intermediate host: Host in which the parasite is in a larval or sexual state.
4) Transport host: It is a carrier in which the organism remains alive but does not undergo
development.

[Ref- Park / 24" /38, 98]
Characteristics of host:
> Demographic characteristics: Age, Sex, Ethnicity.

> Biological characteristics: Genetic factors, biochemical levels of blood (cholesterol), blood
groups, enzymes, blood pressure.

> Social and economic characteristics: socio-economic status, education, occupation, marital status,
housing etc,

> Life style factors: living habits, food habit + colon cancer, exercise —> hypertension, heart
disease. Smoking > lung cancer, alcohol use etc. ‘;
[Ref- Park / 24" /38]

Environmental factors of disease causation:
1) Physical environment: The term physical environment" is applied to non-living things and
physical factors (e.g., air, water, soil etc.) with which man is in constant interaction.

Example:
> Air Air pollution > Health problems,
> Radiation > Radiation hazards —> Health problems,

2) Biological environment: The biological environment is the universe of living things which
surrounds man, including man himself,

Example: Viruses, bacteria, insects, rodents, animals, plants.

3) Psychological environment: It includes a complex of psychological factors which are defined as
‘those factors affecting personal health, health care and community well-being that stem from the

psychological make-up of individuals and the structure and functions of social groups’,

Example: Cultural value, customs, habits, beliefs, attitudes, religion, education, life-style.

Q. Define risk approach. [DU-14Ju,11Ju, RU-18M]
Q. Mention the role of risk on disease causation with example. [CU-17M]
Q. Mention WHO guidelines for defining ‘at-risk’ group. [RU-18M]
Answer
Risk approach / risk groups: . 1 ap
The approach developed and promoted by WHO is to identify precisely the “risk groups” or “target
groups” (e.g. at-risk mothers, at-risk infants etc.) in the population by certain defined criteria and direct
appropriate action to them first. This is known as the “risk approach”.

Guidelines for defining “at-risk” groups:

1) Biological situation:
> Age groups: e.g. infants (low birth weight), toddlers, elderly.

> Sex: e.g. females in the reproductive age periods.

> Physiological state: e.g. pregnancy, high blood pressure, cholesterol level.

> Genetic factors: e.g. family history of genetic disorders.

> Other health conditions: e.g. disease, physical functioning, unhealthy behaviour.

2) Physical situation:

> Rural, urban slums.
» Living conditions, overcrowding.
> Environment: Water supply, proximity to industries.

Social class.

Spectrum of disease

Q. What is disease spectrum?
Q. Explain infectious disease spectrum.
Answer
Disease spectrum: It is a graphic representation of variation in the manifestation of disease. It is as follows —
Y The different manifestations are simply reflections of individual different states of immunity and
receptivity.
Y Leprosy is an excellent example of the spectral concept of disease. For almost every disease, there
exists a spectrum, with few exceptions such as rabies.
Y Ininfectious diseases, the spectrum of disease is also referred to as the gradient of infection.
Y The spectrum of disease can be interrupted by early diagnosis and treatment or by preventive
measure.

Q. Poliomyelitis is a disease of “Iceberg” phenomenon — justify the comment. [RU-13Ju]
Answer
Poliomyelitis is a disease of “iceberg” phenomenon:
> Subclinical infection occurs in about 95% of cases, which indicates the submerged portion of
iceberg.
> niieer seed occurs in about 4-8% of cases, which indicates the water-line of iceberg.
> Paralytic polio occurs in less than 1% cases, which indicates the floating tip of iceberg.

Answer
Comparison of pulmonary tuberculosis problem of Bangladesh with ‘iceberg’:

techniques in preventive medicine.

Concept of Control
Disease control, Disease elimination & Disease eradication

eee

Q. Define disease control [DU-12J, SUST-14Ju,13J] / disease eradication [SUST-15J,1 IJu,10Ju/J] /
disease elimination [SUST-12Ju, 1 1Ju]?
Q. Discuss disease control, elimination & eradication. [SUST-17M, 16J]
Q. Explain the term disease control & disease eradication. [SUST-18M]
Answer
Disease control: The term “disease control” describes operations aimed at reducing:
Y The incidence of disease.
Y The duration and the risk of transmission of disease.
Y The effects of infection, including both the physical and psychosocial complications.
Y The financial burden to the community.

Example: Malaria control.
Elimination of disease: It is defined as interruption of transmission of disease.
Example: Elimination of measles, polio and diphtheria from large geographic regions or areas.

Disease eradication:
Eradication literally means to “tear out by roots". Eradication of disease implies termination of all
transmission of infection by extermination of the infectious agent through surveillance and containment.

Example: Today smallpox is the only disease that has been eradicated.
[Ref- Park /24" / 44]

Q. What are the factors in favour of eradication of disease? [SUST-18M, 15J]
Q. What are the common criteria to eradicate a disease?
Answer
Factors responsible for eradicating a disease:
1) Infection & disease limited to human host.
2) No animal reservoir or insect vector; transmitted person to person.
3) Characteristic clinical illness; usually serious, easily diagnosed.
4) Few or no subclinical cases,
5) No long term carrier,
6) Only one causative agent or serotype persists.
7) Short period of infectivity.
8) Immunity is of long duration.
9) Inhibits reinfection, reactivation, reduces or eliminates excretion of organism.
10) Disease has seasonal variation.
11) Absence or interference by maternal antibodies in infants.

* Monitoring: In management, monitoring refers to ‘the continuous oversight of activities to ensure that
they are proceeding according to plan’,

“ Evaluation: It is the process by which results are compared with the intended objectives, or more
simply the assessment of how well a programme is performing. ,

Q. Define surveillance. [RU-15Ju]

Q. Write short note on: Surveillance. [CU-17M,16J,14Ju/J]
Answer

Surveillance: It is defined as ‘the continuous scrutiny of the factors that determine the occurrence and
distribution of disease and other conditions of ill health’.

Example:
> Epidemiological surveillance.
> Demographic surveillance
> Nutritional surveillance.

Objectives:

1) To provide information about new and changing trends in the health status of a population, e.g.
morbidity, mortality, nutritional status or other indicators and environmental hazards, health
practices and other factors that may affect health.

2) To provide feed-back which may be expected to modify the policy and the system itself and lead to
redefinition of objectives, and

3) Provide timely warning of public health disasters, so that interventions can be mobilized.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 44]

Q. List the diseases under surveillance.
Answer
Diseases under surveillance by WHO:

1) Louse-borne typhus fever.

2) Relapsing fever.

3) Paralytic polio.

4) Malaria.

5) Viral influenza-A.

6) SARS.

7) Small pox.

Q. Explain the term impairment, disability & handicap. [RU-16M] _-
Answer ‘
“> Impairment: Any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological, or anatomical structure or
function. Example — loss of foot. .

+ Disability: As a result of impairment, if affected person is unable to perform any activity or to carry out
any activity. Example: Inability of work.

“> Handicap: As a result of disability, if the person experiences some disadvantages in the life. Example:
Unemployment.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 48]

Q. Write the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of a disease.
Q. Early diagnosis and treatment is a part of prevention — explain.
Answer

Importance of early diagnosis and treatment:

1) Treatment of the case is prevention for susceptible hosts: Treatment reduces the communicability of
disease, cuts short the duration of illness and prevents development of secondary cases in the
community. In some diseases like tuberculosis, syphilis, leprosy treatment is of primary importance
in interruption of transmission.

2) In some diseases, early treatment is essential to prevent secondary complications; e.g. syphilis.

3) Rarely treatment is an important part of prevention in respect of certain diseases and conditions,
e.g. carcinoma, cardiovascular diseases.

4) Treatment relieves pain, arrest or cure disease and thus prevent disability and heath.

From above positive supports it is proved that "early diagnosis and treatment is a part of
prevention.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 48]

Q. Define rehabilitation. [RU-16M, 14], SUST-16N, I 5u,13Ju, 113]

Q. Classify rehabilitation, [RU-16M,14J, SUST-I6N,13Ju,11J]

Q. Mention different types of rehabilitation with example. [SUST-16N]

Q. For the street beggars with disability which type of health care is suitable? [CU-17N,16N]
Q. Write short note on: Rehabilitation. [SUST-18N,17N,1 Ju, 10J]

Answer
Rehabilitation: Rehabilitation is the combined and coordinated use of medical, social, educational and

vocational measures for training and retraining the individual to the highest possible level of functional ability.

Types of rehabilitation:

1) Medical rehabilitation: Restoration of function.

2) Vocational rehabilitation: Restoration of the capacity to earn a livelihood,
3) Social rehabilitation: Restoration of family and social relationships.

4) Psychological rehabilitation: Restoration of personal dignity and confidence.

Examples of rehabilitation:

> Establishing schools for the blind.
> Provision of aids for the crippled.
> Re-constructive surgery in leprosy etc.

Community diagnosis

Q. Define community diagnosis. [CU-11J,10J]

Q. Explain community diagnosis. [DU-18M,16M]

Q. Discuss community diagnosis with example. [SUST-10Ju/J, RU-16J,11Ju]

Q. Write the importance of community diagnosis in the prevention of diseases. [CU-12J]

Answer

Community diagnosis:

It may be defined as the pattern of disease in a community described in terms of the important factors
which influence this pattern.
[Ref- Park / 24" /53]

Or,
Community diagnosis generally refers to the identification and quantification of health problems ina

community in terms of mortality and morbidity rates and ratios and identification of their correlates for the

purpose of defining those individuals or groups at risk or those in need of health care.
[Ref- Park / 24" /96]

Data for community diagnosis:
1) Age and sex distribution of the population; the distribution of population by social groups.

2) Vital statistical rates such as the birth rates, death rates.

3) Incidence and prevalence of important diseases in the community.
[Ref- Park / 24/54]

Importance of community diagnosis in the prevention of diseases:
1) By quantification of health problems, we lay down priorities in disease control and prevention.
2) Quantification of morbidity and mortality can serve as a benchmark for the evaluation of health services

at a later date.
3) Quantification of health problems can be a source of new knowledge about disease distribution,

causation and prevention.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 96]

awit down the aims and objectives of epidemiology. [DU-17N,12Ju, CU-05M]
nswer

: According to International Epidemiological Association (IEA), the aims

Aims and objective of epidemiolo
‘

& objectives of epidemiology are:
> To describe the distribution and magnitude of health and disease problems in human populations

> To identify aetiological (risk factors) in the pathogenesis of disease : and
> To provide the data essential to the planning implementation and evaluation of services for the
prevention, control and treatment of disease and to the setting up of priorities among those services.

The ultimate aim of epidemiology: To lead effective action.

> To eliminate or reduce the health problem or its consequences.

> To promote the health and well-being of society as a whole.

Epidemiological approach

Q. What are the epidemiological approaches to problem of health? [RU-16M]
Q. Write the appropriate epidemiological approaches. [RU-13J]
Answer
‘ Epidemiological approach: The epidemiological approach of health and disease two major foundations —
\ - Asking questions.
- Making comparison.

** Asking questions:
Related to health events:
What is the event? (the problem)
What is the magnitude?
Where did it happen?
When did it happen?
Who are affected?
Why did it happen?
Related to health action:

> What can be done to reduce this problem and its consequences?
How can it be prevented in the future?

What action should be taken by the community? By the health services? By other sectors?
Where and for whom these activities be carried out?

What resources are required? How are the activities to be organized?
What difficulties may arise, and how might they be overcome?

“+ Making comparisons: The comparison may be between two groups- one group having the disease and
another group not having the disease.

Proportional mortality rate (PMR) expresses the “number of deaths due to a particular cause (or ina

Total number of deaths from the specific disease in a year

Description of epidemiological methods / studies:

“* Descriptive epidemiology / descriptive study: Descriptive studies are concerned with observing the
distribution of disease or health related characteristics in human populations and identifying the
characteristics with which disease in question seems to be associated.

Descriptive studies basically ask the following questions:
>» When is the disease occurring? — Time distribution
> Where is it occurring? — Place distribution.

>

> Who is getting the disease? — Person distribution

Uses of descriptive epidemiology:
Provide data regarding the magnitude of disease problem in the community

Provide Clues to disease aetiology & help in formulation of an aetiological hypothesis
Provide background data for planning organizing and evaluating preventive curative services.

They contribute to research by describing variation in disease occurrence by- time place &
person.

Procedure steps of a descriptive study:
1) Defining the population to be studied: Study population may be people, tree, houses, patient

~ etc. The study population is to be described in terms of-

Cross sectional study

Q. Define cross sectional study.
Q. Write down the advantages of cross sectional study. [DU-11J]
Q. Write short note on: Cross-sectional study.

fswer
Cross sectional study / lence study:
> Cross sectional study is the simplest form of an observational study.

> Itis based on a single examination of cross section of population at one point in hae the eg of -
which can be projected on the whole population provided the sampling has been done correctly.

> Cross sectional study is also known as ‘prevalence study’. [Ref- Park /24"/ 744

Advantages of cross sectional study:
1) Itis the simplest form of observational study.
2) A single observation is done.
3) Usually less time consuming.
4) Less expensive.
5) Useful for chronic diseases, e.g. lung cancer.
6) Randomization.
7) Free of selection bias because the investigator has no control to select study group and control

group.

Disadvantages of longitudinal studies:

> Provides very little information about the natural history of disease & rate of occurrence of new
cases (incidence).

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 94)

— study

\
; Q. Define longitudinal study.
Q. Write short note on: Longitudinal study.
Answer
Longitudinal studies:
In longitudinal study, observations are repeated in the same population over a prolonged period of time
by mean of follow up examinations,

Importance of longitudinal studies: Longitudinal studies are useful-

1) To study the natural history of disease and its future outcome,

2) For both acute and chronic diseases,

3) For identifying the risk factors of disease.

4) Finding out incidence rate or rate of occurrence of new cases of disease in the community.

Advantages of longitudinal studies:

> nial Studies provide valuable information which the cross-sectional studies may not
provide.

Disadvantages of longitudinal studies:

1) Difficult to organize,
2) More-time Consuming,

[Ref- Park / 24" / 74]

Q. Write short note on: Case control study. [CU-14J]

a hose
Case control study: . a . .
A case control study involves two populations - Case (with disease) & Control (without disease).
In case-control studies, the unit is the individual rather than a group. The focus is on.a disease or some

other health problem that has already developed. 2
[Ref- Park /24 176)

The case control study has three distinct features:
1) Both exposure & outcome (disease) have occurred before the start of the study.
2) The study proceeds backwards from effect to cause.
3) It uses a control or comparison group to support or refute an inference.
4) Other features:
> Itis usually first & easier to test a causal hypothesis.
> Ituses a fewer number of subject.
> Study yields relative quick results.
> Relative inexpensive.
> Suitable to study rare diseases.

Basic steps of case control study: There are four basic steps in conducting a case control study-

1) Selection of cases and controls:
a) Selection of case:
Y Definition of case: It involves two specification
> Diagnostic criteria: The diagnostic criteria of the disease and the stage of
disease e.g. breast cancer stage I.
> Eligibility criteria: Only newly diagnosed cases.

Y Sources of case: Hospitals, General population.

b) Selection of controls: The control must be free from the disease under study. They must be
as similar to the cases as possible except for the absence of the diseased under study. Asa
rule comparison group is identified before a study is done.

Source of controls:
> Hospital controls,
> Relatives
> Neighborhood controls
> General population.

2) Matching: It is the process by which controls are selected in such a way that they are similar to
cases with regard to certain pertinent selected variables (e.g. Age).

3) Measurement of exposure: It is obtained by interviews, questionnaires, studying post, and records
of cases such as hospital record employment records etc,

4) Analysis & interpretation: It finds out-

> Exposure rate among cases and controls to suspected factor.
> Estimation of disease risk associated with exposure.

Q. Discuss about the biasness in case control study.
Answer :
Biasness of case control study: Many varieties of bias may arise in case control study; e.g.
1) Bias due to confounding: A confounding factor is defined as one which is associated both with the
exposure and disease, and is distributed unequally in study and control groups.
2) Memory or recall bias.
3) Selection bias: The cases and controls may not be representative of cases and controls in’ the
general population.
4) Berkesonian bias: The bias arises because of the different rates o admission to hospitals for people
with different cases.
5) Interviewer’s bias: Bias may also occur when the interviewer knows the hypothesis and also

knows who the cases are.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 78]

A What is cohort? [CU-14J, RU-12Ju]
5 Answer

Cohort: In epidemiology, the term “cohort” is defined as a group of people who share a common characteristic
or experience within a defined time period (e.g. age, occupation, exposure to a drug or vaccine, pregnancy,
insured persons etc.).

Example:
> A group of people born on the same day or in the same period of time (usually a year) form a birth

cohort. .
> A group of males or females married on the same day or in the same period of time form a
marriage cohort.
> Persons exposed to a common drug, vaccine or infection within a defined period constitutes an
exposure cohort.
[Ref- Park / 24/80]

Q. Mention the advantages and disadvantages of cohort studies. [DU-12J, CU-11Ju, RU-11Ju]
Q. Why cohort study is more valid and reliable than case-control study? [DU-10J] :

Heat wer
Merits / advantages of cohort studies:
1) Incidence can be calculated.

2) Several possible outcomes can be studied simultaneously.
3) It provides a direct estimate of relative risk.

4) Dose-response ratios can also be calculated. 4
5) Chance of bias is minimum as comparison groups are formed before disease develops.

Demerits disadvantages of cohort studies:

1) It involves a large number of people and is generally unsuitable for investigation of uncommon
disease.

2) It takes a long time to complete the study and obtain results.

3) Certain administrative problems such as loss of experienced staff, loss of funding and extensive
record keeping are inevitable.

4) There may be loss of substantial proportional of the original cohort.

5) The selection of the comparison group is a limiting factor.

Q. Write short note on: Relative risk or risk ratio.

Q. What is relative risk or risk ratio? Interpret relative risk of 6.2 of particular phenomenon.

{SUST-10J]

‘Answer
Relative risk (RR): It is defined as the ratio between the incidence of disease among exposed persons and

incidence among non-exposed. It is given by the formula —
Incidence of disease (or death) among exposed

No disease

Relative risk =
Incidence of disease (or death) among non-exposed

Example:
A relative risk of 1 indicates no association.

A relative risk >1 suggests ‘positive’ association between exposure and the disease under study.
A relative risk of 2 indicates that the incidence rate of disease is 2 times higher in the exposed

group as compared with the unexposed.
A relative risk of 6.2 indicates that the incidence rate of disease is 6.2 times higher in the exposed

group as compared with the unexposed.
A relative risk of 0.25 indicates a 75% reduction in incidence rate in exposed individuals as

compared with the unexposed.

[Ref- Park / 24" /83]

Q. Write short note on: Population-attributable risk.

Answer
Population-attributable risk: It is the incidence of the disease (or death) in the total population minus the
incidence of disease (or death) among those who were not exposed to the suspected causal factor.

The concept of population attributable risk is helpful in that it provides an estimate of the amount by
which the disease should be reduced in that population if the suspected factors were eliminated or modified.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 83]

Experimental Epidemiology

Q. Discuss experimental epidemiology.

Answer

Experimental epidemiology / experimental study:
> Meant the study of epidemics among colonies of experimental animals such as rat & mice.
> In modern usage, experimental epidemiology is often equated with randomized controlled trials

Aims of experimental studies:
Y To provide scientific proof of etiological (or risk) factors.

Y To provide a method of measuring the effectiveness and efficiency of health services.

Types of experimental studies:
1) Randomized controlled trials (RCT).

2) Non-randomized trial or non-experimental trials.

Advantages of experimental studies:
1) The experimental animal can be bred in laboratories & manipulated easily according to the wishes

of the investigators.
2) They multiply and enable the investigators to carry out certain experiments (i.e. genetic
experiments which in human population would take several years and involve many generations.

Disadvantages / limitations of experimental studies:
1) Not all human diseases can be reproduced in animals.
2) a the conclusions derived from animal experiments may not be strictly applicable to human
eings.
3) Costly.
4) Ethical problems.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 85, 86, 90]

Note: \n modern usage, experimental epidemiology is often equated with ‘randomized control trial’.

[Ref- Park /24"/85]

Q. Define randomization.

Q. Why randomization is called the heart of a control trial?

Answer

Randomization: :

Randomization is a statistical procedure by which the participants are allocated into groups usually
called “study” and “control” groups, to receive or not to receive an experimental preventive or therapeutic
Procedure, maneuver or intervention. ;

Randomization is an attempt to eliminate “bias” and allow for comparability.

Randomization is called the heart of a control trial:

It is an attempt to eliminate ‘bias’ and allow for comparability. Randomization is mr ee
Participant has entered the study, that is after having been qualified for the trial and has given his inform
Consent to participate in the study.

Randomization is best done by using a table of random numbers.

Randomization is the ‘heart’ of a control trial. It will give the greatest confidence that the groups are
comparable so that like can be compared with like. It ensures that the investigator has no ha me a
of participants to either study or control group, thus eliminating what is known as selection | ias”. In other
words, by random allocation, every individual gets an equal chance of being allocated into either group or any
of the trial groups. lied Patkioaty ni

Infectious Disease Epidemiology

Q. Define endemic [SUST-16M], sporadic & pandemic [SUST-16M].
Answer
Endemic: (En = in; demos = People)

It refers to the constant presence of a disease or infectious agent within a given geographic area or the
Population group, without importation from outside; may also refer to the "usual" or expected frequency of the
disease within such area or population group.

Example: Cholera is endemic in Bangladesh, malaria in hill tracts, and goitre at Rangpur.
Sporadic:

When a disease occurs in an inchoate fashion in different areas of a country without having a common
Source of causative agent. When a disease occur irregularly, haphazardly from time to time, and generally
infrequently without having a common source of infection is known as sporadic.

Example: Polio, tetanus, herpes-zoster and meningococcal meningitis,

Pandemic:

An epidemic usually affecting a large Proportion of the population, occurring over a wide geographic
area such a section of nation, the entire nation, a continent or the world,

Scanned with CamScanner

Chapter-03: Principles of epidemiolo, & Epidemiological methods — 81

Example: Influenza pandemics of 1918 & 1957, cholera Eltor in 1962 (still continuing) and acute
haemorrhagic conjunctivitis in 1971 & 1981,

[Ref- Park/ 24" / 98]

> Hyperendemic: The term “hyperendemic” expresses that the disease is constantly present at a high
incidence and / or prevalence rate and affects all the age groups equally.

¢ Holoendemic; The term “holoendemic” means a high level of infection beginning early in the life and
affecting most of the child population leading to a state of equilibrium such that the adult population
f the disease much less commonly than do the children, as in the case of malaria.

Q. Define epidemic. [DU-17M, RU-17N, 14Ju,13Ju,11J , SUST-18M, 16M, 15Ju,12J, CU-18M]
Q. Classify epidemic with example. [DU-18M,16J,15Ju,1 1Ju,10J, RU-17N, 14Ju,13Ju,11J, CU-10J]
Q. Write short note on: Epidemic. [CU-16N/J, SUST-13J]
Q. Write short note on: Types of epidemic. [SUST-13Ju]
Answer
Epidemic: (Epi = Upon, demos = people)
Epidemic means the unusual occurrence in a community or region of disease, specific health-related

behaviour (e.g. smoking) or the health related events (e.g. traffic accidents) clearly in excess of ‘expected
occurrence.

Example of epidemic disease:
Y Communicable diseases: Measles, chicken pox & cholera.

Y Noncommunicable disease: CHD, lung cancer.
Y Health-related behaviour: Smoking.
Y Health-related events: Traffic accidents.

Types / classification of epidemics: Three major types of epidemic are distinguished —

1) Common-source epidemics:
> Single exposure or point source epidemics (e.g. food poisoning, Bhopal gas tragedy).

> Continuous or multiple exposure epidemics (e.g. the Legionnaire's disease in the summer of
1976 in Philadelphia (USA), Gonorrhoea).

2) Propagated epidemics:
> Person to person (epidemics of hepatitis-A and polio).

> Arthropod vector.
> Animal reservoir.

3) Slow (modern) epidemics: e.g. cancer.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 69, 98]

Q. Draw and explain different epidemic curves.
Q. Draw and explain the diagram of a course of typical propagated epidemic.
Answer
Epidemic curve:
A graph of the time distribution of epidemic cases is called the “epidemic curve”.
In other word, epidemic curve is a histogram that describes an outbreak of disease by plotting the
number of cases of a disease by date of onset.

The epidemic curve may suggest:
> A time relationship with exposure to a suspected source,

> Acyclical or seasonal pattern suggestive of a particular infection and common source or
propagated spread of the disease.

Different types of epidemic curves:

1) Point source epidemic curve (Holommiantic curve): Point source epidemics occur when an
index case or a "vehicle", such as contaminated feed, exposes most of the susceptible persons ina
group at once. In the case of an infectious agent, this exposure was by a dose sufficient high to
cause clinical disease in most exposed persons. It indicates common-source, single exposure
epidemic. The curve has usually one peak. One point of interest is the “

median incubation
period”. It is the time required for 50% of the cases to occur following exposure. The epidemic
curve rises and falls rapidly.

2) Propagated epidemic curve (Prosodemic curve): Propagating epidemics occur when infected

Persons transmit the infection to susceptible persons over time. Exposure of susceptibles occurs
over time rather than all at once. These epidemics pr

; ; ogress through a group over a period of time
that is considerably longer than the typical incubation period. It indicates common source, multiple
exposure (or continuous exposure).

Some important topics for viva:

Q
%

Contamination: The presence of an infectious agent on a body surface; also on or in clothes, bedding,
toys, surgical instruments, or other inanimate articles or substances including water, milk and food.
Pollution is distinct from contamination and implies the presence of offensive, but not necessarily
infectious matter in the environment. Contamination on a body surface does not imply a carrier state

Infestation: For persons or animals the lodgment, development and reproduction of arthropods on the
surface of the body or in the clothing e.g. lice, itch mite, some authorities use the term also to describe
invasion of the gut by parasitic worms e.g. ascariasis.

Infested articles or premises are those, which harbour or give shelter to animal forms, especially
arthropods and rodents.

Host: A person or other animal including birds and arthropods that affords substance or lodgment to an
infectious agent under natural conditions.

Infectious disease: A clinical manifest disease of man or animals resulting from an infection.

Contagious disease: A disease that is transmitted through contact, examples includes scabies,
trachoma, STD and leprosy.

Communicable disease: An illness due to a specific infectious agent or its toxic products capable of
being directly or indirectly transmitted from man to man, animal to animal or from the environment
(through air, dust, soil, water, food etc.) to man or animal.

Q. Define infection.
Q. What are the levels of infection?
Answer

Infection:
Infection means the entry and development or multiplication of an infectious agent in the body of man,

or animals. It also implies the body responds in some way to defend itself against invader either in the form of
immune response or disease. An infection does not always cause illness.

Types / levels of infections:
1) Colonization: Normally present in the body & lodgment; e.g. S. aureus in skin & naso-pharynx.

2) Sub-clinical infection or inapparent infection: No sign & symptoms, e.g. Polio.
3) Latent infection: c.g. virus of herpes simplex.
4) Manifest or clinical infection: Clinical sign & symptoms present.

[Ref- Park /24"/97]

Q. Define epizootic with examples. [RU-14J]
Answer

Epizootic:
An outbreak (epidemic) of disease in an animal population (often with the implication that it may also

affect human population). Only a few zoonotic agents cause major epidemics. Notable among these are the
agents of anthrax, brucellosis, rabies, influenza, Rift valley fever, Q fever, Japanese encephalitis and equine

encephalitis.
[Ref- Park /24"/99]

Q. What is nosocomial infection? [DU-14J]
Q. Write short note on: Nosocomial infection. [SUST-14Ju]
Answer

Nosocomial infection / Hospital acquired infection;

Nosocomial (hospital acquired) infection is an infection originating in a patient while in a hospital or
other health care facility. It denotes a new disorder (unrelated to the patient’s primary condition) associated with
being in a hospital. That is it was not present or incubating at the time of admission or the residual of an
infection acquired during a previous admission. It includes infections acquired in the hospital but appearing
after discharge and also such infections among the staff of the facility.

Examples: Infection of surgical wounds, hepatitis B and UTI.

[Ref- Park /24" /99|

Q. Define opportunistic infection. [DU-14Ju]
Answer

Opportunistic infection: ,
Infection by an organism that is not normally pathogenic but can cause disease if resistance is lowered

is called opportunistic infection. This is infection by an organism that takes the opportunity provided by a defect
in host defense to infect the host and hence cause disease.

Common organism: Including Herpes simplex (HSV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Toxoplasma etc.

Example: Opportunistic infections are very common in AIDS.
[Ref- Park /24"/99]

Q. Write short note on: Iatrogenic disease.
Answer

Iatrogenic (physician induced) disease:

Any untoward or adverse consequence of a preventive, diagnostic or therapeutic regimen or procedure
that causes impairment, handicap, disability or death resulting from a physician’s professional activity or from
the professional activity of other health professionals is called iatrogenic or physician induced disease. ,

Or,
latrogenic disease is any ill health induced by a medical practitioner’s actions.

Example:
> Allergic reaction caused by penicillin (of a previously known allergic history with penicillins).

> Aplastic anaemia caused by chloramphenicol.
> Hepatitis- B following blood transfusion.

[Ref- Park /24"/99]

Q. Define case.

Q. Classify case.

Q. Write short note on: Primary case. [CU-17N,16N]
Answer
Case:

A case is defined as a person in the population or study group identified as having the particular
disease, health disorders or condition under investigation.

Types of cases: :
1) Clinical cases: It may mild to moderate, typical or atypical, severe or fatal depending upon the

gradient of involvement. Epidemiologically mild cases are more important sources of infection than
severe cases because they are ambulant and spread the infection whenever they go, whenever

severe cases are usually confined to bed.

2) Sub-clinical cases: They are variously referred to as inapparent, covert, missed or abortive cases.
The disease agent may multiply in the host, but does not manifest itself signs and symptoms, e.g.
rubella, mumps, polio, influenza, diphtheria, but measles has no sub-clinical infection. Sub clinical .
infection can be detected only by laboratory test, e.g. antibody response, biochemical & skin
sensitivity test.

3) Latent infection: In latent infection, the host does not shed the infectious agent which lies dormant
within the host- without symptoms. For example latent infection in herpes simplex.

In epidemiological terminology:
1) Primary case: It refers to the first case 0

unit being studied.
2) Index case: It refers to the first case to come to the attention of the investigator.

3) Secondary case: Secondary cases are those developing from contact with primary case.
[Ref- Park /24"7/ 100]

Classification of carriers:

* According to type:

1) Incubatory carriers: Incubatory carriers are those who shed the infectious agent during the
incubation period of disease, These usually occur during the last few days of the incubation
period, e.g. measles, mumps, polio, pertussis.

2) Convalescent carriers: Convalescent carriers are those who continue to shed the disease
during the period of convalescence; e.g. typhoid fever, dysentery, cholera, diphtheria &
whooping cough.

3) Healthy carriers: They are the victims of subclinical infection who have developed carrier

State without suffering from overt disease but are nevertheless shedding the disease agent, eg.
Poliomyelitis, cholera, salmonellosis and diphtheria.

% According to duration: A
1) Temporary carriers: Temporary carriers are those who shed the infectious agent for short
Periods of time. These include the incubatory, convalescent and healthy carrier.

agent

2) Chronic carriers: A chronic carrier is one who shed infectious agent for indefinite period, The

chronic career state occurs ina number of diseases; e.g. typhoid fever, hepatitis B, dysentery,
malaria.

a According to portal of exit:
1)

Urinary carriers,
2) Intestinal carriers,
3) Respiratory carriers,
4) Nasal carriers,
5) Skin eruptions,
6) Open wounds,
7) Blood etc.

Criteria / Elements of carrier state:
1) The presence in the body of the disease agent.

2) The absence of recognizable symptoms and signs of disease.

3) The shedding of the disease agent in the discharges or excretions, thus acting as a source of
infection for other persons.

Q. Give the epidemiological features of vehicle transmission. [RU-14Ju]

Answer

The epidemiological features of vehicle transmission are:

!)

If the dose of contamination is heavy, the outbreak may be explosive as in case of cholera and
hepatitis A epidemics.

Cases are initially confined to those who are exposed to the contaminated vehicle.

When secondary cases occur, the primary case may be obscured.

The distance traveled by the infectious agent may also be great.

It is not always possible to isolate the infectious agent in the incriminated vehicle, e.g. typhoid
bacilli in contaminated water.

When the vehicle is controlled or withdrawn, the epidemic subsides.

The common source of infection is often traceable.
[Ref- Park /24™/ 102]

Q. Enumerate the factors which influence the ability of vectors to transmit disease.
Answer
The factors which influence the ability of vectors to transmit disease are:

1) Host feeding preferences.

2) Infectivity.

3) Susceptibility.

4) Survival rate of vectors in the environment.

5) Domesticity that is degree of association with the man.

6) Suitable environmental factors.

Successful parasitism

Q. What do you mean by successful parasitism?
Answer
Successful parasitism: There are four stages in successful parasitism —
» First, the infectious agent must find a Portal of Entry by which it may enter into the host. There are
many portal of entry, e.g. respiratory tract, alimentary tract, genitourinary tract, skin etc.
> On gaining entry into the host, the organism must reach the appropriate tissue or site of election in
the body where it may find optimum conditions for its multiplication and survival.
> Thirdly, the disease agent must find a way out of the body in order that it may reach a new host and
propagate its species otherwise it may become a dead-end infection. Example — rabies, tetanus,
bubonic plague.
» After leaving the human body, the organism must survive in the external environment for sufficient
period till a new host is found.
[Ref- Park /24" / 104]

Generation time

Q. Define generation time. What is the difference between generation time & incubation period?
Q. Write short note on: Generation time. [CU-18M,17M]
Answer
Generation time: oa. ..

It is defined as “the time interval of time between receipt of infection by a host and maximal infectivity
of that host.”

Difference between generation time (GT) & incubation period (IP):

1) The time of maximum communicability may precede or following the incubation period. For
example in mumps communicability reaches its height about 48 hours before the swelling of the
salivary gland.

2) _1.P. Can only be applied to infections that result in manifest disease, whereas generation time refers
to the transmission of infection, whether clinical or sub clinical. hs

[Ref- Park / 24" / 105]

Communicable period

Q. Define communicable period.
Answer
Communicable period:

The communicable period is defined as “the time during which an infectious agent may be transferred
directly or indirectly from an infected person to another person, from an infected animal to man, or from an
infected person to an animal including arthropods”.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 105]

Secondary attack rate

Q. Write short note on: Secondary attack rate.
Answer
Secondary attack rate (SAR):
It is defined as, "the number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of the
incubation period, following exposure to the primary case". It can be calculated by the following formula.

Number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of the incubation period
SAR =

x 100
Total number of exposed or susceptible contacts

Significance of secondary attack rate:

1) Advantage of secondary attack is that vaccines and non-vaccines from several families can he
added to determine the overall attack rates in the vaccinated and unvaccinated population, provided
the same definitions for the cases and immunization status are used.

Secondary attack rate was initially developed to measure the spread of an infection within a family,
household or any closed aggregated of persons who have had contact with a case of disease.
It is also useful to determine whether a disease of unknown etiology (e.g. Hodgkin's disease) is

communicable or not and in evaluating the effectiveness of control measures such as isolation and
immunization.

Q. Write short note on: Hypothesis.

Answer
Hypothesis: A hypothesis is a supposition, arrived at from or reflection. It can be accepted or rejected, using

the techniques of analytical epidemiology.

An epidemiological hypothesis should specify the following:

> The population- the characteristics of the persons to whom the hypothesis applies

>» The specific cause being considered

> The expected outcome- the disease

> The dose-response relationship- the amount of the cause needed to lead to a stated incidence of the
effect

> The time-response relationship-the time period that will elapse between exposure to the cause and

observation of the effect.

Screening for Diseases

Q. Define screening. [SUST-15Ju,14J]
Q. Classify screening. [SUST-14J]
Q. Write short note on: Screening. [SUST-18N, 17N,16N, 1 1Ju, CU-18N/M,16M,15J,14J,13Ju/J]
Answer
Screening: ;
Disease screening refers to the “identification of hidden or unknown diseases or defects in a large group

of apparently healthy individuals in the community by means of rapidly applied tests, examinations or other
procedures”.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5® / 23]
Example:
1) Pap smear of cervical cancer.
2) Serological blood test for syphilis.
3) Chest X-ray for pulmonary tuberculosis.
4) Test for BP blood sugar, blood cholesterol.

Aims and objective of screening:
1) To sort out from large group of apparently healthy person those likely to have a disease or at
increased risk of the disease under study.
2) To bring those who are apparently abnormal under medical supervision & treatment.
3) To alter the natural history of disease in a significant proportion of those who are identified as
positive by earlier diagnosis & subsequent treatment.

Apparently healthy (screening tests)

Apparently normal Apparently abnormal
(Periodic re-screening) > Normal: periodic re-screening
> Intermediate: surveillance
> Abnormal: treatment

Figure: Possible outcomes of screening.

Uses of screening:
1) Case detection
2) Control of disease
3) Research purposes
4) Education opportunities

1) Mass screening: It implies screening of whole population or a subgroup (e.g. serological test to
know malaria infection amongst the population of an area). ; ; ;

2) High risk or selective screening: Screening in high risk groups e.g. cervix cancer in lower social
group and diabetes, hypertension, breast cancer in higher social group.

3) Multiphase screening: Application of two or more screening tests.

[Ref- Park /24" / 146, 147 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /23]

Q. Mention the procedure for conducting high risk screening for diabetes mellitus in an Upazila,
[DU-18M]
Answer
The purpose of screening is to identify asymptomatic individuals who are likely to have diabetes. Sep;
diagnostic tests using standard criteria are required after positive screening tests to establish a definitive diagnosis

Aim of screening: Generally, screening in asymptomatic populations is appropriate when seven conditions are met:

1) It is an important health problem that imposes a significant burden on the population; ’

2) The natural history of the disease is understood;

3) There is a recognizable preclinical (asymptomatic) stage during which the disease can be diagnosed;

4) Tests are available that can detect the preclinical stage of the disease, and the tests are acceptable and
reliable;

5) Treatment after early detection yields benefits superior to those obtained when treatment is delayed:

6) The costs of case finding and treatment are reasonable and are balanced in relation to health
expenditures as a whole, and facilities and resources are available to treat newly diagnosed cases; ang

7) Screening will be a systematic ongoing process and not merely an isolated one-time effort,

Tests for screening:
¥ Random blood sugar (RBS) or

v Fasting blood sugar (FBS).

False Negative & False Positive

Q. Define false negative & false positive.
Answer
False negative: The term ‘false-negative’ means that patients who actually have the disease are told thatthe,
do not have the disease. It amounts to giving them a ‘false reassurance’.

> The patient with a false a ‘false-negative’ test result might ignore the development of signs g

symptoms and may postpone the treatment.
> A screening test which is very sensitive has few false negatives.
> The lower the sensitivity, the larger will be the number of false negatives.

False positive: The term ‘false-positive’ means that the patient who donot have the disease are told that they
have the disease.
> Inthe ‘false-positive’ cases normal healthy people may be subjected to further diagnostic tess
at some inconvenience, discomfort, anxiety & expense until their freedom from disease is
established.
> A screening test with a high specificity will have few false positives.
> False positives not only burden the diagnostic facilities, but they also bring discredit to
screening programmes.

Conclusion: No screening test is perfect, i.e. 100% sensitive & 100% specific.
[Ref- Park /24*/ 15]
