Communicable Diseases

Q. What is communicable disease?
Answer
Communicable disease:

An illness due to specific infectious agent or it’s toxic products capable of being directly or indirectly
transmitted from man to man, animal to animal or from the environment (through air, dust, soil, water, food
etc.) to man or animal.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 98}

Component:
> Agent: The seed.

> Host: The soil.
> Route of transmission: The climate.
Q. State the cardinal characteristics of infectious diseases.
Answer
Cardinal characteristics of infectious diseases: For an infectious disease to occur, the following conditions or
events must be take place —
1) There must be an aetiologic agent, such as parasite, bacteria, virus, fungus, rickettsia, etc. that
produces disease,
2) There must be a reservoir (human, animal or others) where the biologic agent can propagate (ie.
live, multiply and die in the natural state).
3) There must be a portal of exit from a reservoir and a portal of entry into susceptible host in
order for a disease to be caused elsewhere.
4) An organism (etiologic agent) must be transmitted, either directly or indirectly, from one place
to another.
5) There must be a susceptible host.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /89]

Transmission of Communicable Diseases

ifferent mode of transmission of diseases. [DU-16N]

rae i) different routes of transmission of communicable disease with example. [SUST-

Q. What are the routes of disease transmission? Give examples of each of them. [SUST-12J]

Q. Write short note on: Disease transmission. [CU-16N]
Answer

Modes of transmission of communicable diseases:
* Direct transmission:

1) Direct contact: Infection may be transmitted by direct contract from skin to skin, mucosa
to mucosa or mucosa to skin of the same or another person.

Example: STD and AIDS, leprosy, skin & eye infection.

2) Droplet infection: This is the direct projection of a spray of droplets of saliva and naso-
pharyngeal secretions during coughing, scenting or speaking and spitting. The sizes of the
es are less than S mm and spread is limited to a distance of 30-60 cm between source and

ost.
Example: Common cold, diphtheria, whooping cough.

3) Contact With soil: The disease agent may be acquired by direct exposure to the disease agent
in soil, compost or clearing vegetable matter.

Example: Hookworm, larval, tetanus, mycosis etc.

4) Inoculation into skin or mucosa: The disease agent may be included directly into the skin or
mucosa.

Example: Rabies virus by dog bite, hepatitis B virus through needles and syringes.

5) Transplancental or vertical: Diseases transmitted through placenta.

Example: Syphilis, Toxoplasma gondii, Rubella virus, Cytomegalo virus, Herpes virus,
Varicella virus, Syphilis, Hepatitis B, Coxsacki-B, AIDS etc.

« Indirect transmission: Mainly by 5 ‘F’ (flies, fingers, fomites, food & fluid).

1) Vehicle borne:
> Water & food borne: Acute diarrhoea, typhoid fever, cholera, polio, hepatitis A, food

poisoning.
> Blood borne: Hepatitis B, Malaria, syphilis.
> Organ transplantation: Cytomegalovirus infection.

2) Mector bone:
> Mechanical transmission: Diarrhoea.
> Biological transmission: Plague, malaria.

3) Air borne:
> Droplet nuclei: They are tiny particles (1-10 microns range) with represent the dried
residue of droplets. They may be formed by i) Evaporation of droplets coughed or
"sneezed into air or ii) generated by atomizing devices (aerosols).

Example: TB, influenza, chicken pox, measles.

> Dust: They are larger droplets settle down by their sheer weight on the floor, carpet,
clothes and become part of the dust.
Example: TB, pneumonia, Q-fever etc.

annem EE

> From soil by wind: e.g. Fungal spore.

a Fomite borne: Fomites are inanimate articles or substances other than water or food
cg by the infectious discharges from a patient. Fomites include soiled clothes, towels
inen, cups, spoons etc.

Example: Diphtheria, typhoid fever, bacillary dysentery etc.

5) Unclean hands and fingers: The transmission takes place both directly and indirectly.
Example: Typhoid fever, dysentery, hepatitis A and intestinal parasites.

Q. How transmission of communicable disease can be prevented? [SUST-13J]

Answer
Interruption / prevention of transmission of communicable disease:
A major aspect of communicable disease control relates to “breaking the chain of transmission” or

interruption of transmission. This may mean changing some components of man’s environment to prevent the
infective agent from a patient or carrier from entering the body of susceptible person. For example —

1) Water treatment / water purification: To prevent water borne diseases e.g. typhoid, dysentery,
hepatitis A & E, cholera, gastroenteritis etc.

refrigeration of prepared foods and withdrawal of contaminated foods.

3) Control of the vector: Vector borne diseases can be prevented by control of vectors and their
breeding places.

4) Practice of safe sex,

Q. Define isolation. [SUST-16N]

Q. Write short note on: Isolation. [SUST-18M]

Isolation:

Y Isolation of the patient is the oldest communicable disease control measure.

Y Itis defined as “separation, for the period of communicability, of infected persons or animals from
others in such places and under such conditions, as to prevent or limit the direct or indirect
transmission of the infectious agent from those infected to those who are susceptible or who may

spread the agent to others”.

Purpose / importance of isolation:
1) To protect the community by preventing transfer of infection from the reservoir to the possible

susceptible hosts.
2) Isolation has a distinctive value in the control of some infectious diseases; e.g. Diphtheria, Cholera,

Streptococcal respiratory diseases & Pneumonic plague.

Types of isolation:
1) Standard isolation.
2) Strict isolation.
3) Protective isolation.
4) High security isolation.

Quarantine

Q. Define quarantine. [SUST-16N]
Q. Write short note on: Quarantine. [SUST-18M]
Answer
Quarantine:
It has been defined as “the limitation of freedom of movement of such well persons or domestic animals
exposed to communicable disease for a period of time not longer than the longest usual incubation period of the

disease, in such manner as to Prevent effective contact with those not so exposed.”
[Ref- Park / 24" / 129]

Types of quarantine:

1) Absolute quarantine.

2) Modified quarantine: e.g. a selective partial limitation of the freedom of movement, such as
exclusion of children from school.

3) Segregation: e.g. removal of susceptible children to homes of immune persons.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 129]

Emerging and Reemerging Disease

Q. Discuss ‘emerging & re-emerging diseases’ with example. [SUST-16M]
Q. Write short note on: Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases.
Answer

Emerging diseases:

Emerging infectious diseases are those whose incidence in humans has increased during the last two
decades or which threaten to increase in the near future. The term also refers to newly appearing infectious
diseases or diseases that are spreading to new geographical areas such as cholera in South America and yellow
fever in Kenya. The most dramatic example of new disease is AIDS.

Re-emerging diseases:
The term re-emerging diseases refers to the diseases which were previously easily controlled by

chemotherapy and antibiotics, but now they have developed antimicrobial resistance and are often appearing in
epidemic form.

The factors responsible for emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases:
1) Unplanned and under-planned urbanization.
2) Overcrowding and rapid population growth.
3) Poor sanitation.
4) Inadequate public health infrastructure.
5) Resistance to antibiotics. ' ‘ ere
6) Increased exposure of humans to disease vectors and reservoirs of infection in nature.

7) Rapid and intense international travel. .
[Ref- Park / 24" /373]

Diphtheria

Q. Define diphtheria.
Q. What are the types of diphtheria?
Answer

Diphtheria:

Diphtheria is an acute bacterial disease caused by toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae,
(and occasionally C. ulcerans) and characterized in its typical form by the presence of membrane
(pseudomembrane) in the throat and generalized toxaemia.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /227]

pes of diphtheria: Three major clinical types have been described:

1) Anterior nasal

2) Tonsillar (Faucal)

3) Pharyngeal

There may be other clinical types, e.g. Laryngeal and cutaneous diphtheria. It occasionally involves
the other sites such as eyes (conjunctiva), nose or vagina.

Laryngeal diphtheria is serious in infants and young children, while nasal diphtheria is mild and

often chronic.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /227]

Pathogenesis of diphtheria: The bacilli multiply locally, usually in the throat, and elaborate a powerful

> The formation of a grayish or yellowish membrane (‘false membrane”) commonly over the tonsils,

pharynx, or larynx (or at the site of implantation) with well-defined edges and the membrane cannot
be wiped away.
Marked congestion, oedema or local tissue destruction.
Enlargement of regional lymph nodes and
Signs and symptoms of toxaemia.

Q. Write short note on: Shick test.

Answer

Shick test; Intradermal test which test two things —
Y To know the immune status of the person against diphtheria,
Y To sce the state of hypersensitivity to diphtheria toxin.

Procedure:

___ 0.2 ml of Shick test toxin is injected into the skin of forearm intradermally. Same amount of toxin
inactivated by heat (at 60°C for 15 minutes) is injected as a control into opposite arm.

Reaction: The following reaction may be observed —

1) Positive reaction: A circumscribed area of redness upto 3 cm or more in diameter appears at the
injection area of the test arm within 48 hours. Some swelling and tenderness may be noted. The
injection area of the control arm shows no changes. The positive test indicates that the individual is
susceptible to diphtheria,

2) Negative reaction: Both arms shows no reaction at all. The negative test indicates that the person
is immune to diphtheria.

3) Pseudo-positive Reaction: Here a red flush appears (much less circumscribed) on both the arms
within 6 to 18 hours which fades away completely within 3 to 4 days. The reaction is due to
hypersensitivity to protein and should be interpreted as Schick negative.

4) Combined Reaction: In this case red areas appear on both arms, but reaction at the injection site of
the test arm may persist for 5 to 7 days or more whereas reaction at the control arm disappears on
days 3 or 4 as this is due to allergy. It is a positive reaction which indicates that the person is
susceptible.

Interpretation: On the results of Schick test and throat swab test the following can be inferred:

Enteric fever:

Y The term “enteric fever” includes both typhoid and paratyphoid fevers.

Y Typhoid fever is an acute infectious communicable disease caused by Salmonella typhi and is

Q. How typhoid fever can be diagnosed in the laboratory?
Answer
Laboratory diagnosis of typhoid fever:

1) . Microbiological procedures: The definitive diagnosis of typhoid fever depends on the isolation of |
Salmonella typhi from blood, bone marrow and stools. Blood culture is the mainstay of diagnosis of
this disease.

2) Serological procedure: Widal test measures agglutinating antibody levels against O and H
antigens.

3) New diagnostic test: IDL Tubex test can detect IgM09 antibodies from patients within a few
minutes. Another rapid serological test, typhidot, takes 3 hours to perform. A newer version of the

test Typhidot-m was recently developed to detect specific IgM antibodies only. Another test is
dipstick test.

[Ref- Park /24" / 250, 251]

Tetanus
Q. Define tetanus. Classify tetanus.
Answer
Tetanus:

It is an acute disease caused by exotoxin of Clostridium tetani and characterized by painful paroxysmal
spasm of the voluntary muscles.

[Ref- Park /24" / 328 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 232]

Classification of tetanus:
1) Traumatic tetanus: Trauma is a major and important cause of tetanus. Sometimes, tetanus may
result from insignificant or even unnoticed wounds.
2) Puerperal tetanus: A post abortal uterus is a favourable site for the germination of tetanus spores:
So tetanus is more common after abortion than normal pregnancy.
3) Qtogenic tetanus: Ear may be a rare portal of entry. Foreign bodies such as infected pencils,
matches, and beads may introduce the infection. It is more common in children then adults.

Q: Discuss the important epidemiological features of tetanus.
Answer

Epidemiological features of tetanus:
° Occurrence: Tetanus is the worldwide in distribution; rare in developed countries. Still a problem in
developing countries.

“ Epidemiological triad:
1) Agents factors: Cl. tetani isa gram-positive, anaerobic, spore forming organism.
2) Host factors:
> Age: 5 to 40 yrs.
> Sex: higher incidence in male, female are more exposed to the risk of tetanus during
delivery & abortion.
> Occupation: Agricultural workers are special risk of tetanus because of contact with
soil.
> Rural urban differences: The incidence of tetanus is much lowering in urban than
tural areas,
> Immunity: No age is immune unless protected by previous immunization.

3) Environment factors:
> The occurrence of tetanus depends upon man’s physical & ecological surrounding the
soil, agriculture, animal husbandry.
> Unhygienic customs & habits.
> Unhygienic delivery practice.

«* Natural history:
1) Reservoir of infection: Infected animal intestine (cattle, goats, and sheep)

2) Source of infection: Soil, dust, earth, human & animal excreta, contaminated articles

3) Carrier: Air and dust

4) Mode of transmission: Infection by contamination of wound with tetanus spores, trival
pinprick, skin abrasion, puncture wound, burns, unsterile surgery, human bite, animal bite.

5) Incubation period: The incubation period is usually 6 to 10 days. It may be are short as one

day & as long as several years.

Q. How tetanus occurs after RTA?

Q. Write down the pathogenesis of tetanus.
Answer

Mechanism of tetanus after RTA: d fractures b
Spores of Cl. tetani enter through penetrating or punctured wounds or through compound frac ya

L

- d and growth of

Germination of spores is favoured by necrotic tissue and poor blood supply in the wound and gr 0 |
|

|

aerobic organisms which utilizes the oxygen producing anerobic condition.
Then the spores germinate and vegetative organisms grow.
The toxin (tetanospasmin) produced intracellularly and release after the death of the bacilli.

The toxin binds to the receptors on peripheral nerve endings and reaches the neurons of spinal cord and
brain stem through retrograde intra-exonal transport.

There the toxin inhibits the release of inhibitory neurotransmitter- glycine and GABA and the motor
neurons are not inhibited.

The inhibition of the release of inhibitory neurotransmitter allows the more powerful muscle to prevail
hyper-reflexia, muscle spasm and spastic paralysis result.

Death usually results from respiratory muscle paralysis.

Q. Why ATS is not used now as a method of immunization?
Q. Mention the disadvantages of ATS.
Answer
ATS is not used now because —
1) It causes sensitivity reaction in many people
2) ATS is rapidly excreted from the body, as it is foreign to the body.
3) ATS stimulate the formation of antibodies to it. Hence a person who has one received ATS tends to
rapidly eliminate subsequent doses.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 330]

Q. Why antibiotic is indicated in tetanus?
Answer

The method of tetanus prophylaxis is active immunization but it is of no immediate effect in non-
immune persons. ATS as an agent for immediate protection has its drawbacks, For this Treason antibiotics are
indicated.

* Mode of transmission:

Q. State the international measures against plague.
Answer
International measures against plague:
1) Telegraphic notification within 24 hours by goveraments to WHO.
2) Measures applicable to ships, aircrafts and land transport arriving from plague affected areas are

specified in International Health Regulation.

3) Vaccination against plague cannot be required as a condition of admission to a territory.

4) On arrival of an infested or suspected ship or an infested aircraft, travelers may be kept under
surveillance for a period of not more than 6 days from the date of arrival.

5) Plague is one of the quarantinable diseases, and as much special measures are taken at the ports in

accordance with International Health Regulation.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5™/235]

Q. Discuss the control measures of anthrax. [DU-11J]
Answer
Control measures of anthrax:
1) Enforcement of health measures in the industries dealing with skin and hides, wool and hairs, bone
and bone products, etc.
2) Vaccination of animals at risk.
3) Education of people about the mode of transmission of the disease.

4) Vaccination of high-risk groups, such as veterinarians and those handiing potentially contaminated
industrial raw materials.

5) Notification to local health authority.

6) Disinfection of soiled articles.

7) Specific treatment: Penicillin is the drug of choice. Ciprofloxacin, Sulphonamides,
chloramphenicol and tetracycline have also been used successfully.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5” /235]

Tuberculosis

Tuberculosis:
; Tuberculosis is an ancient disease. Hippocrates termed it.as phthisis and the word tuberculosis was first
used in 1839, The disease is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rarely by Mycobacterium bovis. The_

common site of lesion is the lungs as tubercle bacilli grow best in high oxygen content. It also affects
extrapulmonary tissues. The disease usually runs a chronic course with varying clinical manifestations.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /347]

Q. Define drug resistance. Why TB becomes resistant? How will you prevent drug resistance?
Q. Write short note on: Drug resistance.

Answer

Drug resistance:

_Drug resistance means that certain strains of tuberculosis bacilli are not killed by the antituberculosis
drugs given during the treatment.

Causes of drug resistance:

Drug resistance is caused by inadequate treatment'and poor tuberculosis control programmes. The most
common reasons for the development of resistance are:

> Incorrect prescription.

> Irregular supply of drugs.

> Non-compliance of treatment.

> Lack of supervision and follow-up.

Types of drug resistance: The resistance may be of two types —
1) Primary or pre-treatment resistance: It is the resistance shown by the bacteria in a patient, who
has not received the drug in question before.
2) Secondary or acquired resistance: Here the bacteria were sensitive to the drug at the start of the
treatment but became resistant to the particular drug during the course of treatment with it.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 189, 211]

Prevention of drug Resistance:
1) Treatment with two or more drugs in combination.
2) Using drugs to which the bacteria are sensitive
3) Ensuring that the treatment is complete, adequate and regular.

Q. Define MDR and XDR tuberculosis.

Q. Write short note on: Multi-drug resistant (MDR) TB.
Answer

Multidrug resistant TB (MDR-TB):

WHO defines a multi-drug resistant (MDR) strain as one that is at least resistant to 2 first line drugs:
isoniazid and rifampicin.

Consequence of MDR tuberculosis:

> Much more difficult to treat, even where second line drugs are available (most serious danger of
MDR-TB).
Treatment of MDR tuberculosis can take at least two years and the results are poor.
2™ line drugs cost 30 times as much as drugs used in treatment of non-resistant tuberculosis
patients.
Patients with MDR tuberculosis may need to be hospitalized and isolated which adds to the cost of
treatment, to prevent transmission of primary resistant strains to others.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 189, 211]

tuberculosis (XDR-TB) and are defined as occurring when M. tuberculosis is resistant to
Y Atleast rifampicin and isoniazid (i.e. MDR-TB).

Q. Discuss the TB control programme in Bangladesh.
Answer
TB control program in Bangladesh:
j Until 1965, TB services were mainly based in 44TB clinics. 8 segregation hospitals and 4 TB hospitals.
Since then different initiatives were taken to control TB, a major health burden in Bangladesh.

The objectives of the national tuberculosis programme (NTP):

+I To bring down the incidence of tuberculosis to such a level that it does not constitute a public health
problem. ;

Targets:
1) To detect at least 70% of existing cases of sputum positive TB.

2) To cure 80% of detected new cases of sputum smear positive TB.

Strategy:
1) Passive case finding through screening of symptomatic patient.

2) Early case detected of sputum smear positive cases by direct microscopy

3) Effective chemotherapy to sputum-smear positive cases and to all other TB patient.

4) Organizing TB treatment delivery up to upazila level.

5) Monitoring results through a standardized recording and reporting system.

6) Providing training and refresher courses to all personnel involved.

7) Integration of NTP and leprosy Elimination programme into general health services and
collaboration and NGO.

DOTS Strategies: The NTP (National Tuberculosis Control Programme) now applies the WHO recommended
DOTS (Directly observed treatment short course) strategy for detection and cure of TB. DOTS introduces in
Bangladesh in 1993, has now expanded to cover 75% of the population with a treatment success rate of nearly
80%. It combines five elements.

1) Political commitment to the programme

2) Reliable microscopic diagnosis

3) Standardized, multi-drug and directly observed treatment.

4) Adequate supply of drugs

5) Proper recording and reporting.

Q. Mention the awareness message for early diagnosis of TB. [CU-06S]
Answer

For early diagnosis of tuberculosis, we should test the sputum of the patients. In this regard, the sputum
positive cases are the targets of the programme. Therefore, utmost importance has to be given for early
detection of cases through direct microscopical examination of sputum of all tubercular symptomatics. The
process is —

3 sputum samples including a fresh morning specimen need to be examined. TB is diagnosed if at least
2 samples becomes positive or contain TB bacilli. The lengthy process of sputum culture comes next. Thus

early diagnosis of TB can be possible.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4" / 335]

Q. Why the prevalence of tuberculosis is higher among HIV infected patients?

Answer
Cause of higher prevalence of TB among HIV infected patients:

The HIV virus damages body’s natural immune protection. It reduces the number of helper T-cells and
thus damages both cell-mediated and antibody-mediated immune systems. Thus it accelerates the speed at
which tuberculosis progresses from a harmless infection to life-threatening condition.

[Ref- Park 24" / 189, 212]

Q. Write about Hansen’s disease (Leprosy).
Q. What is Hansen’s disease? [RU-12J]
Answer
Hansen’s disease (Leprosy): .

Leprosy is a chronic infectious granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae characterized
by-shin lesion, involvement of peripheral nerve resulting in anesthetic patches (in the skin) hypo pigmented
areas, tropic changes producing defect in mucous membrane, muscle, bone.

Leprosy is clinically characterized by one or more of the following cardinal features:
1) Hypopigmented patches.

2) Partial or total loss of cutaneous sensation in the affected areas (the earliest sensation to be affected

is usually light touch). |
3) Presence of thickened nerves, and |
4) Presence of acid-fast bacilli in the shin or nasal smears.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 332]

Q. Write short note on: Lepromin test.
Answer

Lepromin test:

It is a skin test to diagnose leprosy.

Positive reaction indicates immunity to leprosy.
Procedure:

The test is performed by injecting intradermally 0.1 ml of lepromin into the inner aspect of the forearm
and the reaction is read at 48 hours and 21 days.

Observation: Two types of reactions may be observed — ;
1) Early reaction: Redness and induration appears at the site of inoculation within 24 to 48 hours; if
the diameter of erythema is more than 10 mm at the end of 24 hours, the test is positive. ;
2) Late reaction: Here the test result is read at 21 days; if there is a nodule of more than 5 mm in
diameter at the site of inoculation, the test is said to be positive.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5*/351

Q. Mention the treatment of leprosy as per WHO recommendation. [DU-17M, RU-16M, 13J]

Q. Give WHO recommended drug regimens of Hansen’s disease. [RU-15J]
Answer
Treatment of leprosy: The WHO recommends two treatment regimens are:
> Multibacillary leprosy: It includes both lepromatous and borderline leprosy. Three drugs are used —
> Rifampicin- 600 mg, once monthly, given under supervision.
> Dapsone- 100 mg, daily, self-administered.
> Clofazimine- 300 mg, once monthly supervised and 50 mg daily, self-administered.
Duration of treatment: The end point of combined treatment should be for at least 2 years &
continued, where possible, up to smear negativity.

“ Paucibacillary leprosy: It includes tuberculoid and indeterminate forms of leprosy. The WHO

recommends the following treatment.
> Rifampicin: 600mg, once a month for 6 months, supervised.
> Dapsone: 100 mg (1-2 mg/kg of body weight) daily for 6 months, self-administered.

[Ref- Park /24" /341]

Q. Describe the mechanism of OPV.
Q. Write short note on: OPV.
Answer
Mechanism of OPV: J

On administration, the live vaccine strains infect intestinal epithelial cells. After replication, the virus is
transported to the Payer’s patches where a secondary multiplication with subsequent viraemia occurs. The virus
spreads to other areas of the body resulting in the production of circulating antibodies which prevent
dissemination of the virus to the nervous system and prevent paralytic polio.

Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent
infection of the alimentary tract with wild strains of polio virus, and thus is effective in limiting virus
transmission in the community. Thus OPV induces both local and systemic immunity.

The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and
susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized. Thus widespread
“herd immunity” results, even if only approximately 66% of the community is immunized.

Advantages of OPV:

1) Since given orally, it is easy ‘o administer and does not require the use of highly trained personnel

2) Induces both humeral and intestinal immunity (PV induces only humoral immunity but not local or
intestinal immunity).

3) Antibody is quickly produced, even a single dose elicits substantial immunity.

4) The vaccine excretes the virus and so infects others who are also immunized thereby (herd
immunity).

5) Useful in controlling epidemics.

6) Relatively inexpensive.

Complication of OPV: OPV is remarkably free from complications. However, being living viruses, the
vaccine viruses, particularly type-3 do mutate in the course of their multiplication in vaccinated children, and
Tare cases of vaccine-associated paralytic polio have occurred in recipients of the vaccine, & their contacts,

Contraindications of OPV:
1) Acute infectious diseases.
2) Fever.
3) Diarrhoea & dysentery.

Scanned with CamScanner

4) Patients suffering from leukaemias and malignancy.
5) Those receiving corticosteroids. F.
[Ref- Park / 24" /22y ;

Q. Why IPV is used in developed countries?
Answer
Use of IPV in developed countries:

Since the efficacy of OPV is not 100%, even with potent vaccines properly administered, some Cases
May occur. Universally, it is being considered that the enhanced inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) for the
first one or two doses in a continuation regimen with OPV may prevent post-vaccine poliomyelitis. So,
although it is costly IPV is used in developed countries.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"/ 237-238)

Q. Which vaccine can cause provocative reaction?
Q. Why provocative reaction (PR) occurs?

Answer

Provocative reaction:

OPV can cause provocative reaction. Several provocative or risk factors have been found to precipitate
an attack of paralytic polio in individuals already infected with polio viruses. They include fatigue, trauma,
intramuscular injections, operative procedures, such as tonsillectomy undertaken especially during epidemics of
polio and administration of immunizing agents particularly alum-containing DPT.

Hepatitis-B

Hepatitis B:

Hepatitis B (formerly known as “serum hepatitis” is a systemic infection with major pathology in the
liver, caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV) and transmitted usually by the parenteral route.

Persistent hepatitis B virus infection may cause progressive liver disease including chronic active

hepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 227]

There are at least 15 different types of avian influenza that routinely birds around the world. The

Bird flu is not the same as SARS (sever acute respiratory syndrome). Although their symptoms are

causing

So far in this outbreak, human cases have blamed contact with infected chickens and their

disease is generally miler in those who caught it from an infected person rather than from birds,
> If the virus mutates and combines with a human influenza virus, it could be spread through
"person-to-person transmission in the same way the ordinary human flu virus is spread.
History:
> The current outbreak of bird flu is different from earlier ones in that officials have been unable

to people, but it was much more quickly contained: A total of 18 people were hospitalized with

Q. Why measles is treated with vitamin A?
Answer
All cases of severe measles, and all cases of measles in areas with high case-fertility rates should be
treated with vitamin A, as many children develop acute deficiency of vitamin A, which may lead to
keratomalacia and blindness from corneal scarring.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 158]

Q. How eradication of measles is possible?
Answer

Measles is amenable to eradication. Measles immunization has in its favour the fact that only one dose
is needed and that a measles vaccines has now been developed which is more heat stable.

It requires:
> Achieving immunization coverage at least 96% of children under 1 year of age.

> The cumulation in the immunity gap be prevented.
[Ref- Park /24"/ 159]

Q. Write down the control measures of measles outbreak.
Answer
Control measures in case of outbreak of measles:
1) Isolation for 7 days after onset of rash.
2) Immunization of contacts within 2 days of exposure (if vaccine is contra-indicated immunoglobulin
should be given within 3 - 4 days of exposure.)
3) Prompt immunization at the beginning of an epidemic is essential to limit the spread.

[Ref- Park /24"/ 159]

Q. Why small pox eradication was possible?
Q. Mention the epidemiological basis of eradication of small pox. [SUST-10J]
Answer
Epidemiological feature responsible for eradication of small pox:
1) No known animal reservoir.
2) No long-term carrier of the virus.
3) Life-long immunity, after recovery from the disease.
4) Easy recognition of the cases even by non-medical personal.
5) Persons with sub-clinical infection did not transmit the disease.
6) Availability of a stable, potent vaccine. -

Q. When and how small pox has been eradicated?
Answer

History of small pox eradication:
Edward Jenner introduced vaccination against small pox in 1796. Through the next two centuries

improvements were brought in the type/ quality of vaccine and vaccination technique both of which occupied
important application in the global eradication program initiated by WHO in 1958 and intensified since 1967.

The last case of naturally occurring small pox in the world was reported in Somalia on October 26,
1977. Finally on May 8, 1980, the World Health Assembles declared “The World and all its people have won
freedom from the small pox an unprecedented achievement in the histories of public health.”

“ [Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 249]

Q. State the epidemiological features of rabies. [RU-10J]
Q. Give outline of epidemiology of rabies.
Answer
Epidemiological features of rabies:
“ Occurrence: It occurs throughout the world except in developed countries. Rabies is endemic in
Bangladesh.
“ Epidemiological triad:
> Agent: Lyssavirus type-I (rabies virus), family- rhabdoviridiae.
> Host: Rabies virus can infect all warm blooded mammals. Man is infected accidentally.
> Environment: It may occur at any time but is more prevalent in the summer months.

“* Natural history:
1) Reservoir: stray and pet dogs, cats, fox, wolf, jackal, hyena etc.

2) Source of infection to man: Saliva of the rabid animals. .
3) Infectious period: In dogs and cats, 2 to 5 days before onset of signs and symptoms and during
the course of the illness.

4) Mode of transmission:

Y Animal bites: By rabid dog bites. .

Y Licks: Licks on abraded skin and scratches on the mucosa can also transmit the

disease.
Y Non-bite route: Air borne transmission by oral and milk borne route is unusual.

5) Incubation period: Commonly 1 —3 months, but may vary from 7 days to many years. ;
6) Period of communicability: In dogs and cats, 3 to 5 days before onset of symptoms and signs,
and during the course of the disease. Bats shed virus during the course of the disease.

[Ref- Park / 24" /294 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 250]

Q. Describe modes of transmission of rabies?
Answer

Modes of transmission of rabies:

1) Animal bites: Most of the human rabies results from the biting of-
> Rabid dog,
> Also cat, monkey, jackal, horse, & sheep etc. As a pre-requisite to transmission, the saliva

of the biting animal must contain rabies virus at the time of bite.

2) Licks:
> Licks on abraded skin and mucosa
> Injury with bone splinter or other object contaminated by the saliva of a rabid animal.

3) Aerosols:
> Only in certain caves harbouring rabies infected bat.
> In the laboratory, aerosols created during homogenization of infected animal brains can
infect lab workers.

4) Person to person:
> Child biting to others.

> Corneal & organ transplantation.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 295]

Q. How rabies differs from other communicable diseases? [RU-1 1Ju]
Q. Incidence of Rabies is increasing-discuss. [CU-17M]

Answer

Peculiarities of rabies from other communicable diseases:

1) It is the only communicable disease of man that is always fatal.

2) Highly variable incubation period in man, commonly | — 3 months following exposure but may.
vary from 7 days to many years. The incubation period depends on the site of the bite, severity of
the bite, number of wounds, amount of virus injected, species of the biting animal, protection
provided by the clothing and treatment undertaken, if any. In no other communicable disease
incubation period is so variable and dependent on so many factors.

[Ref- Park /24" /294]

Q. Write short notes on (i) Street virus & (ii) Fixed virus.
Answer
Street virus: The virus recovered from naturally occurring cases of rabies is called street virus. The virus is
excreted in the saliva of affected animals. The virus as it occurs in nature is known as street virus.
> The virus can be also isolated from human cases.
>  Itis pathogenic to all mammals.
> Itcan multiply in the neuronal and extra-neuronal tissue(muscles).
> It has a long variable incubation period (20-60 days) in days.
> It forms Negri bodies.

Fixed virus: It is defined as one that has a short, fixed and shortened incubation period when collected after
serial brain-to-brain passage of the natural virus into a suitable animal. Serial brain-to-brain passage of the street
virus in rabbits modifying the virus to form fixed virus.

> It can multiply in the neuronal tissue but not in extra-neuronal tissue(muscle)

> Direct injection to brain produce encephalitis.

Q. Why fixed virus is called fixed virus?

Answer a ‘
Serial brain-to-brain passage of the street virus in rabbits modify the virus such that its incubation —
period is progressively reduced until it becomes fixed between 4-6 days. So the virus isolated at this stage is

called a fixed virus.

Q. Write down the clinical features of rabies in dogs.

Answer

Clinical features of rabies in dogs: The disease in dogs may manifest in the following forms-
“* Furious type:

1) It is the common type and is more frequent.

2) The dog is easily irritated and may bite.
3) Later on, it becomes restless, excited, furious, may bite anybody and has a tendency to snap at

anything that comes on its way.
4) The dog will attempt to eat indigestibles like stick, straw, paper, etc.

5) It will leave its home and roam about.
6) Its eyes are wide open and have fixed gaze, conjunctivae is injected, voice changes, paralysis

starts at hind limbs and then on fore limbs.
7) The rabid dog dies within 10 days.
“* Dump type:
1) There is no irritability.
2) The animal hides in dark corners of the house and suffers from sleepiness and melancholia.

3) Paralysis of jaw and limbs sets in.
4) Death occurs within 3 days after the onset.
5) Dog here usually does not bite.

“ Mixed type.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5" /250, 251]

Note: The characteristic symptoms of hydrophobia are absent in animal.

Q. How will you diagnose a case of rabies from dog bite?
Answer

< Clinical diagnosis:
> History of rabid animal bite.
> Characteristic symptoms and signs.
« Laboratory diagnosis :

Q. How rabies can be controlled?
Q. How the morbidity & mortality of rabies can be reduced? (CU-17M]
Answer
Preventive and control measures of rabies:
1) Immunization of pet dogs and cats annually.
2) Licensing of dogs.
3) Quarantine measures for entry of dogs in rabies free areas.
4) Collection and destruction of stray dogs.
5) Ten-days detention and observation of dogs and cats known to have bitten a person or showing
suspicious signs of rabies.
6) Unvaccinated dogs or cats bitten by known rabid animals should be destroyed.
7) Immediate submission of intact head of animal that die of suspected rabies for laboratory
examination.
8) Pre-exposure immunization of high-risk groups e.g. veterinarians, dog handlers and laboratory
workers with HDCV given IM in 3 doses (1 ml each) on days 0, 7, 21 or 28.
9) Post-exposure measures:
> Local treatment of wound.

> Immunization.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /251]

Q. Write in short the prevention and control measures of dengue fever? [DU-18N, SUST-15Ju]
Answer
Prevention and control measures of dengue fever:

1) Mosquito control:

> Elimination of breeding places in and around houses controlled by individual & community
action.

> Anti-larval action:
¥ Environment control: Discarded tins, empty pots, broken bottles should be got rid
of water holding container.
Y Chemical control: Larvicides (abate).
> Anti-adult measures: Residual sprays.

2) Host individual protection:
> Mosquito net.
> Screening.
> Use of long clothes & gloves.
> Repellents.

3) Vaccines: So far, there is no satisfactory vaccine and no immediate prospect of preventing the
disease by immunization. Live attenuated vaccine is affective.

4) Notifications: Occurrence of epidemics should be reported.

5) Health education about dengue fever.

6) Appropriate treatment of DHF and DF:

> Fluid replacement, blood transfusion & corticosteroids are indicated in the haemorthagic
varieties.

> Patients need full bed rest.
> Severe pain can be relieved by paracetamol.

Yellow fever

Yellow Fever:

Yellow fever is a zoonotic disease caused by an arbovirus.

It is a severe infectious and life threatening disease characterized by toxic jaundice, yellow skin, high
fever, severe body ache, nausea, vomiting and albuminuria accompanied by haemorrhages from stomach, nose

and mouth.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 255]

Protozoal Diseases

Amoebiasis

Q. Define amoebiasis. How you can prevent and control it?
Answer
Amoebiasis:
; The term ‘amoebiasis’ has been defined by WHO as the condition of harbouring the protozoan parasite
Entamoeba histolytica with or without clinical manifestations.

Types:
> Intestinal amoebiasis.
> Extraintestinal amoebiasis involving fiver (liver abscess), lungs, brain, spleen, skin etc.

Prevention and control:
* Primary prevention:
1) Sanitation:
> Safe disposal of human excreta.
> Washing hands after defecation and before eating.

2) Water supply:

> Protection of water supply against faecal contamination.
> Filtration and boiling of water.

3) Food hygiene: Food handlers should be periodically examined, treated and educated in food
hygiene practices such as hand washing.
4) Health education.

“* Secondary prevention:
1) Early diagnosis:

> Demonstration of trophozoites containing red cells is diagnostic.
> Serological test: Indirect haemagglutination test (IHA).

> Newer techniques: Counter immuno-electrophoresis (CIE).

> ELISA.

2) Treatment:
> Symptomatic cases: Metronidazole orally 30 mg/kg body weight/day, divided into 3
doses after meals, for 8-10 days.
> Asymptomatic infections: Oral diodohyroxyquin, 650 mg t.d.s. (adults) or 30-40
mg/kg of body weight/day (children) for 20 days, or oral diloxanide furoate, 500 mg

t.d.s. for 10 days (adults).
[Ref- Park / 24" / 255, 256]

Q. What do you mean by Roll Back Malaria? [DU-06M]

Answer . ‘

Roll back malaria: By mid-1995 all malaria endemic countries in the region had adopted the revised malaria

control strategy to reduce Morbidity and mortality and to reduce its area of distribution particulars of multi-drug

resistance malaria, Vector resistance to insecticides has necessitated the use of more expensive pyrethroid

thereby limiting the coverage. Malaria control added impetus through Roll back Malaria initiative was launcheg

by WHO, UNICEF, UNDP & the World Bank in 1998, The main strategies of these Initiative are given below.
* Strengthen health System to ensure better delivery of health care, especially at district and

community level. .

Ensure the Proper and expanded use of insecticide treated mosquito nets.

Ensure adequate access to basic health care and training of health care workers, -

Encourage the development of simpler and more effective means of administering medicines such

as training of village health workers and mothers on early and appropriate treatment of malaria,

especially in children. .

Encourage the development of more effective and new anti-malaria drugs and vaccines.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 236)

Ancylostomiasis (Hook worm disease)

Q. Write down the epidemiology of hook worm infestation.
Answer
Epidemiology of ancylostomiasis / hook worm disease:
Occurrence: Ancylostoma duodenale and the Necator americanus are found in every country
where the freezing temperature does not last for long and the sanitation is poor.
> Agent: Ancylostoma duodenale and the Necator americanus.
> Reservoir: Man is the only reservoir.
> Host: Negroes are less susceptible than others. Males are affected more than females because of
greater exposure. ‘
> Environment: Agricultural land and mines are ideal for the development of hookworm larva.
Moist, loose, sandy soil rich in organic matter favours larval development.
> Mode of transmission: The larva enters the body by penetrating the skin when and where it comes
in contact with it. The most common sites include the skin between the toes, dorsum of the feet, and
inner aspect of the sole.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 269]

reduce the worm burden and frequency of transmission. Several effective drugs are available for the

Q. Discuss the stages of lymphatic filariasis?
Answer
The following stages have been described in lymphatic filariasis:
1) Asymptomatic amicrofilaraemia: In all endemic areas a proportion of population does not show
Mf or clinical manifestations of the disease although they have the same degree of exposure to
infective larvae as those who become infected. With presently available diagnostic procedures it is
not possible to determine whether persons in this group have detectable infections or whether they
are free from infection. é

2) Asymptomatic microfilaraemia: A considerable proportion of people are asymptomatic, although
their blood is positive for Mf. They may remain without any symptoms for months-in some
instances for years. They are an important source of infection in the community. These carriers are
usually detected by night blood examination.

3) Stage of acute manifestations: In the fast months and years there are recurrent episodes of acute
inflammation in lymph glands and vessels. The clinical manifestations comprise filarial fever,
lymphadenitis, lymphoedema of the various parts of the body and of epididymo-orchitis in the
male.

Q. Explain “Twin Pillars of filariasis elimination”. [DU-12Ju]
Answer
Twin pillars of filariasis elimination: Controlling morbidity and interruption of transmission of filariasis is
called the twin pillars of filariasis elimination,
1) Controlling morbidity: Community level care of those with disease —

» Lymphoedema.

> Acute inflammatory attacks.

> Hydrocele repair.

2) Interruption of transmission:

> Research during the past few years has demonstrated that a single 6 mg/kg dose of
diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is virtually as effective in killing adult W. bancrofti and in
producing long-term suppression of microfilaria in the blood as the previously
recommended 12-day course of treatment,

Single-dose ivermectin (400ug/kg) is even more effective than DEC in suppressing
microfilaremia.

> The long-term microfilarial suppression of DEC and ivermectin is enhanced when they are
given together or with albendazole.

Taeniasis
Q. What is taeniasis?
Answer
Taeniasis:

Taeniasis is an intestinal infection caused by cestode Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) and Taenia
solium (pork tapeworm).

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" 1274)

Q. Write down the preventive measures of taeniasis, [DU-11J]
Answer

Preventive measures of taeniasis:

1) Eating raw or undercooked meat of the intermediate hosts, i.e. beef and pork must be avoided.

2) Slaughter houses should be strictly inspected by health authority.

3) Sanitary contro! of sewage disposal should be ensured.

4) Patients should be effectively treated to prevent infection of the intermediate hosts. The drug of
choice for specific treatment are praziquantel and niclosamide.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /274]

Q. How will you diagnose AIDS?
Q. Enumerate WHO case definition for AIDS surveillance in adults. [RU-16J]
Q. Enumerate the major & minor signs given by the WHO for AIDS surveillance. [RU-16N]
Answer
Diagnosis of AIDS:
“> Clinical diagnosis:

A) WHO case definition for AIDS surveillance: For the purpose of AIDS surveillance an adult
or adolescent (> 12 years of age) is considered to have AIDS if at least 2 of the following major
signs are present in combination with at least 1 of the minor signs listed below, not known to be
due to a condition unrelated to HIV infection.

¥ Major signs:
1) Weight loss > 10% of body weight
2) Chronic diarrhoea for > | month.
3) Prolonged fever for > 1 month (intermittent or constant)

Y Minor signs:
1) Persistent cough for > | month.
2) Generalized pruritic dermatitis.
3) History of herpes zoster.
4) Oropharyngeal candidiasis.
5) Chronic progressive or disseminated herpes simplex infection.
6) Generalized lymphadenopathy.

B) Expanded WHO case definition for AIDS surveillance: For the purpose of AIDS
surveillance an adult of adolescent (> 12 years of age) is considered to have AIDS if a test for
HIV antibody given a positive result , and one or more of the following conditions are present:

1) >10 % body weight loss or cachexia, with diarrhoea or fever or both, intermittent or
constant, for at least | month.
2) Cryptococcal meningitis.

** Laboratory diagnosis of AIDS: . ; :
Y Principle: AIDS is diagnosed by serological test for antibody detection against the HIV.

Electron microscope examination is done in reference laboratory. Cell culture is done for
research purpose, Nucleic acid based techniques are used in special cases.

¥ Specimen collection: Blood for serological test & culture.

Y Procedure:

1) Isolation of virus: HIV can be cultured from lymphocytes in peripheral blood or
infected people. The most sensitive virus isolation technique is to co cultivate. The test
sample with uninfected, mitogen stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cell
(PBMC) which takes 7-14 days.

2) Detection of viral antigen: ELISA.

3) Detection of antibody: ELISA confirmed by western blot and ICT, RIA, IFT.

4) Detection of viral nucleic acid: PCR.

5) Immune function test: By counting CD4+ number; e.g. CD4+ cell count below
200/mm/ indicates cell mediated immunity severely suppressed & the patient is
suffering from opportunistic infection.

6) Non-specific tests:

Raised ESR.

Leucopenia.

Lymphopenia.

Reversal CD4 & CD8 cell ratio.

Functional abnormality in macrophage & B cell.

Q. Explain AIDS related complex (ARC). [DU-06M]
Answer
AIDS related complex (ARC):

A person with ARC has illnesses caused by damage to the immune system, but without the
opportunistic infections and cancers associated with AIDS, but they exhibit one or more of the following
clinical signs —

1) Unexplained diarrhoea lasting longer than a month.

2) Fatigue.

3) Malaise.

4) Loss of more than 10 per cent body weight.

5) Fever.

6) Night sweats.

7) Other milder opportunistic infections such as oral thrush,

generalized lymphadenopathy or enlarged
spleen.

Patients from high-risk groups who have two or more of these manifestations ically includin
generalized lymphadenopathy), and who have a decreased number of T- (typically including

; helper lymphocytes idered to
have AIDS-related complex. Some patients with AIDS related complex sheers y develop AIDS.

[Ref- Park / 24" /365]

Q. Briefly describe the HIV-AIDS situation in Bangladesh. [SUST-15Ju, 14J,12J}
Answer

HIV-AIDS situation in Bangladesh:

Although Bangladesh continues to be a low prevalence area, it is surrounded by high prevalence
countries (High prevalence of HIV/AIDS in neighboring India).

Unemployment, slum housing, family fragility, frequent cross-border movement of people, lack of
information, unsafe blood transfusion, physical and sexual abuse-that create a "risk environment" of violence
for many young People in the region. In addition increased number of migrant workers, unsafe Practice in health
Service, unsafe sex practice etc. movement of population, less use of condom, polygamy, homosexuality, extra.
marital relations, further increases the susceptibility.

> The country faces a concentrated epidemic, and its very low HIV-prevalence rate is partly due to

Prevention efforts, focusing on men who have sex with men, female sex workers, and intravenous
drug users.
Number of HIV-positive individuals has increased steadily since 1994 to approximately 7,500
people in 2005 according to the International Center for diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh.
UNAIDS estimates the number to be slightly higher at 11,000 people.
> HIV prevalence amongst “most at risk populations (MARPs)” is 0.7%.
as 2.7%, for instance among casual sex workers in Hili, a small border to
Bangladesh.

» Many of the estimated 11,000 people living with HIV are migrant workers,

to complete the developmental cycle of the agent, e.g. Human taeniases, Echinococcosis.

Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS)

Q. Write short note on: SARS.

Q. What is SARS? State clinical features, prevention and control of SARS.

Answer

SARS: Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) is a communicable viral disease, caused by a new strain of
coronavirus, which differs considerably in genetic structure from previously recognized coronavirus.

Clinical features:

Fever.

Malaise.

Chills.

Headache.

Myalgia.

Dizziness.

Cough.

Sore throat.

Running nose.

Chest X-ray findings typically begin with a small, unilateral patchy shadowing, and progress over
12 days to become bilateral and generalized, with interstitial / confluent infiltration.

Acute Diarrhoeal Disease

Q. Define diarrhoea. [SUST-18M]
Q. Define diarrhoeal disease.
Answer
Diarrhoea:
Diarrhoea is defined as the passage of loose, liquid or watery stools more than three times a day.

However it is the recent change in consistency & character of stools rather than the number of stools
that is important.

Diarrhoeal diseases:
The term “diarrhoeal diseases” should be considered only as a convenient expression for a group of
diseases in which the predominant symptom is diarrhoea.
The term is not a nosological or epidemiological entity.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 236]

Q. What are the risk factors of diarrhoeal disease?
Answer
Risk factors for diarrhoeal disease:

Risk factors or Can

“> Host Factors:
1) Incidence highest in the age group 6-11 months when weaning occurs.
2) Babies under 6 months of age fed on cow’s milk or infant feeding formulas.
3) Malnutrition
4) Poverty
5) Prematurity
6) Reduced gastric acidity
7) Immunodeficiency
8) Lack of personal and domestic hygiene
9) Incorrect feeding practices.

“Environmental factors:
1) Bacterial diarrhoea occurs most frequently during warm season.
2) Viral diarrhoea (particularly rota viral) peak during the winter.
3) In tropical areas, rotavirus diarrhoea occurs throughout the year, increase frequency during the
drier cool mouths. And the bacterial diarrhoea peak during the warmer, rainy season.

[Ref- Park /24" / 237]

Role of ICDDR,B in controlling diarrhoeal disease in Banglade

Q. Discuss the role of ICDDR,B in the control of diarrhoeal disease. [DU-05M]
Q. How ICDDR,B helps in control of diarrhea? [DU-12Ju]

Answer

Role of ICDDR,B in the control of diarrhocal disease:

Bangladesh is the host country for the international center for diarrhoea disease research, Bangladesh
(ICDDR,B) it was formerly known as cholera research laboratory and was established in 1960.The cholera
research laboratory was transformed into ICDDR,B in 1978 she current mandate of the ICDDR,B is to
undertake and promote research on diarrhoea disease and the related subjects of nutrition and fertility with the
aim to prevent and control diarrhoea diseases and improving health care. The major achievements of the center
are briefly described below.

1. Development of ‘Dhaka solution’: Dhaka solution containing physiologically balanced
electrolytes to replace the loss of water and salts caused by cholera. This single solution is now
used to rehydrate patients with severe dehydration due to any diarrhoea and is made by a
Bangladesh government plant as cholera saline.

2. Development of oral rehydration therapy (ORT): Since intravenous solution is expensive,
attention was tumed to find less expensive ways to treat dehydration due to diarrhoea. Researchers
in Bangladesh and in India found that if glucose is added to a fluid of similar composition to the
Dhaka solution, absorption of water and salts is resumed during diarrhoea and rehydration by oral
route becomes possible. Since then glucose based oral rehydration salts (ORS) was tried world over
for ORT and was shown to be effective for prevention and correction of dehydration due to
diarrhoea caused by any enteropathogen. It is now the mainstay of the global programme of WHO
for control of diarrhoeal disease.

3. Development and evaluation of cholera vaccine: A series of vaccine trials had been conducted in
the Matlab field station of the center and the classical bacterial cholera vaccine was found to be
useless for all practical purposes as it conferred limited and short -lived immunity. Largely due to
the results of these trials. It was decided to withdraw the requirement of the cholera vaccine
certificate for international travel. However, search for effective cholera vaccine is still on.

4. Development of improved ORS: Though glucose based ORS is effective for rehydration, cheaper
and better substitutes for glucose were searched for. Sucrose (table sugar) was found to be equally
effective. '

5. Rice -ORS: Molla and his colleagues at ICDDR B. found that when cereal starch was substituted
for glucose in ORS, the ORS could reduce the stool volume and the duration of diarrhoea
significantly. Now cereal based ORS (rice - ORS) is routinely used in the ICDDR,B treatment

centers for diarrhoea patients.
6. Dissemination of knowledge on diarrhoea research: This is done through ICDDR,B’s

publication and library services.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 328, 329]

Food poisoning

Q. Define food poisoning. [RU-17N]
Answer

Food poisoning:
Food poisoning is an acute gastro-enteritis caused by ingestion of food or drink contaminated with

either living bacteria or their toxins or inorganic chemical substances and poisons derived from plants and
animals.
The condition is characterized by-
> History of ingestion of a common food
> Attack of many persons at the same time and

> Similarity of signs and symptoms in the majority of cases.
[Ref- Park /24" / 253]

Q. How outbreak of food poisoning can be prevented in the community? [RU-17N]
Answer
Preventive & control measures of food poisoning:
1) Food Sanitation :
> Meat inspection: The food animals must be free from infection. This can be ensured by
their examination by veterinary staff, both before and after slaughter.
> Personal hygiene: Among individuals engaged in the handling, preparation and cooking of
>

food.

Food handlers: Those suffering from infected wounds, boils, diarrhoea, dysentery, throat

infection etc. should be excluded from food handling.

Food handing techniques: The handling of ready-to-eat foods with bare hands should be

reduced to a minimum. Time between preparation and consumption of food should be kept

short. The importance of rapid cooling and cold storage must be stressed. Milk, milk

products and egg products should be pasteurized. Food must be thoroughly cooked.

> Sanitary improvements: Sanitation of all work surfaces, utensils and equipments must be
ensured. Food premises should be kept free from rats, ice, flies and dust.

> Health Education: Food handler should be educated about clean habit and personal

hygiene.

2) Refrigeration of food: In the prevention of bacterial food poisoning, emphasis must be placed on
proper temperature control. Food should not be left in warm pantries. Foods not eaten immediately
should be kept in cold storage to prevent bacterial multiplication and toxin production. “Cook and
eat the same day” is a golden rule. Cold is bacteriostatic at temperature below 4°C, and refrigeration

temperature should not exceed this level.

Vv

3) Surveillance: Food samples must be obtained from the food establishments periodically and
subjected to laboratory analysis if they were unsatisfactory. Continuing surveillance is necessary to

avoid outbreaks of food-borne diseases.

Q. Define non-communicable diseases.
Answer
Non-communicable diseases: oo.
These are a group of chronic diseases where the causative agents are not clearly identified, but a set of
tisk factors have been identified to be associated.

Q. State the cardinal characteristics of non-communicable diseases. [DU-06S]

Answer

Cardinal characteristics of non-communicable diseases: The commission on chronic illness in USA has
defined “Non communicable disease” which have one or more of the following characteristics —

They are permanent.

They leave residual disability.

They are caused by non-reversible pathological alternation.

They require special training of the patient for rehabilitation.

They may be expected to require a long period of supervision, observation or care.

Risk factors of non-communicable diseases:
1) Cigarette use and other forms of smoking.

3) Failure or inability to obtain preventive health services (e.g. hypertension control, cancer detection,

[Ref- Park /24" / 381] ;

1) Absence of a known agent:
> Whereas in some chronic diseases the cause is known (e.g., silica in silicosis, asbestos in

mesothelioma).
> For many chronic diseases the causative agent is not known.
> The absence of a known agent makes both diagnosis and specific prevention difficult. |

2) Multifactorial causation:
> Most chronic diseases are the result of multiple causes.
> Chronic diseases appear to result from the cumulative effects of multiple risk factors.
> These factors may be both environmental and behavioral or constitutional.

3) Long latent period:
> Natural history of chronic disease is the long latent (or incubation) period between the first

exposure to "suspected cause" and the eventual development of disease (e.g., cervical
cancer).

> This makes it difficult to link suspected causes (antecedent events) with outcomes, ¢.g., the
possible relation between oval contraceptives and the occurrence of cervical cancer.

> Examples include hypertension, diabetes, stroke, etc.

4) Indefinite onset:
> Most chronic diseases are slow in onset and development, and the distinction between
diseased and non-diseased states.

Q. How can you measure the burden of CHD?
Answer
Measurement of the burden of CHD: The burden of CHD may be estimated in various ways-
1) Proportional mortality ratio: The proportion of all deaths currently attributed to it.
2) Loss of life expectancy: It is the average gain in life expectation that would follow a complete
elimination of all cardiovascutar deaths if another mortality rates remain unchanged.
3) CHD incidence rate: This is the some of fatal and non-fatal attack rates.
4) Age specific death rates: It suggests a true increase in incidence.
5) Prevalence rate: the prevalence of CHD can be estimated from cross-sectional surveys using ECG
for evidence of infarction and history of prolonged chest pain.
6) Case fatality rate: This is defined as the proportion of attacks that are fatal within 28 days of
onset.
7) Measurement of risk factor levels: This includes measurement of levels of cigarette smoking,
blood pressure, alcohol consumption and serum cholesterol in the community.
Medicalares Measurement of levels of medical care in the community are also pertinent.

Rule of halves:

Hypertension is an ‘iceberg’ disease. Only about half of the people in the general population of most
developed countries are hypertensive. Half of them are aware of the condition, half of them are being treated,
and only about half of those treated were considered adequately treated. It is known as “Rules of halves”.

6) Diagnosed but untreated
7) Diagnosed and treated
8) Inadequately treated

Q. Comment on “tracking” of blood pressure. ‘
Answer

Tracking of blood pressure:
If blood pressure levels of individuals were followed up

over a period of years from early childhood into adult life, then
those individuals whose pressures were initially high in the
distribution, would probably continue in the same “track” as
adults.

Blood pressure

In other words, low blood pressure levels tend to remain
ecome higher as individuals grow

low and high levels tend to b
older. This phenomenon of persistence of rank order of blood ——

pressure has been described as “tracking”.
This knowledge can be applied as identifying children and FT
adolescents “at risk" of developing hypertension as a future date.

Cancer

Q. Define cancer. [DU-04S]
Answer
Cancer: Cancer may be regarded as a group of diseases characterized by-
> An abnormal growth of cells.
> Ability to invade adjacent tissues and even distant organs, and .
> The eventual death of the affected patient if the tumor has progressed beyond that stage when it can
be successfully removed.

Cancer can occur at any site or tissue of the body and may involve any type of cells.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 400]

Q. What are the major categories of cancer?
Answer
Major categories of cancer: .
1) Carcinomas: Arising from epithelial cells lining the internal surfaces of the various organs (e.g.
mouth, esophagus, intestines, uterus) and from the skin epithelium.
2) Sarcomas: Arising from mesodermal cells constituting the various connective tissues (e.g. fibrous
tissue, fat, and bone).
3) Lymphomas, myeloma and leukaemias: Arising from the cells of bone marrow and immune
systems.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 400]

Q. Wrife‘dofn the warning signs [SUST-12Ju, RU-16N] / danger signs [DU-14J, RU-14Ju] / early
y 4 ng signs [RU-18M] of cancer.

arning signs / danger signs of cancer:

1) Unusual bleeding or discharge from any natural orifices.

2) A lump or thickening of the breast or elsewhere.

3) A sore that does not heal.

4) Change in bowel or bladder habit.

5) Hoarseness or persistent cough. '
6) Constant indigestion or difficulty in swallowing.

7) A change in wart or mole.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /311|

Q. What are the causes of cancer?

Causes of cancer:
A) Environmental factors:
1) Tobacco: Cancer of the lung, larynx, mouth, pharynx, esophagus, bladder, pancreas, and
probably kidney.
2) Alcohol: Esophageal, liver and rectal cancers.

beef consumption to bowel cancer and a high fat diet to breast cancer.

asbestos, polycyclic hydrocarbons, etc.
5) Viruses:
Hepatitis B & C: Hepatocellular carcinoma.
HIV infection: Kaposi’s sarcoma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): Burkitt’s lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Cytomegalovirus (CMV): Kaposi’s sarcoma.

Q. Write about cancer screening?
Answer

Cancer screening:

Individuals above age 35 years, who can afford it, may undergo a thorough annual medical check-up by a
competent physician, with a view to detect early cancers, Laboratory tests may also be carried out as indicated.
While a complete medical history may provide symptoms of a localized or generalized cancer, a thorough
pee _ is likely to reveal cancers of the skin, mouth, thyroid, breast, uterus, vagina, rectum, penis
and testicle.

Investigations for cancer screening:

1) A chest or other X-ray, as indicated, could provide evidence of lesions in the chest, pleura, lungs, and
bone.

2) A blood count (CBC) not infrequently provides the initial findings of leukaemias, multiple myelomas,
or other blood dyscrasias. Blood biochemistry provides proof of liver and kidney damage.

3) A positive stool examination for blood may point to a GI tract cancer.

4) Pap smear screening may reveal a lesion of the cancer cervix.

5) Mammography helps in the early diagnosis of breast cancer.

6) Sigmoidoscopy may reveal colorectal cancers.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /312]

Cancer emergencies:

2. Pericardial effusion.
3. Intestinal obstruction.
4. Urinary retention.
5. Biliary obstruction.
6. Airway obstruction.
7. Raised intracranial pressure.

Q. Write short note on: Insulin resistance syndrome.
Answer
Insulin resistance syndrome:

In obese patients with type-2 diabetes, the association of hyperglycaemia, hyperinsulinaemia,
dyslipidaemia, and hypertension, which leads to coronary artery disease and stroke, may result from a genetic
defect producing insulin resistance, with the latter being aggravated by obesity.

Q. Discuss the diet of a diabetic & hypertensive patient. [SUST-14Ju]
Answer
Dietary management of DM:
1) Healthy eating:
> Carbohydrate: (45-60%, sucrose up to 10%) Recent studies suggest short-term (6
months), very low carbohydrate diets (containing as little as 50g/day-13% of daily energy)
are safe and effective means of reducing weight and improving glycaemic control.
Fat: (< 35% with < 10% as saturated fat & 10 — 20% from monounsaturated fat).
Protein: (10-15%) Should not exceed 1 g/kg body weight/day.
Fruit / vegetables: 5 portions daily.
Salt: Not more than 6g daily. Further restriction of sodium intake (to less than 3 g daily) is
important in treating hypertensive diabetic patients.
2) Weight management: In addition to reducing calorie intake, overweight patients should be
strongly encouraged to take regular exercise, in the form of walking, swimming or cycling, for
approximately 30 minutes daily. (Management of obesity is discussed in ‘Chapter-04’)

VvVVY

3) Diabetic food and sweeteners: Low-calorie and sugar-free drinks and sorbitol containing foods.

4) Alcohol: Alcohol can be consumed in moderation unless there is a coexisting medical problem that
requires abstinence.

iswer
Prevention and care of diabetes mellitus:

1) Primary prevention:
a. Population strategy:

> Primordial prevention — prevention of emergence of risk factors in countries in which
they have not yet appeared.

> Maintenance of normal body weight through adoption of healthy nutritional habits and
physical exercise.

> The nutritional habits include an adequate protein intake, a high intake of dietary fiber
and avoidance of sweet foods.

> Elimination of protein deficiency and food toxins.

b. High-risk strategy:
> Avoidance of sedentary life-style, over-nutrition and obesity.
> Avoidance of alcohol.
> Avoidance of diabetogenic drugs such as oral contraceptives.
> Reduction of factors that promote atherosclerosis e.g. smoking, high blood pressure,
elevated cholesterol and high triglyceride levels.

2) Secondary prevention:

e Adequate treatment of diabetes mellitus.

¢ Routine checkup of blood sugar, urine for protein and ketone bodies, blood pressure, visual acuity
and weight should be done periodically.

¢ There should be an estimation of glycosylated haemoglobin at half-yearly intervals.

¢  Self-care — i.e. the diabetic should take a major responsibility for his own care with medical
guidance.

¢ Home blood glucose monitoring.

3) Tertiary prevention:

Y Organization of specialized clinics (diabetic clinics) and units for detection and management of
complications of diabetes such as blindness, kidney failure, coronary thrombosis, gangrene of
lower extremities etc.

Q. What do you mean by ‘vector’?
Answer
Vector:

In communicable disease terminology, the word ‘vector’ means “an arthropod or other invertebrate

which transmits infection by inoculation into or through the skin or mucous membrane by biting, or by deposit
of infective materials on the skin or on food or other objects”.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 805]

Q. How arthropod borne diseases are transmitted? [DU-1 Ju]
Q. How diseases are transmitted by arthropods? [RU-15J]
Q. How arthropods transmit disease to man? [RU-12J]
Q. Discuss the mode of transmission of arthropod borne diseases. [CU-10Ju/J]
Q. Discuss biological transmission of arthropod borne diseases. [DU-12Ju]
Q. Mention different types of transmission of arthropod borne diseases. [RU-18M, 13Ju]
Q. Discuss the transmission of vector-borne diseases? [DU-18M]
Q. What do you understand by mechanical transmission of disease? [SUST-13J]
Q. “At present arthropod-borne disease contribute a major public health”- explain it with the
mechanism of transmission of disease by arthropod. [RU-14Ju]
Answer
Transmission of arthropod-borne disease: 3 types of transmission —
1) Direct contact: the arthropods are directly transferred from man to man through close contact e.g.
scabies and pediculosis.
2) Mechanical transmission: the disease agent is transmitted mechanically by the arthropod, e.g.
diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid fever, food poisoning & trachoma by the house fly.
3) Biological transmission: When the disease agent multiplies or undergoes some developmental
change with or without multiplication in the arthropod host, then it is called biological transmission.
This may be of 3 types -
> Propagative: When the disease agent undergoes no cyclical changes, but multiplies in the
body of the vector; e.g. plague bacilli in rat fleas.
> Cyclo-propagative: the disease agent undergoes cyclical changes and multiplies in the
body of the arthropod; e.g. malaria parasite in anopheles mosquito.
> Cyclo-developmental: When the disease agent undergoes cyclical change but does not
multiply in the body of the arthropod; e.g. filarial parasite in culex mosquito and guinea

worm embryo in cyclops.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 805]

Integrated vector control measures:

It has been defined as utilization of all appropriate technology and management techniques to

bring about an effective degree of vector suppression in a cost effective mariner,
The essential requirement for integrated vector control is the availability of more than one method of

control.
It is important to realize that for most vectors, sanitation, water & habitat management, waste

management, source reduction & pesticides will remain the major components of integrated vector control
approach.

Q. What are the habits of mosquito?

Q. Mention important habits of mosquito. [RU-16J]
Answer

Habits of mosquito:

1) Feeding habits: The males never bite. They subsist on plant juices. The females on the contrary are
haematophagous. They require a blood meal, once in 2 —3 days for the development of eggs.

2) Time of biting: In general, mosquitoes bite in the evening or in the early part of the night.

3) Resting habits: Mosquitoes obscure themselves during the day in dark and cool corners.

4) Breeding habits: The anopheles prefer clean water for breeding, the culicines prefer dirty and
polluted water, the aedes prefer artificial collections of water. The mansonia breed in water
containing certain types of aquatic vegetation.

5) Hibernation: They hibernate in the adult stage.

6) Dispersal: Don’t generally fly far from the place where they breed unless swept by currents of
wind.

7) Life span: It is influenced by temperature and humidity. Both high and low temperatures are fatal.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 808]

Q. List the mosquito borne diseases prevailing in Bangladesh. [DU-14Ju, SUST-16M]
Answer
Mosquito borne diseases prevailing in Bangladesh:

1) Dengue (viral, by Aedes aegypti).

2) Chikungunya (viral, by Aedes aegypti).

3) Malaria (protozoal disease, by Anopheles).

4) Filariasis (helminthic disease).

Q. Mention the control measures of mosquito, [DU-10J, CU-18N,16J,15J,10J, SUST-16N, 13J]

Q. What are the control measures of mosquito at Dhaka city [DU-15J] / hill tracts [RU-14Ju]?
Q. Write down the vector control measures for malaria, [CU-I Ju]

yet Personal protective measures for disease prevention, [DU-17N]

Mosquito control measures;

A) Anti-larval measures:

1) Environmental control: Elimination of the breeding places (source reduction) of
Mosquitoes is the most important step.
2) Chemical control: .
> Mineral oils: Diesel oil, kerosene, other crude oil, mosquito larvicidal oil (MLO).
> Paris green: It is copper acetoarsenite which should contain 50% arsenous oxide kills
mainly the Anopheles larva.
> Synthetic insecticides: Abate, Malathion, Fenthion, Chloropyrifor.

3) Biological control: Guppy fish can be used in burrow pits sewage oxidation ponds, ornamental
ponds, cisterus and farm pond as guppy fish feed on mosquito larval.

B) Anti-adult measures:
1) Residual sprays: Adult mosquitoes are most effectively controlled by spraying houses with
residual insecticide such as- DDT, Lindane, Malathion, OMAS-33.
2) Space sprays: Insecticide is sprayed into the atmosphere in the form of a mist or fog to kill
Mosquito. The common space sprays- Pyrethrum extract, Malathion, Fenitrothion.
3) Genetic control;
Male sterilization
Chromosomal translocation.
> Sex distortion.
> Gene replacement
> Cytoplasmic incompatibility.

Vv

C) Protection against mosquito bites / personal protection:

1) Mosquito net: White, rectangular net.

2) Screening of buildings with copper or bronze gauze.
3) Repellents

Diethyltoluamide

Q. Why organochloride compound is not suitable for larviciding operations? [DU-10J]
Answer
Organochloride compound (e.g. DDT, HCH) is not suitable for larviciding operation, because of:
1) Their long residual effect,
2) Water contamination and

3) Increased risk of developing resistance in the vector mosquitoes.

Viva Q. A knowledge of breeding habits is required for conducting mosquito control operation.
-Why?
Answer
A knowledge of breeding habits is required for conducting mosquito control operation: Source reduction
Tequires an accurate knowledge of the breeding habits of mosquitoes. t
> IfCulex mosquitoes are a problem: There should be a programme for the abolition of domestic
and peridomestic sources of breeding such as cesspools and open ditches; and arrangements should
be made for adequate collection, removal and disposal of sewage and waste water,
> IfAedes mosquitoes are a problem: The environment should be cleaned up and got rid of water
holding containers such as discarded tins, empty pots, broken bottles, coconut shells and similar
other artificial collection of water.
> If Anopheles mosquitoes are a problem: There breeding places should be looked for and
abolished by appropriate engineering measures such as filling and drainage.
> IfMansonia mosquitoes are a problem: The aquatic plants to which the larvae attach themselves
should be removed or destroyed by herbicides.

Source reduction method generally produces results that are permanent.

Q. Discuss habits of houseflies. _
Q. Illustrate the relation between habit of house fly and disease transmission. [RU-14J]
Answer

Mi :
Breeding habits: The most important breeding places of flies in order of importance are —

i. Fresh horse manure

ii.Human excreta

iii. Manure of other animals

iv. Garbage

v. Decaying fruits and vegetables

vi. Rubbish dumps containing organic matter

vii. Ground where liquid wastes are spilled.

2. Feeding habits: The housefly does not bite. It is attracted to food by its sense of smell. It can not eat
solid foods. It vomits on solid food to make a solution of it and sucks in a liquid state. Adult flies
delight in sputum, faeces, discharges from wounds and open sores.

3. Restlessness: The fly is a restless insect and moves back and forth between food and filth. This helps in
the spread of infection mechanically,

4. Vomit drop: The fly vomits frequently. The 'vomit drop’ is often a culture of disease agents.

5. Defecation: The fly has the habit of defecating constantly all the day. Thus it deposits countless
bacteria on exposed food.

6. Resting habits: Flies have a tendency to rest on vertical surfaces and hanging objects. They have a
tendency to fly towards light.

7. Dispersal: Normally houseflies remain close to their breeding places, but they disperse frequently up to
4 miles, and sometimes even more from the point of their origin.

[Ref- Park /24"/ 811]

Q. Discuss transmission of diseases by houseflies.
Q. How house fly acts as a vector in context of communicable disease? [DU-15Ju]
Answer
Mechanism of disease transmission by house flies:
1) Mechanical transmission: they transport micro-organisms on their feet and hairy legs. House flies
are called porters of infection.
2) Vomit drop: The regurgitated stomach content or vomit drop is a rich bacterial culture. By its habit
the house fly infects food and thereby transmits disease.
3) Defecation: The excrement of housefly has been found to contain numerous micro-organisms as

well as cysts and ova of intestinal parasites.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 811]
