Q. Describe the life cycle of sand fly.
Answer
Life cycle of sand fly: The life cycle of sand fly is characterized by
complete metamorphosis, e.g. having following four stages-
1) Egg: The eggs are laid in damp dark places in the vicinity of
cattle sheds and poultry.
2) Larva: They are hairy maggots with a distinct head and
become pupa in about 2 weeks.
3) Pupa: This stage lasts for about | week.
4) Adult: The average life of a sand fly is about 2 weeks,

[Ref- Park /24" / 812]

Figure: Adult sand fly.

Q. Mention habits of sand fly.
Answer
Habits of sand fly:
1) They infest dwellings during night and take shelter during day in holes and crevices in walls, wholes in
trees, dark rooms, stables and store rooms.
2) The females alone bite and their bite is irritating and painful.
3) They are incapable of flying over long distances, they merely hope about from one place to another.
4) They are generally confined to within 50 yards of their breeding places.

[Ref- Park /24"/ 812]

Q. How to control sand fly in a community? [DU-16J,13Ju]
Q. Outline the control measures of sand fly. [RU-11Ju]
Q. Write down the vector control measures for kala-azar. [CU-1 Ju]
Answer
Control of sand flies:
Sand flies are easily controlled because they do not move long distances from the place of heir

breeding.

(1) Insecticides: Resistance to DDT has not been demonstrated. A single application of 1 to 2 g/m2 of
DDT or 0.25 g/m? of lindane has been found effective in reducing sand flies. DDT residue may
remain effective for a period of | to 2 years, and lindane only for a period of 3 months. Spraying
should be done in the human dwellings, cattle sheds and other places.

(2) Sanitation: Sanitation measures such as removal of shrubs and vegetation within 50 yarns of

dwells, filling up cracks and crevices in walls and floors, and location of cattle sheds and poultry
houses at a fair distance from human habitations should receive attention.

Q. What is the public health importance of “blocked fleas”? [RU-17M]
Q. Enumerate epidemiological importance of blocked flea. [CU-12J] |
Q. Write short note on: Blocked fleas. |
Answer |
Blocked flea:

A flea may ingest up to 0.5 cu mm of blood which may contain as many as 5,000 plague bacilli. The
bacilli multiply enormously in the gut of the rat flea and may block the proventriculus so that no food can pass
through. Such a flea is called a "blocked flea". A blocked flea eventually faces starvation and death it is unable
to obtain a blood meal. It makes frantic efforts to bite and suck blood over and over again; and in so doing, it
inoculates (regurgitates) plague bacilli into the bite wound each time it bites.

A partially blocked flea:
It is more dangerous than a completely blocked flea because it can live longer. Infected fleas may live

up to a year, and certain species survive in the burrow microclimate for as long as 4 years.
[Ref- Park /24™ / 816]

Q. What are the different types of louse?
Answer
Types of louse:

1) Head louse (Pediculus capitus)

2) Body louse (Pediculus corporis)

3) Pubic or crab louse (Phthirus pubis)

[Ref- Park /24"/814] |
Q. Discuss stages in the life history of lice.

Answer
Life history of lice:

Figure: Life cycle of a louse.

There are three stages in the life history of lice: egg, larva & adult. Metamorphosis is gradual.

(1) Egg: The eggs called “nits” are laid singly or in groups, firmly attached to the hair or seams of clothing
by a cementing substance. The eggs are small, white ovoid bodies, pointed at one end and truncated and
pitted at the other end. A female lays upto 300 eggs at the rate of 4 to 9 a day. Under favourable
conditions of temperature, the eggs will hatch in 6 to 9 days. The eggs will not hatch if the temperature
is below 22°C.

(2) Larva or nymph: The larva looks very much like an adult, except for its smaller size. It feeds on the
host and develops into an adult after passing through 3 moults. The larval stage may take 10 to 15 days.

(3) Adult: The entire life cycle from the laying of an egg to the appearance of the adult louse takes about
15 to 17 days under favourable conditions. Adult lice live from 30 to 50 days.

[Ref- Park /24"/814]

Itch mite & Scabies

Q. Describe itch mite.

Q. Define scabies.

Answer

Itch mite / Sarcoptes scabiei | Acarus scabiei:

The itch mite (Sarcoptes scabiei or Acarus scabiei) is an extremely small, globular arthropod just
visible to the naked eye. The female parasite burrows into the epidermis where it breeds and causes the
condition known as scabies or itch.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 818]

Q. What are the main diagnostic features of scabies?
Answer
Main diagnostic features of scabies are:
1) Intense itching at night.
2) More than one member in the family has affected in adults,
3) Face and scalp are not usually affected in adults.
4) Itching of nipples in female and itching papules in males of penis or scrotum.
5) Examination reveals follicular lesion at the affected site.
6) Secondary infection leads to crusted papules and pustules.
7) Confirmatory diagnosis — Searching of parasite in skin debris under microscope.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5 / 289 + Park / 24" / 819]

Q. Discuss control measures of scabies. [DU-10Ju, CU-17M,13J]
Q. Write short note on: Control of scabies. [SUST-18N]
Answer
Controls of scabies:
1) Sanitation control:
a) Improvement of personal hygiene.
b) Allaffected persons of a family should be treated simultaneously.
c) Affected children should be excluded from the school until the day after treatment.
d) Before treatment all patients should have a good soap and warm water bath.

2) Chemical control (treatment of scabies patient):
a)

Benzyl benzoate (25%) emulsion- smeared all over the body from neck to feet except face
and genital areas for successive days. Application should be repeated after 12 hours and
after a further 12 hours a bath should be taken.

b) Permethrin cream (5%).

c) Monosulfiram (Tetmosol) (5%) - thrice daily applications.

d) Sulphur ointment (2.5 to 10%): Daily for 4 days.

School health service

Q. Define school health service.
Answer

School health service:
The school health service is a personal health service delivering comprehensive health care service to
the school students and school personnel throughout the school years.

[Ref- Park /24" /614)

Q. Write down the importance of school health programme / school health services.

Answer

Importance of school health service / school health programme:

1. To control communicable disease among the students.

2. It is important place of learning.

3. Itis the formative period, where what you educate the children they will practice then in adulthood.

Qbjectives of school health services:

“* General objectives: To provide comprehensive health care — promotive, preventive, curative &
rehabilitative — to school students in order to prepare them physically, mentally and socially for entry
into adulthood as a step towards achieving the goal of ‘Health For All’.

“* Specific objectives:
1) The promotion of positive health,

2) The prevention of disease.

3) Early diagnosis, treatment and follow up of defects.
4) Awakening health consciousness in children.

5) The provision of healthful environment.

Q. Write down the importance of school health services. [SUST-10J]
Answer

Importance of school health service / school health programme:

1) The health of the school children is a common concern of the school, parents and the community.

2) Achild has to be healthy to learn, and the school is an important place, next to home, where a child
learns to be healthy.

3) Atthe time of entering the school, the children are in the most formative period.

4) the schools represent gathering places for a population of age $ — 17 years, which is particularly
prone and susceptible to many communicable diseases and vulnerable physical, mental and moral
hazards with which the students may come in contact in conception with their school experience.

5) Moreover, a considerable proportion of school children particularly in the underdeveloped and
developing countries, suffer from malnutrition and deficiency diseases and as such they naturally
deserve special attention for their physical and intellectual development.

Periodic medical examination

Q. What do you mean by periodic medical examination?
Answer
Periodic medical examination:

_ Periodic medical examination means periodic physical examination or screening of students to
determine their health and nutritional status, for early detection of physical, behavioral and mental health
problems and intelligent quotient (1Q) by the medical officer, assisted by the public health nurse.

Frequency of examination:

The frequency of such examinations will vary according to the workload. However screening by the
health professionals should be performed, at least three times — once during the first year of enrollment at the
primary level and thereafter once in 2 to 3 years during their school life.

Examination includes:
The initial examination should be through and should include a careful history and physical
examination of the child, with tests for vision, hearing and speech.
A routine examination of blood and urine should be carried out.
Clinical examination for nutritional deficiency and examination of faeces for intestinal parasites are particularly
important. ‘
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5" / 183 + Park / 24" / 615]

Q. What is health appraisal? [DU-10Ju]

Q. What do you mean by health appraisal in school health?

Answer

Health appraisal: Health appraisal consists of periodic medical examinations and observation of children by
the class teacher. The health appraisal should cover not only the students but also the teachers and other school
personnel. It includes —

Periodic medical examinations.

Medical examination of the teachers and other school personnel.

Daily morning inspection.

Uses of school desk: They are used in schools for the following reasons:

General activities:

1) School health programme (SHP) will conduct training for school teachers, one from each school
(primary, secondary and madrasa). The priority topics to be included in the training are safe water,
sanitation, personal hygiene and first aid. . . .

2) Two medical officers and four support stuff, assigned to each school health clinic will provide services
to the school children at the clinic as well as the nearby schools. .

3) SHP will provide preventive, promotive, limited curative (first aid) services, and health education
tegarding personal and environmental hygiene. . .

4) A referral system will be developed to provide curative services through the existing health facilities,
Every student will be provided with a ‘health card’ and ‘referral form’.

5) Inaddition to the on-going activities, the following will be implemented through SHP —

> Deworming of school children at Community Clinics, UHF WCs / RDs at union level and
UHCs at upazila level using albendazole 400 mg single dose.

> Promotion and monitoring of iodized salt consumption through one-day workshop /
dissemination seminar at the union and thana levels.

> Strengthening of child nutritional activities by promoting breast feeding, improving weaning
practices, and through the distribution of vitamin A capsules and multivitamin tablets at the
community, union and upazila levels.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5" / 187]

Q. What is deworming? [CU-12Ju]
Answer

Deworming:
Deworming is the giving of an anthelmintic drug to an individual to rid him/her of intestinal parasites.

Q. How school health service developed in Bangladesh?
Answer
Development of school health service in Bangladesh:

Following the preparation of a Master Plan in 1993 for the development of a comprehensive and viable
School Health Programme in the country, the project proforma was signed in June 1996 for the implementation
of School Health Pilot Project (SHPP) in 4 districts under the World Bank's Fourth Population Project.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4/168]

Mid-day meal programme

Mid-day meal programme:

The mid-day programme (MSMP) is also known as School Lunch Programme. The major objective of
the programme is to attract more children for admission to schools and retain them so that literacy improvement
of children could be brought about,

Q. What is mid-day school meal?
Answer
Mid-day school meal:

In order to combat malnutrition and improve the health of school children, it is now an accepted
procedure in all advanced countries to provide a good nursing meal to school children on a ‘no profit no loss’
bias. It is the mid-day school meal.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 698]

Q. Write down the criteria of mid-day school meal. [RU-17M, SUST-18N, 1 5Ju,13J,11J, CU-16N]
Answer
Criteria of a mid-day school meal:
1) The meal should be a supplement and not a substitute to the home diet.
2) The meal should supply at least one third of the total energy requirement, and half of the
protein need.
3) The cost of the meal should be reasonable low.
4) The meal should be such that it can be prepared easily in schools, no complicated cooking process
should be involved.
5) As far as possible, locally available foods should be used in the menu with a view to reduce the cost
of the meal and
6) The menu should be frequently changed to avoid monotony.

Handicap may be intrinsic or extrinsic.
Intrinsic > e.g. blindness
Extrinsic — e.g. loss of parents

Classification: 3 types,
A) Physically handicapped; e.g. blind, deaf and mute.
Causes:
1) Birth defect.
2) Infections.
3) Accidents.

B) Mentally handicapped: e.g. mental retardation.
Causes:
1) Genetic condition: e.g. Down’s syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome etc.
2) Antenatal factors: e.g. neural tube defect, Rh incompatibility etc.
3) Perinatal factors: e.g. birth injuries. . . i
4) Postnatal factors: e.g. head injuries, accidents, encephalitis, physical and chemical
agents such as lead and mercury poisoning may result in mental retardation.
5) Miscellaneous: e.g. maternal malnutrition, PEM, iodine deficiency etc.

C) Socially handicapped: e.g. parental inadequacy, environmental deprivation etc.

Prevention:
1) Primary prevention:

a
> Genetic counseling.

> Identification of the people at risk.

> Immunization against poliomyelitis, rubella etc.

> Nutrition. ;

> Others: Health care of mothers and children through pre-natal, natal and post-natal periods.

2) Secondary prevention (management):

> Early diagnosis of handicap.
> Treatment.

> Training and education. as
[Ref- Park / 24” / 618]

For viva:

Categories of mental retardation:

Mild mental retardation > IQ = 70-50
Moderate mental retardation > 1Q = 49 — 35
Severe mental retardation + IQ = 34 - 20
Profound mental retardation + IQ = Under 20
[Ref- Park / 24" / 618]

Q. One of the family members of an extended family norm is mentally handicapped. How this
wretched fellow should be managed in that family?

Answer

Management of handicapped children (secondary prevention):

The broad objective for all children whatever their condition or problem is to bring them as close to

normality as possible — physically, mentally and socially. This will involve —

(a) Early diagnosis of handicap: Parents themselves have the responsibility to bring the child to
paediatrician and seek advice, Investigation of the child requires full history, assessment of the
degree of handicap and perhaps special investigations including the natural potentialities of the
child. This should be done through MCH and school health services and such other agencies.

(b) Treatment: Handicapped children need specialized treatment. The purpose of treatment is to
improve the physical condition of the patient.

Q. Define demography. [DU-10Ju, RU-16M, CU-12Ju,10Ju, seal be ee val
Q. Define demography with its observable phenomena. [SUST-18N,17N, 16J,
Peale! Demography is the scientific study of human population) which mainly concentrates on —
/\)_ Changes in population size (growth or decline) ;
2) The composition of the population (age, sex, ethnic groups etc.) and
P) The distribution of population in space (urban, rural etc.).

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"/ 190 + Park /24" /513]

Q. List the uses of demography. [RU-10J]
Q. What are the uses of demographic data?
Answer
Uses of demography:
1) Demography focuses its attention to three readily observable human phenomena —
> Changes in population size (growth or decline)
> The composition of the population (age, sex, ethnic groups etc.) and
> The distribution of population in space (urban, rural etc.).

2) Itdeals with five demographic processes namely fertility, mortality, marriage, migration and social
mobility. These five processes are continuously at work within a population determining size,
composition and distribution. .

3) The health and healthcare needs of a population cannot be measured or met without a knowledge of
demography.

4) The knowledge of demography is a prerequisite for making forecasts about future population size
and structure, which should underpin healthcare planning. .

5) Demography is largely concerned with answering questions about how population change and how
its changes can be measured.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5" / 190 + Park /24"/513]

Q. Explain the stages of demographic cycle where the population growth remains static.
Answer

|
Stages of demographic cycle where the population remain static: |
1) 1I''stage (high stationary): This stage is characterized by a high birth rate and a high death rate |

which cancel each other and the population remains stationary, ¢.g. India was in this stage till 1920. |

2) 4" stage (low stationary): In this stage, both birth rate and death rate fall. As a result, the growth
of population becomes stationary, €.g. UK, Denmark, Sweden, Belgium etc.

Stages of demographic cycle where population growth is not static:

leading to increase in population growth. A number of countries in south Asia & Africa are in this |

stage.
2) 3° stage (late expanding): Death rate declines still further, and the birth rate tends to fall. The
population continues to grow, because births exceed deaths, e.g. Bangladesh, India, China,
Singapore etc. ;

Q. What are the salient features of population growth?
Answer

Salient features of population growth:
> Approximately 95% of this growth is occurring in developing countries.

> Currently, one third of the world’s population is under the age of 15 years and will soon enter the
reproductive bracket, giving more potential for the population growth.

> The UNFPA estimates that world population is more likely to near double to 10 billion people in
2050, peaking at 11.6 billion reaching 20.7 billion a century later.

> The expected number of birth per woman, at current fertility rate, is: Africa 6.1, Latin America 2.0,
Europe 1.6.

> World population is currently going at 176 people per minute, 10564 people per hour, 25,35,425

people per day, and 9,25,43,000 people per year.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4" / 172]

Q. What are the causes of declining death rate?
Answer

Causes of declining death rate:

1) Absence of natural checks, e.g. famines, and large-scale epidemics.

2) Mass control of disease, e.g. smallpox, plague, cholera, malaria etc. :
3) Advances in medical science, e.g. extensive use of chemotherapeutics, antibiotics and insecticides.

4) Better health facilities, e.g. establishment of primary health centers and more treatment centers.
5) Impact of national health programmes.

6) Improvements in food supply.

7) International aid in several directions.

8) Development of social consciousness among the masses.
[Ref- Park /21"/54]

Q. Define life table. [RU-10J]
Q. What are the uses of life table?

Answer
Life table: It is an effective method in measuring the force of mortality in a population.

Uses of life table:
1) It enables one to calculate the average life time a person can expect to live after any age.

2) To study population growth and to forecast size and age distribution of population at a future date.
3) Estimation of compensation for injury or death in an industry.

4) To measure the risk of certain infectious disease.

5) To forecast the school-going population in connection with school building programme.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4" / 122, 123]

Q. Brilliant children of Bangladesh go abroad for higher study and after completion of study,
never return in country. What problems will result for the families and the country
ultimately? [CU-18N]

Answer

Problems may include one or combination of the followings:

> The country will be deprived from the service of these students.
> The country will lose its meritorious students as they get attracted by foreign countries with
lucrative benefits abroad.

> The country has invested a lot in these students with little or no return in terms of money and other
resources.

> Their families will be deprived and social insecurity may arise, as it is difficult for the older
people to migrate.

> When the students settle in other countries, many of them may adopt foreign culture that will in
tum affect values and other family norms.

Q. Explain NRR.
Q. Illustrate the importance of Net Reproduction Rate. [RU-10J]

Q. State NRR with the demographic significance of NRR = 1. [RU-13Ju]
Q. Illustrate the importance of Net Reproduction Rate (NRR). [RU-10J]

Answer
Net Reproduction Rate (NRR): It is defined as the number of daughters a newborn girl will bear during her

lifetime assuming fixed age-specific fertility and mortality rates.

Importance of NRR:
1) NRR is a demographic indicator.

2) NRRof 1 is equivalent to attaining approximately the 2-child norm.
3) If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be below

replacement level.

Q. What is total fertility rate (TFR)?
Answer

Total fertility rate (TFR):

It is the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her reproductive
years bearing children at the same rates as the women now in each age group.

Importance: TFR is considered as refined measure of fertility; it gives the approximate magnitude of
“completed family size”.

Q. Define f, wily planning. [RU-15J]

F planning: P “ inki ivi
An Expert Committee (1971) of the WHO defined family planning as “a way of thinking and living that

is adopted voluntarily, upon the basis of knowledge, attitudes and responsible decisions by individuals and
couples, in order to promote the health and welfare of the family group and thus contribute effectively to the

social development of a country.”
[Ref- Park /24" /525]

Concept of family planning:

> Earlier concept — birth control.

> Modem concept > family welfare.
Q. Write down the objectives of family planning. [CU-10Ju, RU-12Ju, SUST-17N,12J,11J]
Answer

Objectives of family planning:
1) To avoid unwanted births
2) To bring about wanted births
3) To regulate the intervals between pregnancies.
4) To control the time at which births occur in relation to the ages of the parent.
5) To determine the number of children in the family.

r. [Ref- Park / 24" /525]

: A WHO Expert Committee (1970)
as stated that family planning includes in its purview:

1) The proper spacing & limitation of births.

2) Advice on sterility.

3) Education for parenthood.

4) Sex education

5) Screening for pathological conditions related to the reproductive system (e.g. cervical cancer).

6) Genetic counseling.

7) Premarital consultation and examination.

8) Carrying out pregnancy tests.

9) Marriage counseling.

10) The preparation of couples for the arrival of their Ist child.

11) Providing services for unmarried mothers.

12) Teaching home economics & nutrition.

13) Providing adoption services.

—_ hd activities vary from country to country according to national objectives and policies with regard
mily planning. This is the modern concept of family planning,

[Ref- Park / 24" /525]

Q. Mention the health outcomes of family planning. [RU-10Ju]

Q. How family planning can improve health of women and children?
Answer

Health outcomes of family planning:

Women’s health:

Family planning, by intervening in the reproductive cycle of women, helps them to control the number,
interval and timing of pregnancies and births, and thereby reduces maternal mortality and morbidity and
improves health. The health impact of family planning occurs primarily through —

1) The avoidance of unwanted pregnancies.

2) Limiting the number of births and proper spacing.

3) Timing the births, particularly the first and last, in relation to the age of the mother.

Child health:
It would seem that family size and birth spacing, if practiced by all, will yield substantial child health
benefits. These are —
1. Child mortality: A birth interval of 2 - 3 years is considered desirable to reduce child mortality.
Family planning is, therefore, an important means of insuring the survival of all children in a family.
2. Child growth, development & nutrition: The child is likely to receive his full share of love and care,
including nutrition he needs, when the family size is small and births are properly spaced. Family
planning, in other words, is effective prevention against malnutrition.
3. Infectious diseases: Children living in large sized families have an increase in infection, especially
infectious gastroenteritis, respiratory and skin infections.
4. Intelligence: Studies have shown a lower IQ scores among children in larger families.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 525]

Answer

Norplant / subdermal implant: .
It is subdermal long term temporary hormonal contraceptive.

Effectiveness: 5 years.

Composition: It consists 6 silastic (silicone rubber) capsules, Each capsule contains 35 mg levonorgestrel. Each

Q. Discuss medical termination of pregnancy.

Answer
Conditions under which medical termination of pregnancy is conducted:
1) Medical: Where continuation of pregnancy might endanger the mother’s life or cause grave injury

to her physical or mental health.
2) Eugenic: Where there is substantial risk of the child being born with serious handicaps due to

4) Socio-economic: Where actual or reasonably foreseeable (whether social or economic) could lead

Miscellaneous contraceptive methods

Q. State the natural methods of family planning (FP), [SUST-14Ju/J]
Answer |
Natural family planning methods: |
1) Basal body temperature (BBT) method: Basal body temperature is the lowest body temperature
ofa healthy person during waking hours. By noting temperature daily and by recording temperature
to successive 3-4 months a woman may determine her time of ovulation. From 24-72 hours after
ovulation a noticeable rise (0.3 — 0.5° C) in temperature occurs. |

2) Cervical mucus method / Billings method / ovulation method: In some women changes in the
character and appearance of cervical secretion and cervix occur just before ovulation. In addition

women may experience ovulatory pain. Observation of these physiological changes can help a Hi
woman to determine her period in the cycle. . i

3) Sympto-thermic method: This method combines 3 fertility awareness methods such as calendar
method, BBT method and the mucus method to identify the fertile period.

[Ref- Park /24" / 542]

Q. Write down the merits & demerits of safe period. [DU-16M]
Answer

Safe period / Rhythm method / Calendar method:
It aims at finding out the time during which a viable ovum is available for fertilization by sperm.

Principle:
> Usually, ovulation takes place at 14" day of menstrual cycle (range: 12 — 16 days).

vum survives 48 hours after ovulation.
Sperm survives 72 hours after ejaculation. |

ulation of safe period:

Ina regular menstrual cycle (28 days)

Y 28-18 = 10th day is the Ist day of the fertile period (1st unsafe day)
Y 28-10 = 18th day is the last day of the fertile period (last unsafe day)

So the total unsafe days are from 10th to 18th day of the menstrual cycle = 9 days
only. All other days before and after the unsafe days are the safe period. |

“ Inan irregular menstrual cycle (26 to 31 days):
Y 26 - 18 = 8th days is the Ist day of the fertile period (Ist unsafe day)
Y 31-10 =2lst day is the last day of the fertile period (last unsafe day)

So the total unsafe days are from 8th to 21st day of the menstrual cycle = 14 days.
All other days before and after the unsafe days are the safe period.

Merits / advantages of safe period:

1) Natural,
2) No cost,
3) Equal participation in sexual act.

1) Need patient education & responsibility,

2) Need abstinence of 9-14 days in a menstrual cycle,

Q. Discuss the traditional family planning methods.
Q. How breast feeding acts as a contraceptive measure?
Answer

Traditional family planning methods: . . .
1. Coitus interruptus: This is the oldest method of fertility control. It continues to be a widely practiced

method. The male withdraws before ejaculation and thereby tries to prevent deposition of semen into
the vagina. The chief drawback of this method is that precoital secretion. If the male may contain sperm
and even a drop of semen is sufficient to cause pregnancy. Therefore the failure rate with this method

may be as high as 25%.

2. Abstinence: Although in theory sexual abstinence is the most effective method in family planning but
in practice it cannot be recommended because it amounts to suppression of a biological need.

3. Breast feeding (lactational amenorrhoea method for 6 month): Numerous studies have documented

the fact that lactation prolongs postpartum amenorrhoea and provide considerable protection against
pregnancy. This is an important method in those countries where prolonged breast-feeding is widely
practiced. In Bangladesh mean duration of breast feeding is about 24 months.

4. Sex without coitus: This non-coital form of sexual intimacy relates to holding of hands hugging,
kissing, massage, mutual masturbation, petting, oral-genital sex and use of stimulation device such as
vibrators etc.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 200]

Q. Write short note on: Birth control vaccine.
Answer
Birth control vaccine:

The vaccine is prepared from beta- subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone produced in
early pregnancy. Immunization with hCGH would block continuation of pregnancy. Antibodies appeared in
about 4 to 6 weeks and reach maximum after about 5 months and reach zero level within 6 to 11 months. The
immunity can be boosted by a second injection.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 542]

Q. Discuss causes of failure of vasectomy,
Answer
Causes of failure of vasectomy:

1) The most common cause of failure is due to the mistaken identification of the vas. That is, instead of
the vas, some other structure in the spermatic cord such as thrombosed vein or thickened lymphatic
has been taken.

2) In some cases, failure may be due to spontaneous recanalisation of vas.

3) Sometimes there may be more than one vas on one side.

4) Pregnancy could also result from sexual intercourse before the disappearance of sperms from the

reproductive tract.
[Ref- Park /24" / 543]

Q. What is MCH package care?
Answer
MCH - package care: . ;

It is package programme for delivering health care to special group i.e. woman in the reproduction age
group (15 — 44/49 years) & children under the age 5 years in the population, which is especially vulnerable to
disease, disability or death. ;

The MCH package services encompass the curative, preventive and social aspects of obstetrics, family
welfare, nutrition, child development and health education.

Q. Mention the new concepts of MCH care. a
Answer \a

New concepts / recent trends in MCH care:

1) Integration of care: The integration is based on the fact that it is inconvenient for the mother to go
to one place to receive care for herself, to another for care for her children, and yet another for her

family planning services. An integrated approach implies that all those involved in maternity care

from the obstetrician down to the local dai, must work as a team.

Risk approach: It is based on the early detection of mothers and children with high risk factors and

are given additional and more skilled care including hospitalization.

3) Manpower changes: A wide range of works are now considered necessary for maternal and child
health work. They include —

Q. Write short note on: MCH based family planning.
he How Bangladesh can achieve MCH based family planning?
nswer

MCH based family planning:

> Itis the family planning service when its delivery is made to the consumer through the units which
usually deliver maternity and child health care. In short, it is the integration of mother and child

health and family planning services.
> Family planning will be highly effective if it is based at MCH centres. Because on these centres are

attended by mothers before, during and after delivery. During these stages mothers and women can
be better motivated in the MCH centres women are accompanied by their husband, so both of them
can be motivated together.

> It is inconvenient for the mother to go to one place to receive care for herself to another place for
care of her children and yet to another place for family planning.

> Family Planning services were being given from existing hospitals, clinics and specially established
family planning clinics. This was a sort of duplication of service, separate establishment, separate
staff, different places.

> Mothers are directly exposed to the risks of child birth, so family planning motivation are more
important for them child care is indirectly related with family planning. With these ideas in the

background came o. the concept of MCH based family planning.
> Now most of the family planning services are being delivered from MCH centers where the same

groups staff are looking after the health of the mother, children and also family planning affairs.
This is definitely beneficial for the government as well as consumers.

For viva:

} “> Importance MCH service:
1) The child bearing mother 22.3% and under five children 15-20% constitute more than 40% of

total population.
2) They are more vulnerable or high- risk group.
3) The infants, under 5 children and maternal mortality rate are very high in developing Countries.

In Bangladesh MMI 3.0/1000 live birth and IMR = 57/1000 (both sex) live birth.
4) By improving the health of mothers and children, we can contribute to the health of total

population or nation.

ist the objectives of antenatal care. [DU-17M, CU-12Ju, RU-18N,16N,13J, SUST-11J]

Objectives of antenatal care:

1) To promote, protect and maintain the health of the mother during pregnancy.

2) To detect “high-risk” cases & give them special attention.

3) To foresee complications and prevent them.

4) To remove anxiety and dread associated with delivery.

5) To reduce maternal and infant mortality and morbidity.

6) To teach the mother elements of child care, nutrition, personal hygienic and environmental
sanitation.

7) To sensitize the mother to the need for famil
termination of pregnancy.
8) To attend to the under-fives accompanying the mother.

Q. Narrate the role of ANC in high risk mothers. [CU-18N]
Answer
High-risk pregnancy (high risk mother):
High-risk mother is defined as one which is complicated by factor or factors that adversely affect the
pregnancy outcome (maternal or perinatal or both).

Criteria of high-risk mother:
1) Elderly primi (30 years & over).

2) Short stature primi (140 cm & below).

3) Malpresentation (e.g. breech presentation, transverse lie etc.).

4) Antepartum hemorrhage, threatened abortion.

5) Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.

6) Anaemia.

7) Twins, polyhydramnios.

8) Previous still-birth, intrauterine death, manual removal of placenta.

9) Elderly grand multiparas.

10) Prolonged pregnancies (14 days after expected date of delivery).

11) History of previous caesarean or instrumental delivery.

12) Pregnancy associated with general diseases, e.g. cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, diabetes,
tuberculosis, liver disease etc.

13) Treatment for infertility.

14) Thrge or more spontaneous consecutive abortions.

Q. Write down the aims of intranatal care. [CU-11Ju]
Q. What are the aims of good intranatal care?
Answer

Aims of good intranatal care:
1) Thorough asepsis.
2) Delivery with minimum injury to the infant and mother.
3) Readiness to deal with complications such as prolonged labour, antepartum haemorrhage,
convulsions, malpresentations, prolapse of the cord ete.
4) Care of the baby at delivery — resuscitation, care of the cord, care of the eyes, etc.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 564]

Q. State the principles of intranatal care.
Answer

Principles of intranatal care:
1) Prevention of infection.
2) Prevention of dehydration and ketosis of the mother.
3) Relief of pain.
4) Prevention of trauma.
5) Prevention of post-partum haemorrhage (PPH).

Q. Write short note on: Domiciliary midwifery service. .
Q. Illustrate the advantages and disadvantages of domiciliary midwifery services. [RU-13Ju]

Answer

Domiciliary midwifery service:
Mothers with normal obstetric history may be advised to have their confinement in their own homes,
provided the home conditions are satisfactory.
In such cases, the delivery may be conducted by the Health Worker Female or trained dai. This is
known as “domiciliary midwifery service”.

Advantages of domiciliary midwifery service:
1) The mother deliver in the familiar surroundings of her home and this may tend to remove the fear
associated with delivery in a hospital.

2) The chances for cross infection are generally fewer at home than in the hospital.
3) The mother is able to keep an eye upon her children and domestic affairs; this may tend to ease her
mental tension.

Disadvantages of domiciliary midwifery service:
1) The mother may have less medical and nursing supervision than in the hospital.
2) The mother may have less rest.
3) She may resume her domestic duties too soon.
4) Her diet may be neglected.

Q. Name some genital tract infections that can be harmful for fetus?

R What are the public health importances of low birth weight baby? [SUST-14Ju]
Q. Write short note on: Low birth weight (LBW) babies. [SUST-18N,17N, 13J]

ZL
Answer

Low birth weight (LBW) baby: A birth weight of less than 2.5 kg (up to and including 2499 gm).
The measurement being taken preferably within the Ist hour of life, before significant postnatal weight

~  loss‘has occurred.
fas of LBW: It may be of two types —
1) Pre-term babies: When the baby born before completed 37 weeks (259 days) of gestation. Their
intrauterine growth may be normal.

2) Small-for-date babies (SFD): Birth weight less than 10th percentile for the gestational age.

Public health importance / Importance of LBW:

Its high incidence is related to a high risk of perinatal & infant mortality and morbidity.

It is the single most important factor determining the survival changes of the child.

The infant mortality rate is about 20 times greater for all LBW babies than for other babies.

LBW is an important guide to the level of care needed by individual babies.

LBW reflects inadequate nutrition & ill health of the mother,

A high percentage of LBW points to deficient health status of pregnant woman inadequate, prenatal
care & the need for improved care of the newborn.

SEAS BIS)

[Ref- Park /24" /570]

For viva:
* Apart from birth weight, babies can also be classified into 3 groups according to gestational age.
1) Pre-term babies: Babies born before the end of 37 weeks gestation (less than 259 days)
2) Term babies: Babies born from 37 completed weeks to less than 42 completed weeks (259-
293 days) of gestation.
3) Post-term babies: Babies at 42 completed weeks any time thereafter (294 days & over) of
gestation.

“Babies weighing less than 1501 gm are designated as very low birth weight babies (VLBW).

For Viva
* Key elements in child survival programme:
The UNICEF has put forward a set of 7 strategies for child health ‘revolution’ popularly known

as GOBIFFF.
G = Growth monitoring (by using growth chart)
O = Oral Rehydration (to treat all mild and moderate dehydration)
B = Breast feeding to nourish and protect the young infant from infection.
I = Immunization (against 6 communicable diseases)
F = Female education.
F = Food supplementation
F = Family spacing/ planning.
Previously the campaign was limited within the Ist 4 strategies and it was known as 4
key elements of child survival.

* Baby friendly hospital initiative (BFHI): :
nurses, health

In 1993 UNICEF & WHO launched the baby friendly initiative annalist doctor,
worker & parent's in hospital & maternity centers to promote, protect & support breast feedings.

Objectives: To reestablish the superiority of breast feeding in order to protect the health by becoming
friendly to the baby.

WHO & UNICEF criteria: 10 steps which the hospital must fulfill —

1) Helping the mother initiate breast feeding within the first hour of birth in normal delivery
and four hours following caesarean section.

2) Encourage breast feeding on demand.

3) Allow mothers and infants to remain together 24 hours a day, except for medical reasons.

4) Give newborn infants no food or drink, other than breast milk unless medically indicated.

5) Exclusive breast feeding should be promoted till 4 — 6 months of age.

6) No advertisement, promotional material or free products for infant feeding should be
allowed in the facility.

7) Show mother how to breast feed and how to maintain lactation even if she is separated
from her infant.

8) Give no artificial teats or pacifiers (also called dummies or soothers) to breast feeding
infants.

9) Encourage mothers to assists each other and to develop breast feeding support groups.

10) Nursing staff should be available to counsel families and mother in support of exclusive
breast feeding.

[Ref- Park /24"/ 575]

Q. What is colostrum? Write down the composition of colostrums.
Q. Explain the importance of colostrums.
Answer

Colostrum:
Colostrum is the secretion of breast following childbirth for the first 2 - 3 days, which contains a great

quantity of proteins and calories in addition to antibodies and lymphocytes.

Composition of colostrum:

1. Protein (moderate)
2. Sugar (few)
3. Minerals (high)
4. Antibody, specially secretory IgA (high)
5. Fat.
Importance of colostrum:
1) Antibodies, especially secretory IgA plays an important role in protection against infection.
2) Colostrum may help to sterilize the small intestine if it becomes contaminated by infected
swallowed during the birth process.
3) Colostrum possesses laxative qualities.

Q. Why breast milk is superior over cow’s milk?
Q. Breast milk is superior to cow’s milk — Justify.
Answer

Mother's milk is superior to cow’s milk because of following reasons:

1) Proteins in breast milk are easily digested as they form a very fine flocculent curd in the stomach, The
curd of the cow's milk is thick and hard to digest for the young stomach due to large proportion of
casinogen.

2) Breast milk contains twice as much iron as in the cow's milk. This iron is essential for the new born &
meets his needs upto 3 months. Anaemia is commonly seen in babies fed on cow's milk even before 3
months.

3) Calcium of breast milk is utilized better as it present in more assimiable form.

4) Vitamin A is present in large quantities in colostrum. Mother's milk contains more vit A than in cows

milk.

Vitamin C of breast milk is related to vit C content of mother's diet, in general it is higher. Cow's mill:

loses its vitamin C due to boiling, dilution & exposure to air.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5* / 172)

Peri-natal mortality rate: The ratio of peri-natal deaths ina given year to the total number of live

* Live birth: It is the complete expulsion or extraction from its mother of a product of conception,

irrespective of the duration of the pregnancy, which after such separation, breaths or shows any other
evidence of life such as beating of the heart, pulsation of the umbilical cord of deflate movement of
voluntary muscles, whether or not the umbilical cord has been cut or the placenta is attached; each
product of such a birth is considered live-born.

* Still-birth: It is defined as synonymous with late foetal death occurring after 28 completed weeks of
gestation or over. In still-birth, there is no evidence of life at or after birth.

Q. High IMR impedes the family planning programme - explain.
Answer .
High IMR impedes the family planning programme:

Family limitation and spacing of births contribute substantially to lowering of infant mortality rate. The
risk of death is greatly enhanced if the last child was born less than two years ago, and if the mother already has
four or more children. Small number of children and longer spacing between pregnancies are associated with all
societies with improved infant and child survival. But high IMR encourages the spouses to take more children
and thus it impedes the family planning programme.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 607]

Q. Write down the importance of 1 — 4 years mortality rate.
Answer
Importance of 1 —4 years mortality rate:

1 — 4 year mortality rate is a more refined indicator of the social situation in a country than infant
mortality rate. It reflects the adverse environmental health hazards (c.g. malnutrition, poor hygiene, infections
and accidents), including economic, educational and cultural characteristics of the family. Mortality in this age
group no longer depends on perinatal hazards and other endogenous factors, which often causes loss of life
during the first year of life.

Q. Write short note on: Universal children’s day.
Answer
Universal children’s day:

November 14 is observed as Universal Children's Day. It was started by the international Union for
Child Welfare and the UNICEF. In 1954, the UN General Assembly passed a formal resolution establishing
universal Children's Day and assigned to UNISEF the responsibility for promoting this annual day.

A non-governmental organization (Defense for Children International, Geneva), was set up in 1979
(during the International Year of the Child) to ensure on - going systematic international action specially
directed towards promoting and protecting the rights of the child.

Perinatal period:

Immunity / host defense against infection:
Immunity is the ability of the body to recognize, destroy and eliminate antigenic material (eg. bacteria,

[Ref- Park /24* 196

Q. Classify immunity with examples. [DU-17N,15Ju, lJ, CU-12Ju,10Ju/J, RU-12Ju,1 Lu, SUST-

Q. Enumerate the different types of natural immunity,
Answer

Classification of immunity:
A) Innate (non-specific) immunity:

1) Genetic / constitutional.
2) Mechanical:
> Keratin layer of skin
> Intact mucous membrane
> Mucocilliary movement
> Reflexes, e.g. coughing reflex, sneezing reflex etc.

3) Humoral:
> Normal bacterial flora
> Acid in gastric juice
> Complement system
> Interferons etc.

4) Cellular:
> Macrophage
> Eosinophil
> Natural killer cells etc.

B) Acquired (specific) immunity:

1) Active: Where antigens are exposed to the body.
> Natural: After clinical & sub-clinical infections, e.g. Hepatitis-A virus infection.
> Artificial: Different types of vaccines, e.g. bacterial vaccines, viral vaccines,
toxoids, live attenuated vaccines etc,

2) Passive: Where antigens are not exposed to the body.
> Natural:
Y Transfer of maternal antibody to foetus through placenta.
¥ Transfer of antibody from mother to infants by breast milk.

> Artificial: Antisera & antitoxins, e.g. TIG (tetanus immunoglobulins), ATS (anti-
tetanus serum), ADS (anti-diphtheria serum) etc.

Q. “Active immunity is superior to passive immunity” — Justify. .
Q. Why active immunity is superior to passive immunity? [CU-14J,12Ju,10J]

Answer

Active immunity is Superior to passive immunity for the following reasons: .
1) Active immunity is long-lasting, whereas passive immunity is short-lasting. . ;
2) Immunological memory is present in active immunity, whereas absent in passive immunity,
3) Secondary immune response occurs in active immunity, whereas it does not occur in passive

immunity, . _ ;
4) There is no risk of type-I and type-II hypersensitivity reactions in active immunity,

5) ADCC (antibody dependent cell mediated cytotoxicity).

Q. Define immune response. What are the fimr
S whale you wcan'by'i types of immune responses? —
van y immune response? [RU-13J]
Immune response: Development of resistance to foreign substance is called immune response.
Types:
1) Primary immune response: When an antigen is administered for the first time to a person who has
er been exposed to it, this initial encounter of a native immunocompetent lymphocyte with the
antigen induces a response which is known as primary response.
2) Secondary immune response: A second or subsequent contract of the host with the same antigen
elicits a more rapid & heightened response which is known is as the secondary response.
. The amplified population of memory cells accounts for the rapidity & intensity that
distinguishes a secondary response from the primary response.

Q. Discuss mechanism of immune response.

Q. How an individual will response to an antigen when introduced for first time? [DU-10J]

Q. Discuss the mechanism of immune response after vaccination.

Answer
Mechanism of immune response: Immunogenic stimulus by vaccination or any foreign antigen > Processing
and presentation of the antigen by macrophage or other antigen presenting cells which are recognized by helper
T cells (Th) > Activation and proliferation of helper T cells >
> Activation of cytotoxic T cells > Delayed hypersensitivity reaction > Cell-mediated immunity.
> Production of B cell growth and differentiation factors (IL-4 & 5) by Th cells > Activation of B
lymphocyte > Proliferation & differentiation of activated B cells to plasma cells > Production of

antibody > Humoral immunity.

Q. Define herd immunity. [CU-12Ju, RU-12J]

Q. State the epidemiological significance of “Herd immunity”. [RU-13Ju]
Q. Mention the significance of herd immunity. [RU-14Ju]

Q. Write short note on: Herd immunity. [SUST-16N, CU-17N,16J,14J,13Ju]

Answer . r
Herd immunity: It is the level of resistance of a community or group of people to a particular disease.

. According to another source, herd immunity implies group protection beyond that afforded by the
protection of immunized individuals. That is, it concerns the freedom from infection of individuals within a
herd by sole virtue of the influence of the herd structure on the transmission among individuals. _

Studies have shown that it is neither possible nor necessary to achieve 100% herd immunity ina
population to halt an epidemic or control disease. To just how much less than 100% is required is a crucial

question, for which no definite answer can be given.

Merits of herd immunity: . .
1) Herd immunity provides an immunological barrier to the spread of disease in the human herd.
2) Ifthe herd immunity is sufficiently high, the occurrence of an epidemic is regarded as highly
unlikely.

3) Ifhigh level of to immunity can be maintained, it may lead to elimination of the disease in due
course. e.g. diphtheria and poliomyelitis. .

4) The epidemic curve tends to decline with a buildup of herd immunity.

[Ref- Park /24"/ 107]

Q. What are the elements of herd immunity? [RU-14Ju]

Q. What are the elements of herd structure? [DU-11J]

Q. What are the preconditions of herd immunity? [CU-1 Ju]
Answer

Elements contribute to herd immunity:

a) Occurrence of clinical and subclinical infection in the herd.
b) Immunization of the herd.

c) Herd structure:
- Host belonging to the herd species.
- Presence and distribution of alternative animal host.

- Possible insect vectors.

Q. Define ring immunity.
Q. State ring immunization. [DU-13Ju]
Answer
Ring immunity:
When an infected non-immune person is surrounded by a barrier of immune persons, then the disease
cannot be transmitted outside. It is called ring immunity. This was applied to eradicate small pox.

Q. Why live vaccines are more potent immunizing agent than killed vaccine? [SUST-09J]
Answer

Live vaccines are more potent thon killed vaccines, because:
Live organisms multiply in the host and the resulting antigenic dose is larger than what is injected.

Live vaccines have all major and minor antigenic components.

Live vaccines engage certain tissues of the body.
There may be other mechanisms such as the persistence of latent virus.

Q. What are the contraindications for vaccination? [SUST-12Ju]
Answer
Contraindications for vaccination:
1) Contraindications of all vaccines:
> Ananaphylactic reaction following a previous dose.
> Current serious illness.

2) Contraindications of live vaccines (MMR, BCG, yellow fever):
> Pregnancy.
> Radiation therapy (i.e. total body radiation).

3) Contraindications of yellow fever vaccine:
> Eggallergy.
> Immunodeficiency (from medication, disease or symptomatic HIV infection).
4) Contraindications of BCG vaccine: Symptomatic HIV infection.
5) Contraindications of influenza & yellow fever vaccine: History of anaphylactic reaction
following egg ingestion.

6) Contraindications of pertussis-containing vaccine:

> Anaphylactic reaction to a previous dose.
> Evolving neurological disease (e.g. uncontrolled epilepsy or progressive encephalopathy),

[Ref- Park /24"/ 128]

Q. Mention the contraindications of live vaccines. [DU-13Ju]
Answer
Contraindications of live vaccines: Live vaccines should not be administered to —
1) Immunodeficiency state.
2) Anaphylaxis.
3) Pregnancy.
4) To persons whose immune response may be suppressed because of leukaemia, lymphoma or
malignancy or because of therapy with corticosteroids, alkylating agents, anti-metabolic agents or
radiation.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 128]

Q. Define monovalent, polyvalent and combined vaccine.
Answer
* Monovalent vaccine: Monovalent vaccines are those which are prepared from only one strain of a
species.

“> Polyvalent vaccine: The term “polyvalent” is applied to vaccines which are prepared from two or more
strains of the same species.

“+ Combined / mixed vaccine: If more than one kind of immunizing agent is included in the vaccine, itis

called a mixed or combined vaccine.

Q. What are the advantages of combination?
Q. Mention the usefulness of combined vaccine.
Answer
Advantages of combination:

1) To simplify administration.

2) To reduce costs.

3) To minimize the number of contacts of the patient with the health system.

[Ref- Park /24"/ 110]

Q. Mention the advantages of DPT vaccine.
Answer
DPT is a combined vaccine. Advantages are —

1) Three vaccines (diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus) are administered at a time.

2) Reduces the cost.

3) Minimizes the number of contacts of the patient with the health system.

4) Simplify administration.

5) Increase the potency.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 110]

Q. Explain toxoid.

Answer

Toxoid: These are vaccines prepared from toxin by inactivation (combining formaldehyde with toxin) which
have no toxigenicity but retain antigenicity.

Example: Tetanus toxoid (TT), Diphtheria toxoid (DT).
[Ref- Park /24™/ 110]

children of the world against six vaccine preventable disease:

Q. What are the causes of giving BCG vaccine just after birth?
Answer ,
Causes of giving BCG vaccine just after birth:
1) To protect the baby from tuberculosis that may be transmitted from the mother (hidden case) or
from other sources.
2) The baby is very much susceptible to this infection because of lacking maternal antibody against
tuberculosis. The earlier is the age the higher level of protection.

nT Eee:

Scanned with CamScanner

406 — ENDEAVOUR COMMUNITY MEDICINE FOR WRITTEN (SAQ, MCQ), VIVA ¢ Ospy

3) It provides a high level of protection particularly by against the severe form of tuberculosis Such
tubercular meningitis, milliary tuberculosis which are most frequent in young children and are ae
fatal. Therefore it should be given early in life as possible in any situation where the risk of
tubercular infection is high.

Q. State complications of BCG.
Answer
Complications of BCG: Complications of BCG vaccinations are more or less related to the strain, dosage ang
age of the child, faulty technique and skill of the vaccinator. The main complications are
1. Local abscess
2. Keloid at the site of injection
3. Axillary lymphadenitis

Again, generalized eczema, infectious dermatitis, hypogammaglobulinaemia may occur.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4" 1337)

For Viva

Viva Q. Why measles vaccine is given at the age of 9 months?
Answer

Measles vaccine is given after 9 month of age, because —
Infants are protected by maternal antibodies up to 6 months of age; in some maternal immunity may

persist beyond 9 months. Measles vaccine is not given to a child before the age of 9 months because it interferes
with the maternal antibodies passively transmitted to a child. However, it has been shown that the matemal

antibodies start declining as early as 6 months, causing at an early age.

Viva Q. Why buttock is not used routinely as an immunization site?

Answer
The buttock should not be used routinely as an immunization site for infants. children or adults because

of the risk of injury to the sciatic nerve. Since the depth of gluteal fat in adult women is usually more than 3.5
cm, which is typically the length of the injecting vaccines into the buttock may result in poor absorption of the

vaccine from fatty tissue.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 411]

Viva Q. Why there is an interval of 4 weeks between doses?

Answer
Giving dose of a vaccine at less than 4 weeks interval may lessen antibody responses. Lengthening the

interval between doses of theses vaccine leads to higher antibody levels. So, there is an minimum interval of 4

weeks between disease.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"/412]

Q. What are the criteria of a thought-out immunization schedule?
Answer

Criteria of a thought-out immunization schedule:

1) Epidemiologically relevant: Vaccination should be included only against diseases which are
public health problems and against which an effective vaccine persists. 4

2) Immunologically effective: Children must be vaccinated at an age when they can benefit from it,

3) Operationally feasible: This includes cost and ability to achieve a high percentage of coverage.

4) Socially acceptable: The vaccination schedule must take into account the local customs, beliefs
and practices.

NID / National immunization day:
National immunization day (NID) is a supplementary vaccination strategy which means vaccination

simultaneously throughout the country with OPV of all children under 5 years repeated twice with four to six
weeks interval. :

Objective / importance:

> Interruption of transmission of poliomyelitis.
> To establish vaccine virus in the community in place of wild poliovirus.

NID in Bangladesh: Ist NID was observed in Bangladesh on March 16 to April 16, 1995.

NID is ongoing each year on particular dates.

Cold chain system

Q. What is cold chain system? [SUST-17N,12J,10J]
Answer

Cold chain:
It is a system of storage and transport of vaccines at low temperature from the manufacturer to the

actual vaccination site. It consists of a series of storage and transport links, all designed to keep vaccines within
an acceptable range until it reaches the user.

VVVVVVVV

Q. What is the importance of cold chain? [SUST-10J]
Answer

Importance of cold chain:

1) To maintain potency of vaccine.
2) For the store of vaccine.
3) For the transportation of vaccine at low temperature.

Disinfection

Q. Define & classify disinfection. [RU-1 IJu,10Ju]
Answer

Disinfection: ;
It is the killing of infectious agents outside the body by direct exposure to chemical or physical agents,

It can refer to the action of antiseptic as well as disinfectants.

Types:

1) Concurrent disinfection: It is the application of disinfection measures as Soon as possible after the
discharge of infectious material from the body of an infected person, or after the soiling of articles
with such infectious discharge, concurrent disinfection consists of usually disinfection of urine,
faeces, vomit, contaminated linen, clothes, hands, dressings, aprons, gloves etc. It prevents further
spread of disease.

2) Terminal disinfection: It is the application of disinfective measures after the patients has been
moved by death or to a hospital or has ceased to be a source of infection or after other hospital

isolation practices have been discontinued. a
Disinfection of water by chlorination, pasteurization of

3) Precurrent (prophylactic) disinfection:

milk and hand washing. z is
[Ref- Park / 24" / 136]

Uses of disinfection: Disinfection of urine, faces, vomit, contaminated cloths, hands, dressing, aprons, gloves,

etc. throughout the course of illness.

Disinfectant
It is usually a chemical agent (but sometimes a physical agent) which destroys disease-causing

pathogens or other harmful microorganisms, but might not kill bacterial spores.
Disinfectants are suitable for application only to inanimate objects.

‘+ Sterilization: It is the process of destroying all organisms including spores.

Q. What are the qualities of ideal disinfectant?

Answer

Qualities of ideal disinfectant:
1) It should not be very poisonous.
2) It should not act on metals and should not spoil fabrics.
3) It should have good germicidal effect and rapid in action.
4) It should act powerfully in presence of organic matter.
5) It should not have any injurious effect on human body.
6) It should not have unpleasant smell.
7) It should act both in acid and alkaline medium.
8) It should not bleach or stain.
9) It should be readily miscible with water.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5" /294 + Park /24" / 136]

Q. What are the mechanisms of action of disinfectants?
Answer

Mechanisms of action of disinfectants:
1) Disruption of the lipid-containing cell membrane (e.g. alcohol, detergent, phenol etc.).

2) Modification of cellular proteins (e.g. chlorine, iodine etc.).
3) Modification of nucleic acids.

4) Interference with bacterial cell wall.

5) Chemical antagonism.

Q. Write short note on: Incineration. [CU-17M, RU-11Ju]
Answer
Incineration:
Incineration is a high temperature dry oxidation process, that reduces organic and combustible waste to
inorganic incombustible matter and results in a very significant reduction of waste volume and weight.

Use: .
The process is usually selected to treat wastes that cannot be recycled, reused or disposed off in a land
fill site. Hospital refuse which is particularly dangerous is best disposed by incineration.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 827]

Q. Write short note on: Auto disabled syringes.
Answer

A-D Syringes:
They are self-locking syringes that can be used only once. They are the preferred equipment for all

types of immunization sessions. Every Ad syringe is sterilized and sealed by the manufacturer.
Parts: 4 parts. Plunger, barrel, needle & needle cap.

The plunger can go back and forth only once, so health workers should not more the plunger
unnecessary and should not try to inject air into the vial, as this will disable the syringes.
Advantages:

i) They can only be used once.

ii) They eliminate the patient to patient disease transmission caused by the use of contaminated needle
and syringes.

iii) They save time for health workers from their heavy work for sterilization.

Q. Mention the mechanism of action of radiation.

Answer

Mechanism of. action of radiation:
1) Formation of thymine dimers and addition of hydroxy! groups to the nucleotide bases. As a result ;

DNA replication is inhibited and the organism can’t grow.

2) Production of free radicals.
3) Direct heat on a covalent bond in DNA, resulting in chain breakage.

Q. Write short note on: Ionizing radiation.

Answer

lonizing radiation (B & y rays):
Ionizing radiation is being increasingly used for sterilization of bandages, dressing, catgut, plastic

syringes, catheter, anesthetic instrument, transfusion set and surgical instruments.

The objects to be sterilized are placed in plastic bags before radiation, and they will remain sterile until
opened. Ionizing radiation has great penetrating powers with little or no heating effect.
This method is most effective but very costly. Commercial methods of sterilization are normally carried
out by gamma radiation (atomic). It is now one of the most viable, safe and economic methods used today.
[Ref- Park /24"/ 137]

Q. Write short note on: Autoclave. |
Answer H
Autoclave:

Sterilizers which operate at high temperatures (in excess of 100°C) and pressure are called autoclaves.

Types of autoclave: They fall into two categories — i
1) Double chamber autoclave &

|
2) Single chamber autoclave |

Time, temperature & pressure used in autoclave:

|
121°C temperature under 15 Ibs/sq inch pressure for 15 minutes. Ht

Principle of autoclave: {i}

1. Atatmospheric pressure, water boils at 100°C i}

2. With the rise of pressure, the boiling point of water also rises e.g.

3. Steam under pressure unmixed with air has more temperature than that mixed with air.

4. Steam under pressure has more penetrating power. This is due to fact that, steam condenses to water on
contact with materials.

5. During condensation of steam to water, a large amount of latent heat is liberated, thus increasing the i|}
efficacy of sterilization.

Uses of autoclaving:
Autoclaving is widely used in hospital and laboratory practice. It destroys all forms of organisms Hi

including spores. It is the most effective method for sterilization of linen, dressings, gloves, syringes, blunt
surgical instruments and culture media. It is not suitable for sterilization of plastics and sharp instruments by
autoclave.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4" /267 + M.R. Choudhury / 5" / 43 + Park / 24" / 137]

Q. Give the mechanism of action of dry heat and moist heat. l
Answer i|
Mechanism of action of dry heat: 1

1. Denaturation of cell protein

2. Oxidative damage

3. Toxic effect of elevated electrolyte. |

Mechanism of action of moist heat: i
1. Loss of functional integrity of cytoplasmic membrane. |
2. Denaturation and coagulation of structural proteins and enzymes. |
3. Breakage of DNA strands.

Q. Mention the advantages of moist heat over dry heat in sterilization. |

Q. Why moist heat is better / superior than dry heat?

Answer

Moist heat is superior to dry heat due to:
1. Moist heat has a better penetrating power at a lower temperature. |
2. It produces latent heat. |
3. Kills the bacteria by denaturing their enzyme & structural proteins. \ |
4. Bacteria are more susceptible to moist heat |

Q. Write short note on: Fumigation.
Answer ;

Fumigation: It is a process of gaseous disinfection by using formaldehyde in the form of vapor.

Uses:
a Disinfection of operation theatre (OT) and hospital ward.
2 Disinfection of books, shoes, leather goods, silk, woolen cloths, toys etc.
) Also used as insecticide e.g. killing of mosquitoes, flies, lice etc.

Condition of the room:
For efficient fumigation, the temperature of the room should be around 70°F and the humidity should be
around 75%.

Procedure:

Boiling commercial formalin in 2 volumes of water (500 ml formalin + 1000 ml of water per 30 cu
meters of space) in a stainless steel vessel over an electric hot plate.

There is vigorous boiling and liberation of formaldehyde gas.

The room is kept closed for 6 — 12 hours to allow disinfection.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 138, 139 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5/294]

Q. How can we prevent and control hospital acquired / nosocomial infection?
Answer

Prevention and control of hospital acquired / nosocomial infection:

1) Isolation: Infectious patients must be isolated.

2) Hospital staff: Those who are suffering from skin diseases, sore throat, common cold, ear
infection, diarrhoea or dysentery or other infectious aliments should be kept away from work until
completely cured.

3) Hand washing: A suitable disinfectant must be employed for hand washin,
patients.

4) Dust control: Suppression of dust by wet d
measures,

5) Disinfection: The articles used by the patients as well as patient's urine, faeces and sputum should
be properly disinfected.

6) Control of droplet infection: Use of face masks, proper bed spacing, prevention of overcrowding
and ensuring adequate lighting and ventilation are important control measures.

7) Nursing techniques: Barrier nursing and task nursing to minimize cross infection.
es: To formulate policies regarding admission of infectious cases, isolation

8) Administrative measur ; i
facilities, disinfection procedures, and in fact all matters relating to control of hospital acquired

Q. Define food. [CU-10Ju/J, RU-I Ju]
Q. What are the functions of food?

Answer
Food: . .
Food is a composite mixture of substances which when consumed performs certain functions in the
body.
These functions are —

i) Yielding energy

ii) Building and maintaining the body.

iii) Protecting the body & regulating the tissue function.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5” / 136]

Q. Write down the functions of non-calorigenic foods.
Answer

Functions of non-caloriegenic foods: (vitamin, mineral, water, dietary fibre).
1) Water is a very essential component of cells, tissues and body fluids. Without water, no

biochemical reaction can take place within the body, and hence, life is not possible.

2) Most of the vitamins are coenzymes of different enzyme reactions of the body. Besides this,
vitamin A helps in vision, vitamin K in blood clotting, vitamin C in collagen formation etc.

3) Minerals are important constituents of ECF and ICF. They takes part in a variety of functions e.g.
action potential, muscle contraction, glandular secretion, membrane transport of other substances

etc.
4) Dietary fibers are essenti

Q. Describe the role of each component of a balanced diet.
Q. Write down the functions of dietary carbohydrate, protein & lipids.

Answer

Functions of dietary carbohydrates (CHO):
1) Major sources of energy: Carbohydrates are the principal source of energy, supplying 60-80% of

the caloric requirements of the body.
2) Protein sparing action: Use of carbohydrates for calorie purpose spares the protein for its body

building & growth function.
in: The brain & other parts of CNS are dependent on glucose for '

3) Absolute requirement by brai
may lead to irreversible brain damage.

energy. Prolonged hypoglycaemia
4) Energy supply for muscle work: The muscle glycogen is broken down to lactic acid (glycolysis)

to provide energy for muscle contraction.
5) Required for the oxidation of fat: Acetyl CoA is the product that is formed in fatty acid oxidation.

For its further oxidation via TCA cycle, Acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate, the latter is

predominantly derived from carbohydrates. It may therefore be stated ‘Fat burns in a fuel of

carbohydrate’. Excess utilization of fats coupled with deficiency of carbohydrates leads to ketosis.
6) Synthesis of pentose sugars: Pentose sugars (e.g. Ribose & deoxyribose) are the constituents of
several compounds in the body, e.g. nucleic acids (DNA, RNA), co-enzymes (NADH FAD) etc.
7) Synthesis of non-essential amino acids: The intermediates of carbohydrate metabolism, mainly
the ketoacids (e.g. pyruvic acid), serve as precursors for the synthesis of non-essential amino acids,
8) Synthesis of fat: Excess consumption of CHO leads to the formation of fat which is stored in the

adipose tissue.

Role of proteins in dict / nutrition: Proteins are traditionally regarded as ‘body building foods’. They play

the following roles — ; ;
1) Proteins are the fundamental basis of cell structure & its function. ;
2) All the enzymes, several hormones, immunoglobulins, transport carriers etc. are proteins,

3) 10-15% of total body energy is derived from protein.
Proteins are involved in osmotic pressure maintenance, blood clotting, muscle contraction etc.

5) Repair & maintenance of body tissue.

6) Milk formation during lactation.

7) Actas buffer & maintain acid-base balance.

8) During starvation, proteins serve as major supplier of energy. Structural proteins serve as ‘storage

proteins’ to meet the emergency energy needs of the body.

9) Fetal development during pregnancy.

Major nutritional functions of lipids: Dietary lipids have 2 major nutritive functions:

1) Supply triacylglycerol (TAG) that normally constitute about 90% of dietary lipids which is a
concentrated source of fuel to the body.
2) Helps in absorption of fat soluble vitamins (A, D, E & K).
Provide essential fatty acids (EFA): Functions of EFA are-
Essential fatty acids are the structural components of biological membranes.
They participate in the transport and utilization of cholesterol.
Prevent fat accumulation in the liver.
They are required for the synthesis of prostaglandins.
Maintain proper growth and reproduction of the organisms.

Q. What are the proximate principles of food?

Answer
Proximate principles of food: Protein, fat & carbohydrates are often called ‘proximate principles of food’ as
they form the main bulk of food. They contribute to the total energy intake in the following proportions:

> Proteins: 7- 15%

> Fats: 10-30%

> Carbohydrates: 65 — 80%
[Ref- Park /24"/ 647]

Q. What is nutrition? [CU-10J]

Answer

Nutrition: Nutrition is the science or practice of consuming and utilizing foods.

In other word, nutrition is the science of foods, the nutrients and other substances in foods, their actions,
interaction and balance in relation to diet, health and diseases.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 136]

Answer
Diet:

A diet may be defined as the kinds of food on which a person or group lives.
[Ref- Park / 23" / 608]

Or,
The food which we are eating and or drinking is called diet.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 136]

Q. Define dietetics.
Answer
Dietetics:
It is the science and art of food, the goal of which is to improve health through optimal feeding

practices.

Q. Define balanced diet. [RU-17M,16M, SUST-15J]

Q. Explain the importance and composition of balanced diet. [SUST-15J,10Ju]
Q. Write short note on: Balanced diet. [SUST-16M]

Answer

Balanced diet:
A balanced diet is defined as one which contains a variety of foods in such quantities and proportions

that the need for energy, amino acids, vitamins, minerals, fats, carbohydrate and other nutrients is adequately
met for maintaining health, vitality and general well-being and also makes a small provision for extra nutrients

to withstand short duration of leanness.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 675]

Or, A balanced diet is one which contains all the proximate principles (e.g. protein, fat & carbohydrate),
minerals and vitamins in due proportions and at the same time meeting the total energy requirements for

maintaining health, vitality & wellbeing of a person.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4 / 135]

Percentage of food item in balanced diet:
> Carbohydrate: 55 - 715%.

> Fat: 15-30%.
> Protein: 10-15%.

Q. Define food hygiene. [CU-15Ju]

Answer
Food hygiene:
Food hygiene implies hygiene in the production, handling, distribution and serving of all types of food.
The aim is to prevent food poisoning and other food borne illnesses.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 692]

Q. Discuss dietary goals.
Q. State the dietary goals recommended by WHO. [DU-14Ju]

Answer
All countries should develop a national nutrition and food

Dietary goals / WHO recommended dietary goals:
prudent diet”) recommended by the

policy setting out "dietary goals" for achievement. The dietary goals (“

various Expert Committees of WHO are as below —

1) Dietary fat should be limited to approximately 15-30% of total daily.

2) Saturated fats should contribute no more than 10% of the total energy intake, unsaturated vegetable
oils should be substituted for the remaining fat requirement.

3) Excessive consumption of refined carbohydrate should be avoided; some amount of carbohydrate
rich in natural fiber should be taken.

4) Sources rich in energy such as fats and alcohol should be restricted.

5) Salt intake should be reduced to an average of not more than 5 g per day.

6) Protein should account for approximately 10-15% of the daily intake.

7) Junk foods such as colas, ketchups and other foods that supply empty calories should be reduced.

|Ref- Park /24" / 675]

Amino acids are a group of organic compounds containing two functional groups- amino and carboxyl.

The amino acids are termed as a-amino acids, if both carboxy! and amino groups are attached to the same
carbon atom. Over 300 amino acids occur in nature but only 20 amino acids act as monomer of proteins.

Q. What do you mean by protein supplementation? [CU-13J]
Q. Explain the supplementary action of protein. [DU-18M,16N,14J, RU-18M,15J]
Q. Explain the importance of supplementary actions of proteins in context of your country. [(CU-

10J)
Answer

Importance of supplementary actions of proteins:

Man derives protein not from a single source, but from a variety of food sources, animal and vegetable.

Cereal proteins are deficient in lysine and threonine; and pulse proteins in methionine. These are known
as “limiting” amino acids. Where two or more vegetarian foods are eaten together (e.g. rice-dhal combination)
there proteins supplement one another and provide a protein comparable to animal protein in respect of essential
amino acids.

Thus with proper planning, it is possible for a vegetarian to obtain a high grade protein, at low cost,
from mixed diets of cereals, pulses and vegetables. This in known as supplementary action of proteins, and is

the basis of counseling people to eat mixed diets.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 648]

Q. Define fat. Classify lipids. What are the sources of fat?
Answer
Fat:

Fats or lipids are made of fatty acids (saturated, polyunsaturated, monounsaturated), triglycerides,

phospholipids, glycolipid etc.
Fats are solid at 20°C; they are called ‘oil’ if they are liquid at that temperature.

Classification of lipid:
1) Simple lipid: e.g. triglycerides.
2) Compound lipids: e.g. phospholipids.
3) Derived lipid: e.g. cholesterol.

Sources of fat:
>» Animal fat: Major source of animal fats are ghee, butter, cheese, eggs, fat of meat & fish etc.
> Vegetable fat: Some plants store fat in their seeds; e.g. ground nuts, mustard, sesame, coconut etc.
> Other sources: Small quantities (invisible fats); e.g. cereals, pulse, nuts & vegetables.

Q. List the needful functions of fat. [RU-17M,16M,13J]
Answer
Functions of the fat: We need fat in the diet for the following reasons.
1) They are high-energy foods, providing as much as 9 kcal/gm.
2) Fats serve as vehicles for fat-soluble vitamins,
3) Fats in the body support viscera such as heart, kidney & intestine.
4) Fat beneath the skin provides insulation against cold.
5) Fats give flavour to food.
6) Fats (especially vegetable fats) are rich sources of essential fatty acids, which are needed by the
body for growth, for structural integrity of the cell membrane & decreased platelet adhesiveness.
7) Essential fatty acids (EFAs) reduce serum cholesterol & low-density lipoproteins (LDL).
8) Cholesterol is essential as a component of membranes & nervous tissue and is a precursor for the
synthesis of steroid hormones and bile acids.
9) Polyunsaturated fatty acids are precursors of prostaglandin now recognized as local hormones.

[Ref- Park /24" / 649]

Q. List the harmful functions of fat. [RU-17M,16M,13J]
Q. Mention diseases associated with high fat intake. [DU-15Ju,13J]

Answer

Diseases associated with high fat intake / Demerits of excess fat in diet:

1) Obesity: Obesity occurs when fat-rich diet is taken. In fatty people adipose tissue may increase

upto 30%. ‘
2) Phrenoderma: Deficiency of essential fatty acids in the diet is associated with rough and dry skin,

a condition is known as phrenoderma or toad skin.
3) Coronary heart disease: High fat intake is the major risk factor of coronary heart disease (CHD).
4) Cancer: High fat diets increase the risk of colon cancer and breast cancer.

» Cellulose: Contributes to dietary fibre.
