Provides main source of energy.

Helps the body to use protein and fat efficiently.

Supplies fiber that helps in the formation of the bulk for better digestion,
Can convert itself into fat.

Essential for the synthesis of certain nonessential amino acids,

Q. What is the vitamin A? Name sources of vitamin A. What are the functions of vitamin A?

Answer
Vitamin-A:

Vitamin A is a fat soluble vitamin which covers both a preformed vitamin, retinol and a pro-vitamin,
beta carotene, some of which is converted to retinol in the intestinal mucosa.

Sources of vitamin-A:
(a) Animal source:

Function of vitamin-A:
1) It is indispensable for normal vision. It contributes to the production of retinal pigments, which are '
needed for vision in dim light. |
2) Itis necessary for maintaining the integrity and the normal functioning of glandular and epithelial
tissue, which lines intestinal, respiratory and urinary tracts as well as the skin and eyes.

3) It supports growth, especially skeletal growth. .
4) It is anti-infective: there is increased susceptibility to infection and lowered immune response in

vitamin A deficiency and
5) It may protect against some epithelial cancers such as bronchial cancers.

Q. Why vitamin D is considered as kidney hormone?
Answer

Vitamin D is considered as kidney hormone:
It has been proposed that vitamin D should be regarded as a kidney hormone because it does not meet

the classic definition of a vitamin, that is, a substance which must be obtained by dietary means because of lack
of capacity in the human body to synthesize it. In fact, vitamin D; is not a dietary requirement at in conditions
of adequate sunlight. It can be synthesized in the body in adequate amounts by simple exposure to sunlight even

for five minutes per day. [Ref: P. k / 24" / 655]

Minerals:

; The human body contains more than 50 chemical elements which are required for growth, repair and

Q. Discuss detrimental effects and intervention measures of nutritional anaemia.

Answer
etrimental effects of nutritional anaemia: The detrimental effects of anaemia can be seen in 3 important

Di

areas:

1) Pregnancy: Anaemia increases the risk of maternal and foetal mortality and morbidity. Conditions
such as abortions, premature births, post-partum haemorrhage and low birth weight were especially
associated with low haemoglobin levels in pregnancy.

2) Infection: Anaemia can be caused or aggravated by parasitic diseases, ¢.g., malaria, intestinal
parasites. Further, iron deficiency may impair cellular responses and immune functions and
increase susceptibility to infection.

3) Work capacity: Anaemia (even when mild) causes a significant impairment of maximal work

Fluorine

Q. Mention the sources of fluorine. Why it is called two-edged sword?
Answer
Sources of fluorine:
1) Drinking water: Major source of fluorine to man.
2) Foods: Fluorides occur in traces in many foods, but some foods such as sea fish, cheese and tea are

reported to be rich in fluorides.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 663]

Fluorine is often called a two-edged sword: . . . ;
Prolonged ingestion of fluorides through drinking water in excess of the daily requirement is associated

with dental and skeletal fluorosis; and inadequate intake with dental caries. The use of fluoride is recognized as

the most effective means available for the prevention of dental caries.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 663]

and alkaline phosphatase)
7) Itis active in the metabolism of glucose & proteins

8) It is required for the synthesis of insulin by the pancreas.

Q. What do you mean by complimentary feeding?
Answer
Complementary feeding:
It means giving other foods in addition to breast milk. These foods and liquids are called

complementary foods as they are additional or complements to basic foods rather than adequate on their own.

Q. “Malnutrition predisposes to infection & infection to malnutrition” — justify the statement.

[DU-10J]
Answer
Malnutrition predisposes to infection & infection to malnutrition:

Infectious diseases are an important conditioning factor responsible for malnutrition, particularly in
small children. Diarrhoea, intestinal parasites, measles, whooping cough, malaria, tuberculosis all contribute to
malnutrition. In fact it is a vicious circle- infection contributing to malnutrition, and malnutrition causing an
otherwise minor childhood ailments to become killers. It has been shown that where environmental conditions
are poor, small children may suffer from some infection or the other for almost half of their first three years of
life. The interrelationship between malnutrition and infection has been well documented.

[Ref- Park /21"/ 603]

Q. What are the advantages and disadvantages of Gomez’s classification of PEM? [DU-09J]
Answer

Advantages of Gomez’s classification:
1) It is based on weight retardation.
2) It locates the child on the basis of his or her weight in comparison with a normal child of the same
age.
3) Weight is widely recorded and the classification is easy to compute.
4) This classification has a prognostic value for hospitalized children.

Disadvantages of Gomez’s classification:
1) A cut-off point of 90% of reference is high (80% being approximately equivalent to -2SD or the 3"

percentile). Thus some normal children may be classified as 1* degree malnourished.
2) By measuring only weight for age, it is difficult to know if the low weight is due to a sudden acute

episode of malnutrition or to long-standing chronic undernutrition.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 677]

Clinical stages:
1. Latent stage:
¢ The individual is apparently healthy but when subjected to physical stress exhibits ungainly

gait.
¢ Ifthe pulse is withdrawn from the diet it will result in complete remission of the disease.

2. No stick stage: The patient walks with short jerky steps without the aid of a stick.

3. One stick stage:
¢ The patient walks with a crossed gait with a tendency to walk on toes.

¢ Muscular stiffness makes it necessary to use a stick to maintain balance.

4. Two stick stage: More severe.
e = The gait is slow & clumsy.
¢ The pt gets tired easily after walking a short distance.
e The patient needs two crutches for support.

5. Crawler stage: Final stage
¢ The knee joints cannot support the weight of the body so the erect posture becomes impossible,
e = There is atrophy of the thigh & leg muscles.
"The patient is reduced to crawling by throwing his weight on his hands.

e Steeping method &
e Parboiling.

consumption.

5. Genetic approach:
e Certain strains of Lathyrus contain very low levels of toxin (0.1 %)

Q. Mention different food toxins.
Answer
Food toxins:

1) BOAA (Beta Oxalyl Aminoalanine): the cause of neurolathyrism found in seeds of the pulses -

Lathyrus sativus (Khesari dhal).

2) Aflatoxin: It is a group of mycotoxin produce by certain fungi- Aspegillus flavus & Aspegillus
parasiticus. This fungus Infests groundnut, maize, wheat rice, cotton seeds under condition of
improper storage. These toxins are the most potent hepatotoxin & carcinogenic. ;

3) Ergot: It is also mycotoxin produced by claviceps fugiformis. These fungi infested during the
flowering stage food grains such as bajra sorghum wheat.

4) Sanguinarine: It is a toxic alkaloid from argemone oil which causes epidemic dropsy.

5) Pyrrolizidine alkaloids: Jhunjhunia seeds where found to contain this toxin which are hepatotoxin

cause endemic ascites characterized by rapidly developing ascites and jaundice.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 694]

Q. Define environment.

Q. Classify environment with example. [DU-17M]

Q. Classify macro-environment with example. [DU-18M]

Q. Enumerate the component of physical environment. [SUST-16J]

Answer

Environment:

The term environment implies all the external factors — living and non-living, material and non-material
which surround man,

Classification:
* Internal environment: It relates to tissues, organ, organ system and their harmonious functioning.
“External / macro environment: It is defined as, all that which is external to the individual human host,

living and non-living and with which he is in constant interaction. These include all of man’s external
surroundings such as air, water, food, housing etc.

For descriptive purpose, the environment has been divided into three components, all closely related:
** Physical: Water, air, soil, housing, wastes, radiation etc.

* Biological: Plant and animal life including bacteria, viruses, rodents, insects and animals.

o

* Social / psychosocial: Customs, culture, habits, income, occupation, religion etc.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 742 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5°/ 478]

Q. What do you mean by sanitation?
Answer

Sanitation: The dictionary meaning of sanitation is “the science of safe guarding health”.

The National Sanitation Foundation of the U.S.A has defined sanitation as follows:

“Sanitation is a way of life. It is the quality of living that is expressed in the clean home, the clean farm,
the clean business, the clean neighbourhood and the clean community. Being a way of life it must come from
within the people; it is nourished ty knowledge and grows as an obligation and an ideal in human relations.”

[Ref- Park / 24" / 742]

Q. What do you mean by environmental sanitation? [RU-10Ju]
Q. Write short note on: Environmental sanitation.

Answer

Environmental sanitation / Environmental health:

The term environmental sanitation has been defined by WHO as, “the control of all those factors in
man’s physical environment which exercise or may exercise a deleterious effect on his physical development,
health & survival.

[Ref- Park /24" / 742]

Purpose: To create and maintain ecological; conditions that will promote health and thus prevent disease.

Safe and wholesome water: Safe & wholesome water has been defined as water that is —
1) Free from pathogenic agents
2) Free from harmful chemical substances
3) Pleasant to taste, i.e., free from colour and odour; and
4) Usable for domestic purposes.

Q. Give the uses of water.
Answer
Uses of water:
1) Essential for body functions: Maintenance of vital body functions and personal body physiology.
2) Essential for plants: Plants use water to convert the nutrients in the soil into food, which keeps
them alive and helps them to grow.
3) Domestic use: Drinking, cooking, washing, bathing, flushing of toilets, gardening etc.
4) Public purposes: Cleaning streets, swimming pools, public fountains & parks, fire fighting etc.
5) Industrial purposes: Processing and cooling.
6) Agricultural purposes: Irrigation.
7) Power production: Hydropower and steam power.
8) Waste removal: From all manners of establishments and institutions.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 480]

Q. Give the physiological functions of water.
Answer
Physiological functions of water:
1) Replaces fluid loss from the body.
2) Maintains fluidity of blood and lymph
3) Helps elimination of waste material from the body
4) Acts as a transport for dissolved food
5) Form main constituent of all the body juices
6) Helps in regulation of body temperature.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 480]

water. The area draining into reservoir is called “catchment area”.

Wells:

Q. Discuss the steps in well disinfection with example. [RU-15Ju]
Answer

Steps in well disinfection:
Wells are the main source of water supply in rural areas. The most effective and cheapest method of

disinfecting wells is by bleaching powder. The steps of well disinfections are —

Scanned with CamScanner

Chapter-15: Environment & Health —————

1, Find the volume of water in well:
a. Measure the depth of water column in metre (h)
b. Measure the diameter of well in metre (d)
Take the average of several readings of the above measurements.
c. Substitute ‘h’ and ‘d’ in:

3.14xd?xh

Volume in litres = ———————— x 1000
4

d. One cubic metre = 1,000 litres of water

2. Find the amount of bleaching powder required for disinfection: Estimate the chlorine demand
of the well water by “Horrock’s Apparatus (vide Annex 1) and calculate the amount of bleaching
powder required to disinfect the well. Roughly, 2.5 grms of good quality bleaching powder would
be required to disinfect 100 litres of water. This will give an approximate dose of 0.7 mg of applied
chlorine per litre of water. .

* 3. Dissolve bleaching powder in water: The bleaching powder is placed in a bucket (not more than
100 gm in one bucket) and made into a thin paste. More water is added till the bucket is nearly

three fourth full. The contents are stirred well and allowed to sediment for 5 to 10 minutes when
lime settles down. The supernatant solution which is chlorine solution, is transferred to another
bucket, and the chalk or lime is discarded.

4. Delivery of chlorine solution in to well: The bucket containing the chlorine solution is lowered
some distance below the water surface and the well water is agitated by moving the bucket
violently both vertically and laterally. This should be done several times so that the chlorine
solution mixes intimately with the water inside the well.

5. Contact period: A contact period of one hour is allowed before the water is drawn for use.

Q. Describe the water purification process by surface water treatment.
Answer

Natural purification process in surface water:

1) Sunlight: It bleaches colour, encourages growth of algae or plankton which are active purifiers,
Most important function of algae is reoxygenation of polluted water. Ultraviolet rays are
germicidal.

2) Sedimentation: It is the most important process in standing water; natural coagulation takes place,
removing colour, turbidity and bacteria.

3) Oxygenation and recarbonation of water by pla nts: Carbon dioxide is used up and carbonate is

Precipitated softening the water. Phytoplankton is very important in furnishing needed oxygen.
: 4) Temperature: It affects life in water, sedimentation and chemical process.
5) Dilution: This process lightens pollution load and supplies oxygen. This is the most important for
Stream purification.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 488]

Q. What is biological layer?

Q. ‘Zoogleal layer is the heart of show sand filter’-explain. [RU-15Ju]
Q. Explain zoogleal layer with its importance. [RU-18M]

Q. Write short note on: Zoogleal layer. [RU-13Ju]

Answer

Biological layer / zoogleal layer:

When the filter is newly laid, it acts merely as a mechanical strainer and cannot truly be considered as
‘biological’. But very soon, the surface of the sand bed gets covered with a slimy growth known as
‘Schmutzdecke’, vital layer, zoogleal layer or biological layer.

This layer is slimy and gelatinous and consists of threadlike algae and numerous forms of life including
plankton, diatoms and bacteria. This layer is the heart of the slow sand filter. It removes organic matter, holds
back bacteria and oxidizes ammoniacal nitrogen into nitrates and helps in yielding bacteria-free water.

[Ref- Park /24"/749]

Q. What is break point
Q. Write short note on: Break point chlorination.
Answer
Break point chlorination:
The addition of chlorine to ammonia in water produces Chloramines. If the chlorine dose in the water is

increased, residual chlorine will continue with further increase in chlorine dose and after a stage, the residual

chlorines begin to increase in proportion to the added dose of chlorine. This point at which the residual chlorine

appears and when all combined chlorines have been destroyed is the breakpoint and corresponding dosage is the

breakpoint dosage.

Q. Define chlorine demand. [DU-15Ju]

Q. State the Principles of chlorine demand. [DU-15Ju]
Q. Write short note on: Chlorine demand.

Answer

Chlorine demand:
Chlorine demand is the difference between total chlorine added in the water and residual chlorine,

To purify water supplies and make them suitable for purposes like drinking, cooking and swimming,
chlorine is added. Chlorine demand from the total chlorine added can be explained using the following
equation:

Chlorine demand = Total chlorine — Chlorine residual

The purity of water can be determined by monitoring the value of chlorine demand. If the value is zero,
the water is already free of pathogenic microorganisms. If the value is less than the total chlorine, it shows that
the amount of chlorine added initially to the water was sufficient.

Q. Why coliform organisms are taken / chosen as indicators of faecal pollution of water?
Q. Why E. coli has been considered as important tool for bacteriological surveillance of drinking

water?
Answer
Coliform organisms are chosen as indicator of faecal pollution rather than the water pathogens for the
following purposes:
Y They are constantly present in great abundance in human intestine. These organisms are foreign to
potable waters, and hence their presence is looked upon as evidence of faecal contamination.
Y They are easily detected by culture methods- as small as one bacterium in 100 ml of water.
Whereas the methods for detection of other bacteria are time consuming.
Y They survive longer than the pathogens, which tend to die out more rapidly.
Y They have the greater resistance to the forces of natural purification than the water borne
pathogens. If the coliform organisms are present in a water sample, the assumption is the probable

presence of intestinal pathogens.

Q. Define hardness of water. Classify it.
Q. How can you remove the hardness of water?
Answer

Hardness of water: It is defined as the soap-destroying power of water.

Types: It is of 2 types-
1) Temporary hardness: It is due to the presence of bicarbonates of calcium or magnesium in water
held in solution by carbon dioxide.

2) Permanent hardness: This is due to the presence of sulphates and chlorides of calcium or
magnesium.

Hardness in water is expressed in terms of milli-equivalents per liter. One mEq/Itr of
hardness producing ion is equal to 50 mg calcium carbonate in | liter of water. The terms soft and
hard water are used when the levels of hardness are given as follow:

Very hard water > 6 (> 300 mg/ltr )

Q. Mention the sources of air pollution. [SUST-18M,16N/J, 15Ju, 14J,13J, RU-18N,11J, CU-
17N,16M,14Ju]

Q. Enumerate the sources of air pollution in rural & urban areas / Chittagong [CU-18M] /
Dhaka city [CU-16J].

Answer

Sources of air olution: Air pollution can be caused by a variety of substances and processes:

1) Pollution by natural phenomenon, e.g. volcanoes, forest fires, radioactive substances in the
nature, bacteria, viruses, moulds and spores.

2) Pollution by products of combustion: Combustion of fuel produces smoke, sulphur di-oxide,
nitrogen oxide and fly ashes.

3) Industrial waste e.g. dust, fume and other wastes from factories, mills, power plants, mines,
cement plants pollute the air.

4) Automobiles: Internal combustion engine, spark ignition, gasoline engine, diesel engine contribute
to air pollution by emitting hydrocarbon, carbon mono-oxide, lead, nitrogen oxide, smokes and
aldehyde.

5) Photo-chemical pollution: Volatile hydrocarbon and oxides of nitrogen from vehicle engines in
presence of strong sun light produce ozone and many complex organic compounds.

6) Acid rain (sulphuric and nitric acids).

7) Miscellaneous: Burning of refuse, agricultural activities contribute to some extent to air pollution.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 502]

Control and Prevention of Air Pollution

Q. Discuss WHO strategy for control and prevention of air pollution. [DU-13J, RU-14J]

Q. How you can prevent [CU-12Ju/J, SUST-18M, I 5Ju, 14J,13J,11J, RU-12J] / control [RU-
14Ju,12J] air pollution?

Q. How air pollution can be prevented? [SUST-16N]

Q. How outdoor [RU-11J,10Ju] / indoor [CU-11Ju] air pollution can be prevented?

Answer

Prevention and control of air pollution; The WHO has recommended the following procedures for the

prevention and control of air pollution:

1) Containment: It means prevention of escape of toxic substance into the ambient air which can be
achieved by enclosure, ventilation and air cleaning .A major contribution in this field is the
development of arrestors for the removal of containment.

2) Replacement: It means replacement of a technological process causing air pollution by a process
that does not pollute the air.

3) Dilution: Dilution is valid so long as it is within the self-cleaning capacity of the environment. For
example, some air pollutants are readily removed by vegetation.

4) Legislation: Air pollution can be controlled by legislation and its appropriate application.

5) International action: To deal with air pollution on a world scale, the WHO has established an
international network of laboratories for the monitoring and study of air pollution. They issue
warnings of air pollution when and where necessary.

[Ref- Park /24"/775]

Q. How air borne diseases can be controlled?
Answer
Control of air borne diseases:
1) By giving vaccines we can prevent and control air borne diseases such as- diphtheria, tuberculosis,
pertussis, measles, mumps, chicken pox etc.
2) Inhalation of air pollutants (e.g. silicosis, siderosis, anthracosis, lead poisoning can be prevented by
legislation of law.
3) To reduce the impact of air pollution, location of the industries should be outside from the human
habitation.
4) Industrial air pollution can be controlled by prevention of escape of toxic substances into the
ambient air by engineering methods and by adequate disposal of waste products.
5) Health education is also necessary to prevent the air borne diseases.

[Ref- Park /24" / 775 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"|

Ventilation

Q. Define ventilation. [SUST-13Ju]
Q. Write short note on: Ventilation.
Answer

Ventilation:
Ventilation is a science of maintaining atmospheric conditions which are comfortable and healthful to

the human body.

The modern concept of ventilation:
Replacement of vitiated air by a supply of fresh outdoor air and control of the quality of incoming air

with regard to its temperature, humidity and purity with a view to provide a thermal environment that is
comfortable and free from risk of infection.

Purpose of ventilation:
1) To replace vitiated air.

2) To supply oxygen and fresh air.
3) To control temperature and humidity in order to provide thermal environment.

4) To dilute air borne contamination to an acceptable concentration.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 505 + Park /24"/ 775]

Q. Classify ventilation.

Q. Mention the types of ventilation. [SUST-13Ju]
Answer

Classification of ventilation:

1) Natural ventilation:
> Thewind:
Y Perflation: When air blow through a room.
Y Aspiration: When there is an obstruction, wind bypasses and exerts a suction
action at its tail end- this is called aspiration.
Y  Cross-ventilation: Doors and windows facing each other provides cross
ventilation.

> Diffusion: Air passes through the smallest openings or spaces by diffusion. This is a slow
process.

> Temperature differences: Air flows from the high density to low density. The greater the
temperature differences between inside and outside air, the greater the velocity of the
incoming air.

2) Mechanical / Artificial ventilation:

> Exhaust ventilation: In this system, air is extracted or exhausted to the outside by the
exhaust fans usually driven by electricity. As air is extracted, a vacuum is created which
induces fresh air to enter the room through windows, doors and other walls, high up near
the roof which facilitates removal of the upper layers of the heated light air.

> Plenum ventilation: In this system, fresh air is blown into the room by centrifugal fans so
as to create a positive pressure and displaces the vitiated air. This system is used for
supplying air to air conditioned buildings and factories.

> Balanced ventilation: This is a combination of the exhaust and plenum system of
ventilation.

> Air conditioning: Air conditioning is defined as, “the simultaneous control of all, or at
least temperature, humidity and air movement of the atmosphere within any confined space
or room.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 505]

Q. Illustrate the simplest system of ventilating a small dwelling.
Answer
Please see above the procedures of mechanical / artificial ventilation.

Q. What is air conditioning? State the mechanism of air conditioning.
Answer
Air conditioning:

Air condition is defined as "the simultaneous control of all or at least the first three of those factors
affects both the physical and chemical conditions of the atmosphere within any structure. These factors include
temperature, humidity, air movement, distribution, dust, bacteria, odours and toxic gases and comfort.

Principle of air condition:

Y  Inair conditioning, the air is first filtered and is drained through a layer of fine water jets and while
passing through it, evaporates the water and thereby becomes cooler (due to the loss of heat absorbed
by water during its process of evaporation). This cool air becomes saturated with water vapour. The
excess of moisture is subsequently removed by pass into it over a cold surface. And the air is heated to
the desired temperature before it is supplied.

The temperature difference between the outside air and the air -conditioned air should not be more than
20°F otherwise it gives a sense of discomfort. Generally a difference of 10°F to 15°F is maintained.
Where there is air conditioning "transitional room" is sometimes provided so that people may not be
suddenly exposed to the high or low temperature.

[Ref- Park /24"/7761

Q. What do you mean by comfort zone?
Answer
Comfort zone:

It may be defined as the range of effective temperature at which majority of adults feel comfortable.
Comfortable thermal conditions are those under which a person can maintain a balance between production and
loss of heat at normal body temperature and without sweating.
Pleasant and cool — 69°F
Comfortable and cool — 69-76°F
Comfortable + 77-80°F
Hot and uncomfortable > 81-82°F
Extremely hot > 83°F and above.

SN SGN8

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /504]

Consequences of Ill Ventilation

Q. What are the causes of discomfort?
Answer
Discomfort is a subjective sensation which people experience in an ill-ventilated and crowded room.
For a long time it was believed to be due to increased carbon dioxide and decrease oxygen, resulting from
respiration. This theory has been refuted. It is now established that the causes of discomfort are not due to
chemical changes but physical changes. These are temperature, humidity, air movement and heat radiation.
[Ref- Park /24"/ 776]

Q. Mention the suggestions for improvement of daylight illumination.
Answer
Suggestions for improvement of daylight illumination:

1) Qrientation: Buildings are oriented towards north or south for uniform illumination. When a
building faces east and west, window shades are provided to protect against the direct penetration of
sunlight.

2) Removal of obstructions: Removal of obstructive items either wholly or partly is likely to give the
most effective single improvement in lighting.

3) Windows: Windows should be properly planned, as the natural lighting within any room is
influenced by the amount of visible sky, the size, shape and arrangement of the window openings. A
tall window gives greater penetration of light; a broad window gives greater diffusion of light.

4) Interior of the rooms: In order to obtain the full benefit of the natural illumination, the ceiling
should be white; the upper portions of the walls light-tinted; and lower portions somewhat darker so
as to give comfortable contrast to the eyes.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 777]

Q. Define noise. [SUST-17M, CU-15J]

Q. Write the properties.

Answer

Noise: Wrong sound in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Properties: Noise has 2 important properties —
> Loudness/intensity: It depends upon the amplitude o the vibrations which initiated the noise. It is
measured in decibels (dB).
> Frequency: The frequency is denoted as hertz (Hz). The human ear can hear frequencies from
about 20 to 20,000 Hz.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 778]

Q. Describe the factors related to harmful effects of noise.
Answer
The factors related to harmful effects of noise:
1) Intensity: The loudness or intensity of sound depends on the amplitude of the
acoustic vibration and is measured | decibel (dB).A daily exposure of 85 dB is about the limit
people can tolerate without substantial damage to their hearing.
2) Frequency: Frequency is denoted by Hertz. The sound frequencies audible to human ear range
from 20 to 20000 Hz, but this range is reduced with age and other factors.
3) Duration: The adverse effect of noise is proportional to the duration of the exposure and appears to
be related to the total amount of energy reaching the inner air.
4) Nature: this refers to the distribution of the sound energy over time (stable, fluctuating,
intermittent). Impulsive noise is particularly harmful.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 508]

Q. Tell in brief the approaches to control of noise. [CU-11J]

Q. How can we minimize noise pollution / hazards of noise in a big city?

Q. ‘Sound pollution in Dhaka’- how can be prevented? [CU-15J]

Answer

Control measures for noise: A variety of approaches are needed to control noise. These include —

1) Careful planning of the cities: The following measure should be taken to reduce noise:

> Division of cities into zones with separation of areas concerned with industry and transport.

» The separation of the residential areas from the main street by means of wide green belts.
» Widening of main streets to reduce the level of noise penetration into dwelling.

2) Control of vehicles: Heavy vehicles should not be routed into narrow streets. Vehicular traffic on
residential streets should be reduced.

3) To improve acoustic insulation of buildin : Installation that produce noise or disturb the occupants
within dwellings should be prohibited. Buildings should be sound-proof where necessary.

4) Industries and railways: Special areas must be earmarked, outside the residential areas, for industries,
for railways, marshalling yards and similar installations. Protective green belts must be laid between the
installation and residential areas where necessary,

5) Protection of exposed persons: Hearing protection is recommended for all workers who are
consistently exposed to noise louder than normal,

6) Legislation: Legislation should be adopted to for control of noise.

7) Education: Education through all available media is needed to highlight the importance of noise as a
community hazard.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 780]

Q. What is acute radiation syndrome?
Answer
Acute radiation syndrome:

_ Exposure of whole body to a large dose of over 100 rems penetrating radiation in a single exposure
within 1 to 2 days, resulting in progressive series of sign & symptoms known as acute radiation syndrome. The
symptoms are —

Y Inthe first phase there is short interval between exposure and onset of symptoms

Y Second phase consists of nausea and vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain. There may be
headache, erythema of skin and conjunctivitis.

Y Inthe third phase there may be loss of hair and desquamation of skin.

Y Inthe final stage bone marrow aplasia, thrombocytopenia and agranulocytosis occurs.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / S511]

Q. How radiation hazard can be prevented?
Q. Discuss radiation protection. [DU-09J]
Q. How can you protect radio-imaging technologists from radiation hazards? [DU-14Ju]
Answer
Radiation hazard can be prevented by-
A) Preventive measures for internal irradiation:
1) Notification
2) Advance approval for specified activities where preparation is essential.
3) Specification of dose limits & emissions for exposed persons, energy limits for accidents &
incidents.
4) Classification of work places depending on risk and exposed persons.
5) Introduction of control measures and monitoring.
6) Introduction of competent practitioners for the specialized task of monitoring, evaluation and
control.
7) Critical assessment of new plant & projects.
8) Centralization of calibration, dosimetry & records.
9) Medical surveillance of exposed persons.

B) Preventive measures for external irradiation:

1) Avoidance of unnecessary X-ray examinations particularly of children & pregnant mothers.
2) Adequate control & surveillance of x-ray installations.

3) Improvement in technique.

4) Improved leadings for dose reduction shield, distance, time.

5) Effective protective measures, lead apron, rubber apron.

6) Film badge or dosimeter for workers.

7) Periodic medical examination.

8) Regular working hour.

9) Recreation & holidays.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5" 7511]

Q. What do you mean by global warming? [DU-10Ju, SUST-13Ju]

Q. Enumerate the impacts of global warming in Bangladesh. [CU-17N,16N]

Q. How the situation can be controlled to avoid the future danger? [CU-17N,16N]

Q. Explain the genesis of global warming. [CU-16J]

Q. Write short note on: Global warming. [CU-18N/M,17M,16M, 15Ju,14Ju, SUST-11J]
Answer

Global warming:

Emission of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere has been increasing ever since the beginning of the
industrial revolution. It is generally conceded that the main effects of this include an increase of about 3°C in
the average global surface temperature by the year 2030, a rise in the sea level of 0.1-0.3 meters by 2050 and an
increase in the occurrence of extreme climate events such as cyclones, heat waters and draught. The summer
will become hotter.

Temperate zone warming will induce a decline in soil moisture that impairs grain production. This will
also change the distribution of vegetation and insect vectors. A change of this magnitude would affect local,
regional and global ecosystem, sea levels and ocean currents, prevailing winds, fresh water supplies,
agriculture, forests, fisheries, industry transport, urban planning, demographics and human health.

[Ref- Park /24"/ 785]
Consequences & prevention: Please see below in the ‘consequences and prevention of greenhouse effect’.

Q. What is meant by ‘Green house effects’? [SUST-15J]

Q. ‘Greenhouse effect in Bangladesh’: explain. [CU-15J]

Q. Write short note on: Greenhouse effect. (CU-14J,13Ju]

Q. Write short note on: Green house phenomena. [CU-10J]

Answer

Green house:

; Green house is a kind of glass-house specially designed and built to rear vegetable and other plants
inside while protecting them against excessive heat or cold of the outside environment. The glass panes of he
greenhouse allows the sun light and with it the solar radiation to enter freely inside the house, but the reradiated
solar radiation from within is partially trapped by them and returned back into the green house: this causes the
temperature in a greenhouse to rise to a level higher than of the free air outside.

Q. How can you propose to reduce the greenhouse effect?
Answer

Prevention of greenhouse effect:

1) To reduce the continually increasing carbon dioxide content of the atmosphere by conserving fuel
energy.

2) To place more trees on the use of solar, hydraulic and atomic energy which are reusable.

3) Invent motor vehicle engines, which will require lesser fuel to cover longer mileage.

4) To reduce the use of diesel and other fossil fuels as much as possible and discover suitable

substitutes.
5) To create new forest areas by conserving the existing forests and employing planned aforestation.

6) To encourage use of organic manure in agricultural fields thereby reducing the use of chemical
fertilizers.
7) To stop the use of CFC and invent a cheaper substitute of the synthetic chemical.
8) To build suitable dams and walls in the coastal areas.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5" /520]

Q. Write short note on: Heat stroke. [SUST-15J]

Answer

Heat stroke:
This is attributed to failure of the heat regulating mechanism. It is characterized by very high body

temperature which may rise to 110 °F (43.3 °C). It is often fatal (mortality rate is about 40%).

Clinical features of heat stroke:

Partial or complete loss of consciousness.
Delirium.

Convulsion.

Dry & hot skin.
Classically sweating is absent or diminished (but may present in some case).

VVVVWV

Treatment:
1) Rapid cooling of the body in an ice water bath up to rectal temperature 102 °F.

2) Prevention of hypothermia by ice water bath by cautious monitoring.

3) Monitoring of vital signs & supportive treatment.
4) The patient should be kept in bed under observation until the temperature contro

[Ref- Park /24" / 784]

1 becomes stable.

Q. Discuss about sanitary disposal of refuse at a rural setting. [DU-14Ju]

Q. Write short note on: Refuse disposal. [SUST-16J, 15Ju,14Ju/J,12J]

Q. Write short note on: Solid waste disposal. [CU-10J]

Answer

The principal methods of refuse disposal are: 6 principles of methods.

1) Dumping: Refuse is dumped in low lying areas as an easy method of disposal of dry refuse. As a
result of bacterial action, refuse decreases considerably in volume and is gradually converted into
humus. Due to its certain drawbacks, it is regarded by WHO Expert Committee as the most

unsanitary method of refuse disposal.

2) Controlled tipping / sanitary land filling: It is the most satisfactory method of refuse disposal

where suitable land is available.
Refuse is placed in a trench or other prepared area, adequately compacted and covered with

earth at the end of working day > Temperature rises to over 60°C within 7 days > All the
pathogens are killed & decomposition process is hastened + Cooling down within 2-3 weeks >
Complete decomposition of organic matter within 4 to 6 months into an innocuous mass.
Three methods are used in this operation:
> The trench method.
> The ramp method.
> The area method.

3) Incineration: It is the method of choice where suitable lands are not available. Hospital refuse
which is particularly dangerous is best decomposed by incineration. It is mainly practiced in the

industrialized countries due to lack of suitable land. Due to certain drawbacks incineration has a
limited application in refuse disposal.

4) Composting: It is a method of disposal of refuse along with human excreta or sludge. In this
process the organic matters are broken down by bacterial action resulting in the formation of
compost-relatively stable humus like material. The compost can be used as manure in agricultural

land. The methods commonly used are:
> Hot fermentation method: In this method the heat produced during composting destroys

pathogenic organisms and eggs and larvae of flies. It generally takes 4 to 6 months for the
decomposition of refuse and formation of composts.
> Mechanical or aerobic method

cattle dung, straw and leaves are dumped into the pits and covered with earth after each day’s
dumping. Within 5-6 month the refuse is converted into manure which can be returned to the field.

Q. Which method of disposal of refuse is ideal and why? [SUST-18N, 17M, 13Ju]

Answer

Ideal method of disposal of refuse:

Composting is the best method of disposal of refuse.

Cause:
It is a process of nature whereby organic matter breaks down under bacterial action resulting in the

formation of relatively stable humus-like material, called the compost.
The heat produced during composting, about 60°C or higher, over a period of several days,

destroying eggs and larvae of flies, weed seeds and pathogenic agents.
The end product ‘compost’ contains few or no disease producing organisms, and is a good soil
builder containing slam amounts of the major plant nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates.

Relatively cost effective.
Environment-friendly.

Q. Write short note on: Septic tank.
Answer
Septic tank: It is a water-tight tank into which household sewage is admitted for treatment.
Design feature:
1) Capacity: Minimum capacity of a septic tank should ne at least 500 gallons.
2) Length: It is usually twice the breadth.
3) Depth: From 1.5 to 2 m.
4) Liquid depth: The recommended liquid depth is only 1.2 m.
5) Air space: There should be minimum air space of 30 cm.
6) Bottom: It should b sloping towards the inlet end. It facilitates retention of solid.
7) Inlet and outlet: There is an inlet and outlet pipe, which are submerged.
8) Cover: The septic tank should be covéred by a concrete slab of suitable thickness and provides

with a manhole.
9) Retention period: Septic tanks are designed to allow a retention period of 24 hours.

Working of a septic tank:
The stages are involved in the purification of sewage. The first stage, anaerobic digestion takes place in

the septic tank proper and the second stage, aerobic oxidation takes place outside the septic tank, in the sub-soil.
Together, these two stages complete the purification of sewage.

Operation and maintenance:
1) Use of soap water and disinfectants, such as phenol should be avoided.

2) Undue accumulation of sludge should be removed periodically.
3) Newly constructed septic tank needs to be seeded with sludge from another septic tank in use.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 796 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"/ 495]

Q. Write short note on: Man hole.

Answer

Man hole: They are openings built in the sewerage system. They are placed —
1) Whenever there is a change in the direction of sewage
2) At the meeting point of 2 or more sewers
3) At the distances of 100 meters in long straight runs.

These openings permit a man to enter the sewer for inspection, repairs and cleaning. Workers entering
the manhole are liable to gas poisoning and asphyxiation. Due precaution should be taken.

Sewage

Q. Mention the composition of sewage. Mention aims of sewage purification.
Answer
Composition of sewage:

1) Water: 99.9%

2) Solid: 0.1% (organic & inorganic)

Aims of sewage purification:
1) To stabilize the organic matter so that it can be disposed off safely.

2) To convert the sewage water into an effluent of an acceptable standard of purity that can be disposed
off in to land, rivers or sea.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 799)

For Viva

“+ Methods of disposal of sewage:
1) Sewage disposa} after treatment (purification) — Activated sludge process.

2) Sewage disposal without treatment:
> Sea outfall
> River outfall
> Land treatment
> Oxidation pond.
> Oxidation ditches.

“ Aims & objectives of sewage treatment (purification):

Y To 'stabilize' the organic matter. It means breaking down the organic matter to simple
substances, which will not decompose further. This is accomplished by bacterial action.

Y To produce an effluent which is free from pathogens and which can be disposed of without
causing a nuisance,

Y To utilize the water (effluent) and solids (sludge) economically if necessary, without risk to
health.

[Ref- Park / 24/799]

Q. Give the characteristics of good sewage effluent.
Answer
Characteristics of good sewage effluents are:
1) It should be clear, free from any deposit and should not have any faecal smell
2) When a small living fish is kept in it, it should not die within few hours
3) Ifincubated for a week at 37 deg C there will be no sign of putrefaction
4) Amount of organic ammonia present should not exceed 1 ppm, and
5) It should not absorb more than 2 parts of dissolved oxygen per 100,000 parts, kept at uniform
temperature for 5 days.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 500]

For Viva

** Biological oxygen demand (BOD): It is defined as the amount of oxygen that must be supplied to a
waste material to maintain aerobic condition during decomposition. BOD is computed in terms of parts
of million BOD values range from | ppm in natural water to 300 ppm in unnatural domestic sewage.
BOD greater than 300 indicates strong sewage, whereas BOD less than 100 indicates weak sewage.

Chemical oxygen demand (COD): It is the amount of oxygen required by a sewage for oxidation of
organic matter present in it by a chemical oxidizer.

Activated sludge treatment process: This is the most modern method of sewage disposal. The stages are:
1) Primary treatment: This consists of three stages:
> Screening: Sewage is passed through a metal screen which intercepts large floating objects.
ber allows settlement of heavier solids but allow passage of sewage

> Grit chamber: Grit cham
containing organic matter. The grit collected at the bottom is periodically removed and

disposed by dumping.
> Primary sedimentation: The sewage in the primary sedimentation tank flows very slowly with

a retention period of 6-8 hours. Purification takes place through sedimentation of suspended
matter; 50-70% solids settle down. Fat and grease rise to the surface to form scum which is

removed time to time.

Scanned with CamScanner

528 — ENDEAVOUR COMMUNITY MEDICINE FOR WRITTEN (SAQ, MCQ), VIVA & OSPE

2) Secondary treatment: It consists of 2 stages —
> Biological treatment: The sewage effluent containing organic matter and micro-organisms is
subjected to biological treatment in an aeration tank. In the aeration tank, the mixture of
activated sludge and sewage is subjected to aeration for 6-8 hours by forcing air from the
bottom of the aeration tank. During aeration aerobic bacteria of the activated sludge oxidize the
organic matter of the sewage into carbon monoxide, nitrates and water. The pathogenic

microorganisms are destroyed.
> Final sedimentation: The oxidized sewage from the aeration tank is allowed to pass into the
final or secondary settling tank where it is detained from 2-3 hours. The sludge collected at the

settling tank is called activated sludge. Part of this activated sludge is pumped back into
aeration tank for biological action.

3) Disposal of sludge: The sludge disposed either by composting or by digestion in the digestion
chamber.
4) Disposal of effluent:
> Disposal by dilution: After chlorination it can be disposed into the sea or river.
> Disposal inland: If suitable land is available the effluent can be used for irrigation purposes.

Arsenicosis

Q. What is arsenicosis? [DU-12Ju]

Q. Explain the genesis of arsenic contamination of drinking water in Bangladesh. What efforts
are taken by the GOB to tackle the situation? [CU-18N, 17M,16M, | 5Ju,14Ju]

Q. How can you prevent arsenicosis? [SUST-17M]

Q. Write short note on: Arsenicosis. [SUST-15J,13Ju,1 Ju]

Answer

Arsenicosis:
‘Arsenicosis means the clinical conditions that develop due to excess level of arsenic in the blood.

Arsenic problem in Bangladesh:

Background information:
In the late 1970s, United Nations agencies such as UNICEF provided the rural people with | million

shallow tube wells. The villagers dug 3 million more such wells at their own cost. Not only shallow tube wells,
thousands of deep tube wells were also installed throughout the country in the last two decades and have been in
use to irrigate the cultivated lands and support the ongoing development in the agricultural sector. 1993 the tube
well water was found to be contaminated with arsenic in certain areas of the country which was first sounded by
a Kolkata chemical analyst in 1988. Continued investigation since 1993 detected water from shallow tube wells
in many places of 4 districts out of 64 districts of Bangladesh to have been contaminated with arsenic- throwing
about 15 million people at risk of slow arsenic poisoning. As per WHO standard the recommended limit of
arsenic concentration in potable water is 0.01mg/liter, in Bangladesh that limit has been set at 0.05mg/liter.

Scanned with CamScanner

~~

530 — ENDEAVOUR COMMUNITY MEDICINE FOR WRITTEN (SAQ, MCQ), VIVA & OSPF

Causes of arsenic poisoning: The groundwater arsenic problem in Bangladesh arises because of an

unfortunate combination of three factors:
v Asource of arsenic (arsenic is present in the aquifer sediments),
Y Mobilization (arsenic is released from the sediments to the groundwater) &
Y Transport (arsenic is flushed away in the natural groundwater circulation).

Clinical features:
> Primary Stage or stage 1: Melanosis, kerotosis, conjunctivitis, gastroenteritis, inflammation
respiratory tract.
> Secondary Stage or stage 2: Leukomelanosis, hyperkeratosis, non-pitting oedema of feet and legs,
peripheral neuropathy, liver and kidney disorder, ; ,
> Tertiary Stage or stage 3: Gangrene of distal organs or parts of the body, cancer of the skin, lungs
urinary bladder, kidney and liver failure. ,

Prevention & control of arsenicosis:
1) Detection of contamination,

2) Identification of cases,

3) Cessation of arsenic contaminated water intake,
4) ,Provision of safe drinking water,

5) Treatment of arsenicosis:

> Symptomatic treatment of cases:
Y Adequate nutrition, sufficient protein supplementation & anti-oxidants (vitamin A,

C, E) therapy can help in reversal of early arsenicosis.
Y Liniments of 20% urea & 10-20% acetyl salicylates in petroleum jelly base are
used locally as keratolytic treatment on thickened palms & soles.

> Treatment with specific antidotes: D-Penicillamine, Dimercaprol & Dimercaptosuccinic
acid are established chelating agents in acute arsenic poisoning (sequester arsenic away
from the blood, common side effect is hypertension).

> Treatment of complications.

6) Rehabilitation of patients,
7) Social advocacy & counseling to raise morale.

Bangladesh program for tackling the problem:

Government of Bangladesh has formed a national steering committee for arsenic contamination
mitigation activities. The steering committee consists of al! agencies working in the field of arsenic related

problems. The government has so far taken three major strategies:
Phase-one: To identify the arsenic contaminated tube-wells and mark them with red colour and

mark the non-contaminated ones with green colour.
> Phase-two: To provide deep tube wells as well as emergency measures in those locations where

most of the tube wells are found to be contaminated by arsenic.
> Phase-three: To provide treated safe surface water through pipes to the people. Simultaneously

efforts are to be taken to create awareness among the people.
Three projects under the ministry of Health and Family Welfare have just completed their phase one.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 485-487]

Provision of safe water in an arsenicosis affected community:

1) Sono filter.
2) Boiling of pond, well & river water.

3) Rain water.
4) Potash alum mixed in pond, well & river water.

Lead poisoning / Plumbism

Q. Define plumbism.
Q. List at risk workers for plumbism. [DU-14Ju]
Q. Write short note on: Plumbism. [RU-17N,16M]

Answer ,
Plumbism /saturnism: Chronic exposure of lead (Pb) is called plumbism.

1) Facial pallor.
2) Anaemia. .
3) Lead line / ‘Burtonian line’: A strippled blue line is seen at the gums in 50-70% cases. It appears at

the junction with teeth, within a week of exposure especially in the upper jaw.
4) Colicky pain. |
5) Constipation.
6) Lead palsy. |
7) Lead encephalopathy (present in almost every case & frequently encountered in children). |
8) Effect on CVS: Hypertension & permanent arteriolar degeneration.
9) Effect on kidneys: Chronic intestinal nephritis.
10) Sterility & menstrual abnormality.
11) Lead osteopathy (in case of children and young individuals).
12) Effect on liver: Acute or chronic degeneration may occur.
13) Optic atrophy.
14) Other effects: Dyspepsia, anorexia, emaciation, general weakness, exhaustion, alopecia etc.

Management of chronic lead poisoning:
A) Curative:
1) Removal of the patient from the source of poison.
2) Chelating agent: Disodium calcium edetate is the best chelating agent for Pb.
Dose: 1gm twice daily is given by slow I/V drip over a period of 1 hour, mixed with 5%
glucose saline for 5 days.

3) Potassium or sodium iodide 1-2 gm, thrice daily to eliminate circulatory Pb through urine.

4) Sodium bicarbonate 20-30 gm/day in 4-5 divided doses.

5) To prevent constipation magnesium sulphate purgative is used.

6) For severe colic 0.5-1 mg of atropine sulphate and /or hot compression on the abdomen is
useful.

7) Leg encephalopathy in children may need surgical decompression of the skull.

8) Symptomatic treatment should be given.

B) Prophylaxis:
1) To prevent chronic lead poisoning in the factory: Maintenance of proper ventilation,

maintenance of personal hygiene of the workers and their periodic medical checkup is
necessary.

2) Advice should be given to wash fruits before eating and avoidance of canned foods that are
preserved in containers lined by lead.

3) Lead vermilion, cosmetics and dyes may be used keeping the danger in mind.

Complications of lead poisoning:

1) Gastroenteritis.

2) Malnutrition.

3) Intercurrent infection.
4) Hepatic failure.

5) Respiratory failure.
6) Renal failure.

Ozone Layer Depletion

Q. Define ozone layer.
Q. State the impact of ozone layer depletion on community health. [DU-14Ju]
Answer

Ozone layer / Ozone shield / Ozonosphere:

The ozone layer refers to a region of earth’s stratosphere that absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet (UV)
radiation. It contains high concentrations of ozone (Os) relative to other parts of the atmosphere, although still
very small relative to other gases in the stratosphere. It is situated roughly between 15 and 35 km (9 and 22

miles) above earth’s surface.

Source of ozone layer:
UV light strikes ordinary oxygen molecules containing two oxygen atoms (O,), splitting them into

individual oxygen atoms (atomic oxygen). The atomic oxygen then combines with unbroken O, to create ozone
(Os).
0, + Avyy — 20
0 +02 — 03 ‘
Functions of ozone layer:
The ozone layer absorbs 97-99% of the sun’s medium-frequency UV light (from about 200 nm to
315 nm wavelength), which otherwise would potentially damage exposed life forms near the surface.
The United Nations General Assembly has designated September 16 as the International Day for the
Preservation of the Ozone Layer.

Effects of ozone layer depletion on community health: Ozone layer depletion increases in surface UV ray
which lead to:

1) Basal & squamous cell carcinoma of skin.

2) Malignant melanoma of skin.

3) Cortical cataract.

4) Immunesuppression.

5) Increased oxidation process in human body & aging process.

Q. “Road traffic accidents cause social disaster”-justify the statement. [RU-13J]

Answer
Road traffic accidents cause social disaster: acts,
Of all the types of accidents, road traffic accidents are foremost to cause fatal injuries to occupants of

motor vehicles and pedestrians as well.
WHO studies show that road accidents account for 2.5 percent of the total deaths.
It is among the six leading causes of death and about 300,000 deaths occur annually in the world from
road accidents and the number of persons sustaining non-fatal injuries and requiring periods of treatment and
nursing care are at least 40 times of this figure.

In this way road traffic accidents cause social disaster. ;
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /384]

Q. Discuss disaster management. [SUST-16M]

Q. Write short note on: Disaster preparedness. [SUST-14Ju, 12Ju]

Answer

Disaster preparedness and response:
A) Prevention and alleviation of consequences:
1

) Forecasting the disaster using modern technology.

2) Ascertaining the risk by periodically enlisting the support of various social groups.

3) Evacuation of people to a nearest safe shelter.

4) Promoting community preparedness by such activities like exercise in first aid, exercise in
providing temporary shelter, sanitary exercises including installation and management of safe
water supply, use of sanitary latrines, controlled refuse disposal, fly control , vector control ,
rodent control etc.

5) Improving professional qualities of local health personnel.

B) Immediate emergency care:
1) Whatever be the type of disaster, the local authority is required to set up an emergency
committee. The first task of the committee is to inform or instruct the people by using
loudspeakers and to mobilize volunteers so as to dispel fear and panic.

2) The first Priority following a disaster should be the care of the injured. The injured and afflicted
victims must be removed to the nearest medical establishment for emergency care. Those
requiring specialized surgical care or medical treatment are to be removed by ambulance, motor
boats etc to the nearest medical center with good facilities.

RANASRAAA AAA .
Scanned with CamScanner

Chapter-16: Accident & Disaster ———————— _ 547
C) Management of the aftermath:

1) Environmental sanitation.

2) Public health monitoring and prevention of epidemics.
3) Vaccination against six major children diseases.

4) Food and nutrition.

D) Rehabilitation & reconstruction:

1) Reconstruction and rehabilitation are time consuming. Nevertheless planning for reconstruction
start immediately after the disaster and it is important to include measures for the
reconstruction of the damaged area in the national disaster plan.

2) Planners should play due attention not only to the erection of new households and public
buildings but also to industry, agriculture and all other socioeconomic aspects of
reconstruction.

3) Statistical information on the following points is required before the planning for
reconstruction-

> Number of affected person, there geographical distribution, age group, occupation etc.
> Damage to water supply and health centre.

> Number and standard of house destroyed.

> Available manpower, materials, equipment and financial sources.

4) The authorities responsible for rehabilitation should establish priorities: reconstruct roads and
public buildings, execute programmes for replacing destroyed housing: exercise economic and

technical control of labour and material.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5/390]

Mitigation / reduction of the health effects of disaster: Emergency prevention and mitigation involves
measures designed either to prevent hazards from causing emergency or to lessen the likely effects of

emergencies. These measures include —
> Food mitigation works.
> Appropriate land-use planning.
> Improved building codes.

> Reduction or protection of vulnerable population and structures.

Q. Define triage. [CU-17N]
Q. Write short note on: Triage.
Answer
Triage:

It consists of rapidly classifying the injured on the basis of the severity of the injuries and livelihood of
their survival with prompt medical attention. Triage is the only approach that can provide maximum benefit to
the great number of injured in a major disorder.

Four color code system for triage:

1) Red: High priority treatment or transfer.
2) Yellow: Medium priority.
3) Green: Ambulatory patients.

4) Black: Dead / morbid patients.

Occupational health & Ergonomics

Q. Define occupational health,
Q. What do you mean by occupational health?
Answer

Occupational health:
The Joint ILO/WHO committee on occupational health (1950) gave the following definition —
“Occupational health should aim at the Promotion and maintenance of the highest degree of physical,
mental and social well-being of workers in all occupations; the prevention among workers of departures from
health caused by their working conditions; the protection of workers in their employment from risks resulting
from factors adverse to health; the placing & maintenance of the workers in an occupational environment
adapted to his physiological & psychological equipment and to summarize the adaptation of work to man &

each man to his job.”
[Ref- Park / 24" / 849]

Q. What are the objectives of occupational health? [CU-17N,16N, RU-14Ju]

Answer

Objectives of occupational health:

1) The promotion and maintenance of the highest degree of physical, mental and social well-being of
workers in all occupation.

2) The prevention among workers of departure from health by their working conditions.

3) The protection of workers in their employment from risk resulting from factors adverse to health.

4) The placing and maintenance of the workers in an occupational environment adapted to this
physiological and psychological equipment.

5) The adaptation of work to man and each man to his job.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 208]

Q. Deéfine’ergonomics. [DU-18N]
ite down the objectives of ergonomics. [DU-18N]

nsWer
Ergonomics: The term ergonomics is derived from the Greek ergon, meaning work and nomos, meaning law. It

simply means: ‘fitting the job to the worker’.

Objective: To achieve the best mutual adjustment of man and his work, for the improvement of human
(> efficiency and well-being. :
[Ref- Park / 24" / 840]

Q. What do you mean by occupational environment? [CU-10Ju]
Q. Enumerate types of interaction in working environment.
Answer

Occupational / working environment:

It means “the sum of external conditions and influences which prevail at the place of work and which
have a bearing on the health of the working population.
[Ref- Park /24" / 840]

Q. How occupational environment determines health and disease of workers of factory? Explain.

Q. Enumerate types of interaction in working environment.
Answer

Occupational environment determines health and disease of workers of factory:

Basically, there are three types of interaction in an occupational environment as follow:
1) Man and physical, chemical and biological agent.
2) Man and machine.
3) Man and man.

Man and man:

disturb his sleep. Severe prolonged stress, no matter where it has been aroused, may produce serious physical or

mental symptoms which do not allow man to work efficiently. -

Possible health problems: Coal miner’s pneumoconiosis (anthracosis).

It may have two general phases:

1) The first phase is labeled as simple pneumoconiosis which is associated with little ventilatory
impairment. This phase may require about 12 years of work exposure for its development.

2) The second phase is characterized by progressive massive fibrosis (PMF); this causes severe
respiratory disability and frequently results in premature death. Once a background of simple
pneumoconiosis has been attained in the coal worker, a progressive massive fibrosis may develop
out of it without further exposure to it.

Preventive measures: As there is no cure for this conditions emphasis should be on preventive measures; eg.
> Dust control.
> Personal protection and.
> Periodic medical check-up.

Sili€osis
Q. Write short note on: Silicosis.
Answer
Silicosis:

” It is an occupational disease caused by inhalation of dust containing free silica or silicon dioxide, found
in mining industry, Pottery and ceramic industry, sand blasting, metal grinding, iron & steel industry, building

and construction works and others, Among the occupational disease, it is the major cause of permanent
disability and mortality.

The incidence of silicosis depends upon:
1)

Chemical composition
2) Health status of the person exposed
3) Fineness
4) Concentration of the dust in the air
5) Period of exposure

Size of the particle: 0.5 to 3 micron
Incubation period: It may vary from a few months up to years of exposure.

Pathogenesis:
Particles are ingested by the phagocytes
N

Accumulation and blockage of the lymph
L

Formation of dense nodular fibrosis

Symptoms: .
Initially there is dry irritant cough, dyspnoea on exertion and pain in the chest. In advance cases,

impairment of the total lung capacity is commonly seen. An X-ray of the chest shows “snow-storm” appearance
in the lung fields.

Prevention and control: As there is no effective treatment for silicosis, the only way that silicosis can be
controlled is by —

(i) Rigorous dust control measures, ¢.g. substitution, complete enclosure, isolation, hydro blasting, good
house-keeping, Personal protective measure
(ii) Regular physical examination of the workers.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 843]

Characteristics / criteria of occupational cancer:
1) They appear after prolonged exposure.

3) The disease may develop even after the cessation of the exposure.
4) The average age incidence is earlier than that for cancer in general.
5) The localization of the tumor is remarkably constant in any one occupation.

_Kécident in industry

Q. What are the causes of accident in industry?

Answer
Causes of accident in industry: The causes of accidents are several and may be grouped under 2 headlines —

(A) Human factors:
(i) Physical: The physical factors of the worker may not meet the job requirements; his visual

acuity may be inadequate; his hearing may be inadequate.

(ii) Physiological factors:

a. Sex: Women are known to have more accidents than men.

b. Age: Younger ages are known to be involved more in accidents than older age groups.

c. Time: Accidents are minimum at the beginning of the day and increase gradually as

fatigue sets in.

d. Experience: Experience is an important factor in the occurrence of accidents. The
more the experience the less are the accidents.
Working Hours: An increase in accidents is found whenever the daily or weekly
working hours increase.

e.

(B) Environmental factors: The temperature, poor illumination, humidity, noise and unsafe machines

influence the incidence of accidents.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 847]

out a plan to prevent acci i i
Races p accidents in the industry. [RU-15Ju]
Prevention of accidents in industry: The principles of accident prevention are —
1) Adequate pre-placement examination.
2) Adequate job training.
3) Continuing education.
4) Ensuring safe working environment
5) Establishing a safety department in the organization under a competent safety engineer.
6) Periodic survey for finding out hazards.

7) Careful reporting, maintenance of records & publicity.

Slaughter house

Q. What are the criteria of good slaughter house?
Answer

Criteria of good slaughter house are:
¢ away from human habitation.

1) It should be situated on a high land outside the town an
2) The floor should be cemented having proper slope.
3) It should have good drainage system.

4) It should have a high boundary wall.
5) Provision should exist for proper disposal of skin, bones, intestines, blood etc.

6) Water supply should be adequate.
7) Screening of doors and windows should be provided.

8) It should not be used for sleeping.

Badge of the trade

Q. What do you mean by “badge of the trade”?
Answer

Badge of the trade:

The trauma of a particular occupation often gives rise to characteristic stigma “badge of the trade”. For
example; discoloured nails of photographers and hairdressers, white fingers due to traumatic vasospasm in
workers handling vibration tools, metallic tattooing as a result of explosives.

Q. Mention some factory acts.
Answer

Factory act: The factories act regulating the working conditions of the workers are —
1) Keeping the factory premises clean.
2) Proper disposal of wastes and effluents produced due to manufacturing process.
3) Proper ventilation and adequate measures to protect workers from excessive temperature.
4) Measures to protect workers from inhalation of dust and fumes.
5) Providing artificial humidification in cotton mills.
6) Provision of sufficient space to avoid overcrowding.
7) Arranging sufficient and suitable lighting and preventing glare in the factory.
8) Adequate supply of wholesome drinking water for the worker.
9) Provision of sufficient number of latrines and urinals.
10) Provision of bathing, washing and canteen facilities.
11) Supply of first aid appliances.
12) Prohibiting employment of children below the age of 14 years.

Chapter-18

Mental Health

Q. Define mental health.

Q. What are the warning signals of poor mental health? [RU-18M]
Answer

Mental health:

More recently, mental health has been defined as “a state of balance between the individual and the
surrounding world, a state of harmony between oneself and others, coexistence between the realities of the self
and that of other people and that of the environment”.

[Ref- Park /24" / 15]

Warning signals of poor mental health:
1) Worrying all the while.

2) Inability to concentrate.

3) Continually unhappy.

4) Loses temper easily.

5) Regular sleep disturbance.

6) Incapacitating fluctuations of mood.

7) Continual disliking of people's company.

8) Easily upset by disturbed daily routine.

9) Having constant pain and aches without physical cause.

10) Fear and panic without real cause.

11) Feeling own decisions always right and other's wrong.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder 15" / 425 + Park /24™ / 868]

Q. Enumerate the criteria of a mentally healthy person. [RU-18M]

Answer

Criteria of a mentally healthy person:
1

) Is free from internal conflicts.
2) Is well adjusted.
3) Searches for identity. .
4) Hasa strong sense of self-esteem.
5) Knows himself; his needs, problems & goals.

6) Has good self-control.
7) Faces problems and tries to solve them intelligently.

Health information

Q. State health information system. [RU-08Ju]
Q. What are the components of health information system?
Q. Enumerate the sources of health information in Bangladesh. [RU-08Ju]

Answer

Health information system:

Health information system is defined as “a mechanism for the collection, processing, analysis and
transmission of information required for organizing and Operating health services, and also for research and

training”.
Components of health information system:
1) Demography and vital events.
2) Environmental health statistics,
3) Health status — mortality, morbidity, disability and quality of life.
4) Health resources — facilities, beds, manpower.
5) Utilization and non-utilization of health services — attendance, admissions, waiting lists.
6) Indices of outcome of medical care.
7) Financial statistics (cost, expenditure) related to the particular objective.

Uses of health information:

1) To measure the health status of the people of a community and to quantify the health problems and
medical & health care needs of a community.

2) For local, national and international comparison of health status.

3) For planning, administration and effective management of health services and programmes.

4) For assessing whether health services are accomplishing their objects in terms of their effectiveness
and efficacy.

5) For assessing the attitudes and degree of satisfaction of the beneficiaries with the health system.

6) For research into particular problems of health and disease.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 876]

stics

Statistics & Biostati

Q. Define statistics. Describe in brief the function and use of statistics.

Answer

Statistics:
According to Croxton and Cowden, statistics may be defined as “the science of collection, presentation,

analysis and interpretation of numerical data.”

Function and uses of statistics;
1. Collection of information in the best possible way.

Simplification of huge complex sets of data.

Elucidation of ideas- formulation of hypothesis.

Community health diagnosis.

Measurement of association between two or more variables.

Prediction and forecasting,

Designing experimental study.

Analyzing data and drawing conclusions,

Providing information support to planning, management, monitoring and evaluation of health
service programmes.

[Ref- Higher secondary statistics book / A.K. Azad + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 110]

Q. Define bio-statistics.

Q. State the uses of bio-statistics. [DU-16N]
Answer

Bio-statistics:

Bio-statistics is that branch of statistics concerned with mathematical facts and data relating to

biological events.

Uses of Bio-statistics:

1) To define what is normal or healthy in a population and to find the limits of normality in variables

such as weight and pulse rate.

2) To test whether the difference between two populations, regarding a particular attribute is real ora

chance occurrence,

3) To study the correlation or association between two or more attributes in the same population.

4) To evaluate the efficacy of vaccines, sera etc by control studies

5) Ro locate, define and measure the extent of morbidity and mortality in the community in the

community.

6) To evaluate the achievements of public health programs.

7) To fix priorities in public health programs.

Q. State the major events of vital statistics. [DU-13J]

Q. Write short note on: Vital statistics.
Answer
Vital statistics:

[Ref- Gupta /3™ /371]

Vital statistics is that branch of statistics that deals with collection, compilation and presentation of data

about the vital events of life.

Vital events are those events which have to'do with individuals entrance into or departure from life

with change in civil status. It includes:
> Birth.
> Death.
> Marriage.

Sources of vital statistics:
1) Census
2) Vital registration method
3) Health and demographic surveys
4) Hospital and other institutional records
5) Sample vital registration system
6) Surveillance

Uses of vital statistics:
1) To describe health status of a community.
2) To diagnose health problems of a community.

3) To determine priorities, planning and evaluation of health programmes.

4) To promote health legislation.
5) For research purposes.

Previous surveys,
> Professional journals etc,

“* On the basis of nature:

vaccinated; anaemic, not anaemic etc,

Q. What are the methods of data presentation? [RU-17N,16M,15J,14J,11Ju, SUST-18M,13J,12J,

10J]
Q. How data can be presented? [DU-15J, SUST-15J]

Q. How can you present your research findings? [RU-13J]
Q. What are the types of statistical table? [RU-10J]
Q. Write short note on: Methods of data presentation. [SUST-17N]

Answer

Methods of data presentation:

A) Tabulation: Three types of tables are in use:
1) Master table: In this table all initial readings as per designed proforma are serially recorded.

When the number of observation is large and several attributes have to be studied, the master
table is must.

2) Simple table: In this the characteristic under observation is fixed and the number of frequency
of events is small.

3) Frequency distribution table: this is the most important table in statistical work. In a
frequency table large, unsorted data is presented in a small manageable number of groups. This

can be prepared using either type of data, qualitative and quantitative data.

B) Drawings (charts, diagrams & maps):
1) Bar chart: bar charts are way of presenting a set of numbers by the length of a bar-the length
of which is proportional to the magnitude to be represented. The following are some examples

of bar charts:
Y Simple bar chart: Bars may be vertical or horizontal. The bars are usually separated

by appropriate spaces with an eye to neatness and clear presentation.
Y Multiple / compound bar charts: In this type, two or more bars can be grouped

together.
¥ Component bar chart: In this type, the bars are divided into two or more parts, each

part representing a certain item and proportional to the magnitude of that particular
item.

Histogram: It consists of a series of blocks. The class intervals are given along the horizontal

axis and the frequency along the vertical axis.

3) Frequency polygon: It is simply a derivation from the histogram obtained by joining the
midpoints of various histogram blocks.

4) Frequency curve: When the number of observations is large, the polygon loses angulations
and it becomes a frequency curve.

5) Line chart or graph: It shows the trend of an event over a period of time.

6) Scatter or Dot diagram: A graphic presentation is made here to show the extent and nature of
correlation between two variables such as height and weight.

7) Pie or Sector diagram: In this type, data are presented in a circle. Degrees of angles and the
area of the sectors denote the relative frequency.

8) Map diagram or Spot map: These are prepared to show geographical distribution of the
frequencies of the characteristics. The spot map also helps in locating the index case in an
epidemic.

9) Pictogram: In this type, small picture:
method of presentation of data to the man in the street and to those who cannot unde!

orthodox charts.

Q. Describe histogram.
Answer
Histogram:
It is a pictorial diagram of frequency distribution. It is a special form of bar chart of frequency
distribution that represents classes of continuous data.
Criteria:
1) Consist of a series of blocks.
2) The class intervals are given along the horizontal axis.
3) Thee frequencies are given along the vertical axis.
4) The area of each block or rectangle is proportional to the frequency.

Q. Discuss pie diagram. [SUST-12J]

Answer

Pie chart / sector diagram:

A pie chart is a system of presentation of data in a circle subdivided into parts to reveal the various
components of the data.

A circle has 360 degrees at the centre which are divided into sectors in proportion to the components of
the data. Sectors are coloured or shaded differently. This permits comparison between the different components
of the same phenomenon.

Q. Define survey.
Answer

Survey:
Collection of data on a particular disease especially its epidemiological aspects is called survey.

Hypothesis

Q. Write short note on: Hypothesis.
Answer
Hypothesis:
A hypothesis is a supposition, arrived at from or reflection. It can be accepted or rejected, using the

techniques of analytical epidemiology.

Types of variable:
A) Qualitative / categorical variables: The values of variables which are expressed in

numeric narrative values. Example — doctor, engineer, teacher, urban, rural etc.
B) Quantitative / numerical variables: The values of variables which are expressed in numbers, e.g. age,
weight, monthly income etc. It is of two types —
1. Continuous variable: A continuous variable is one which can have an infinite numbers of
possible values in a given interval. For example — height in cm, weight in kg etc.
2. Discrete variable: A discrete variable is one which can have only a finite numbers of values in
a given interval. For example — number of hospital bed, number of family members ete.

is termed as a dependent variable.

3. Extraneous / Confounding variable: Independent variables that are not related to the purpose
of study, but may affect the dependent variable are termed as confounding variable. Example —

Alcohol consumption causes oesophageal cancer. Smoking influences oesophageal cancer.
Here, alcohol is independent variable, oesophageal cancer is dependent variable, and smoking

is confounding variable.
