Discuss different sampling methods. [DU-18M,16N]
Q. Give the characteristic features of simple random sampling. [RU-18M]
Q. Write short note on: Sampling techniques. [CU-13J]
Q. Write short note on: Simple random sampling. [RU-11J]

Answer

Classification of sampling / different methods of sampling / sampling technique:
A) Probability sampling / Chance sampling / Random sampling:

1) Simple random sampling: This method is applicable when the population is small,
homogenous and readily available. The simple is drawn in such a way that each unit has an

equal chance of being drawn in the sample. So, this method is also called unrestricted random
sampling. To ensure randomness of selection, lottery method or table of Random Number can

be adopted.
2) Systematic sampling: In a systematic sampling, the selection of the first unit is made at
random and subsequent units are selected at certain interval.

3) Stratified sampling: The sample is deliberately drawn in a systemic way so that each portion
of the sample represents a corresponding stratum of the universe. This method is particularly

useful where one is interested in analyzing the data by a certain characteristics of the
population, viz Muslims, Hindus, Christians.

4) Multistage sampling: This method refers to the sampling procedures carried out in several
stages using random sampling techniques.

5) Cluster sampling: A cluster is a randomly selected group. This method is used when units of
population are natural groups or clusters such as villages, wards, blocks, slums of a town,

factories, workshops or children of a school etc. As per module approved by WHO, it is the
most often used to evaluate vaccination coverage in Expanded Program of Immunization and

Universal Immunization Programme.

6) Multiphase sampling: In this method, part of the information is collected from the whole
sample and part from sub-sample.

B) Non-probability sampling:
1) Deliberate sampling / Purposive sampling / Judgment sampling: In this method, items for
her; his choice concerning the items remains

the sample are selected deliberately by the researc!

supreme.

2) Quota sampling: Under quota sampling the interviewers are simply given quota to be filled
from the different strata, with some restriction on how they are to be filled.

3) Accidental sampling: When the sample is collected without the intension of the researcher to
collect the sample of that occasion.

4) Convenient sampling: When the sampling is carried out according to the convenience of the

researcher.

Central tendency: In case of large number of observation there is generally a tendency of the observation to
cluster around a central point. This is known as central tendency. There are mainly 3 main measure of

central tendency:
> Mean

> Median
> Mode

‘> Mean: There are three types of mean:
¥ Arithmetic mean
¥ Geometric mean
Y Harmonic mean
Arithmetic mean: It is widely used in statistical calculation. It is sometimes called simply the
mean. It is the sum of all the observations divided by the number of observations. Symbolically
an arithmetic mean is ‘X’
X = YX/N; Y-X= Summation of all the observations
N= Number of observation
X = Mean value

For example, pulse rate of some 10 individual were 68, 74, 56, 64, 75, 66, 59, 73, 55 & 60.
Here, X= 68+ 74+ 56+ 64+ 75+ 66+ 59+ 73+55 +60 = 650
N= 10
X = DX/N= 650/10 = 65.
Advantage: It is easy to calculate and understand.
Disadvantage:
> Sometimes it may be unduly influenced by abnormal values in distribution.
> Sometimes it may even look ridiculous.

b. Geometric mean: It is the ‘n’th root of product of ‘n’ observations.

Median: It is the middle most value of a series when observations are arranged in ascending or
descending order. If n is odd, the value in the (n+1)/2th position is the median. For example, in the
following series the value of (9+1)/2th e.g. 5" position that is so 10 is the median.

4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14

If there is an even number of observations (‘n’ is even), then there is no single middle value
i.e. there are two middle positions, these are n/2 & (n/2 +1). The median is then usually defined to the
arithmetic mean of the two middle values in the n/2 & (n/2 +1)th position.

fe

Mode: Mode is the value which occurs most frequently, i.e. a value which has the highest frequency in
the series is the mode. For example in the series: 7, 9, 8, 6, 9, 11, 14 9 is the mode.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"/ 118]

Q. Write short note on: Measures of dispersion. [CU-14J]

Answer
Dispersion: Dispersion means scattering of values of the variable.

Measures of dispersion: There are several measures of variation of which the following are widely known:

1) The range.
2) The mean or average deviation.
3) The standard deviation.

“ The range: It is defined as the difference between the highest and lowest figure in a given sample.

Example: From the following record of DBP of 10 individuals-
83, 75, 81, 79, 71, 90, 75, 95, 77, 94
Here, the highest value is 95 and the lowest value is 71. So range will be difference between 95
and 71; i.e. range = 95 — 71 = 24.

“+ The mean deviation: It is the average of the deviations from the arithmetic mean.

Formula: It is given by the formula-

M.D. =¥ (X - X)/N
Example: The diastolic blood pressure of 10 individuals was as follow: 83, 75, 81, 79, 71, 95,75,
77, 84 & 90.

Q. Write short note on: Types of communication. [SUST-14Ju, 13Ju]

Answer

Types of communication:

1) One way communication (Didactic method).
2) Two way communication (Socratic method).
3) Verbal communication.
4) Non-verbal communication.
5) Formal and informal communication.
6) Visual communication.
7) Telecommunication and internet.
[Ref- Park /24"/891]

Explanation of any two:
“ One-way communication (Didactic method): The flow of communication in "One way" from the

communicator to the audience.
Examples: Lectures, films, printed materials, radio and posters.
Drawbacks:

Knowledge is imposed.

Learning is authoritative.

Little audience participation.

No feedback.

Does not influence human behaviour.

“Two-way communication (Socratic method): The Socratic methods is a two-way method of
communication in which both the communicator and the audience take part. The audience may raise
questions, and add their own information, ideas and opinions to the subject. The process of learning is

active and ‘democratic’. It is more likely to influence behaviour than one-way communication.

VVVVV

Examples: Interviews, discussions, demonstrations, and contrived situations.
[Ref- Park / 24" / 892]

Q. Briefly discuss the functions of health communication. [RU-17M, #5J,13Ju,12J]

Q. State the importance of good health communication.
Q. Why counseling is preferred to advising health communication? [RU-

Q. Write va Persuation. [RU-18N]

15J]

Answer
Functions ofhealth communication: Health communication has to cater to the following needs —
\\_1y Information: The primary function of health communication is to provide scientific knowledge or
information to people about health problems and how to maintain and promote health.
2) Education: Education of the general public is an integral part of a prevention-oriented approach to
health and disease problems; and the basis of all education is communication.
3) Motivation: It is the power that drives a person from within to act. One of the goals of health
communication is to motivate individuals to translate health information into personal behaviour
and lifestyle for their own health. Motivation includes the stages of interest, evaluation and decision

making.
4) Persuasion: It is the art of winning friends and influencing people. It is an art that does not employ

force or deliberate manipulation.
5) Counseling: It is a process that can help people understand better and deal with their problems and
communicate better with those with whom they are emotionally involved.
6) Raising morals: It is the capacity of a group of people (or team) to pull together persistently or
consistently.
Communication can play a powerful role in health development by helping

7) Health development:
diffuse knowledge in respect of the goals of development and preparing the people for the roles

expected of them.
8) Organization: Communication is the life and blood of an organization.

[Ref- Park /24"/893]

Q. Why communication skills are essential in providing health education? ,
Answer

Importance of communication skills in providing health education:
Communication is part of our normal relationship with other people. Our ability to influence others
depends on our communication skills; e.g. speaking, writing, listening, reading and reasoning. These skills are

much needed in health education.
Communication revolution is important to put today’s health information at the disposal of families, to

help people to achieve health by their own actions and efforts.

Answer

Communication process / key elements of communication process: 5 key elements.

a

“Sender (source)

** Receiver (audience)
“* Message (content)

“> Channel (s) (medium)
“Feedback (effect)

1) Sender: The sender (communicator) is the originator of the message. To be an effective communicator,
he must know:
> His objectives, clearly defined.
> His audience, it’s interests & needs.
> His message.
> Channels of communication.
> His professional abilities and limitations.

2) Receiver: All communications must have an audience; this may be a single or a group of people. They
are the consumers of the message.

3) Message: A message is the information which the communicator transmits to his audience to receive,
understand, accept and act upon. It may be in the form of words, pictures or signs. Health
communication may fail in many cases, if its message is not adequate. A good message must be —

In line with the objective (s).

Meaningful.

Based on felt needs.

Clear and understandable.

Specific and accurate,

Timely & adequate.

Fitting the audience.

Interesting.

Culturally & socially appropriate.

VVVVVVVVV

4) Channels of communication: By channel is implied the ‘physical bridges’ or the media of
communication between the sender and receiver. The total communication effort is based on 3 media
systems:

Interpersonal communication.

Mass media.

Traditional or folk media.

VVV

}

The choice of the medium is an important factor in the effectiveness of communication.

5) Feedback: It is the flow of information from the audience to the sender. It is the reaction of the
audience to the message. Feedback is generally obtained through opinion polls, attitude surveys and
interviews.

Q. Discuss the channel of communication.

Answer

Channel of communication: Message can be communicated through some channels. Channels are implied as
“physical bridges" or the media of communication between the sender and the receiver.

Message can be communicated through:
1) Interpersonal communication: This is the most common channel of communication. It is more

persuasive and effective than other ways of communication.

2) Mass media: Mass media such as, Television, radio, newspaper, printed material, direct mailing ,
posters and internet play an important role in communication of message.

3) Folk media: such as keerthan, katha, folk songs, dances and drama, puppet show also convey
messages.

4) Group approaches: such as- lectures, demonstrations, and other discussion methods like-group
discussion and panel discussion, symposium, workshop and conferences also play vital role in

transmitting messages.
[Ref- Park / 24/892]

Health Education

Q. Define health education? [RU-17N, SUST-18N/M,17N,16N, 13J,10Ju]
Answer
Health education:

The definition adapted by the national conference on preventive medicine in USA, is ‘health education
is a process that informs motivates and helps people to adopt and maintain health practices and life styles,
advocates environmental changes as needed to facilitate this goal and conducts professional training and
research to the same end.’

Or,

The dynamic definition of health education by Alma- Ata Declaration is as follows:
“a process aimed at encouraging people to want to be healthy, to know how to stay healthy, to do what they can

individually and collectively to maintain health and to seek help when needed".
[Ref- Park / 24" / 894]

Q. Write down the changing concept of health education.

Answer

Changing concept of health education: Historically health education has been committed to disseminating
information and changing human behaviour. Following Alma -At declaration the changing concepts are —

- Prevention of disease and promotion of healthy lifestyles.

- The modification of individual behaviour to modification of "social environment" in which the
individual lives.

- Community participation and community involvement.

- Promotion of individual and community "self-reliance".
[Ref- Park /24"/895]

Q. What are the aims and objectives of health education? [CU-10Ju]
Q. Highlight the objectives of health education. [SUST-18N,17N]
Answer
Aims and objectives of health education:
1) To encourage people to adopt and sustain health promoting life style and practice.
2) To promote the proper use of health services available to them.
3) To arouse interest, provide new knowledge, improve skill and change attitudes in making rational
decisions to solve their own problems; and
4) To stimulate individual and community self-reliance and participation to achieve health
developments through individual and community involvement at every step from identifying

problems to solving them.
[Ref- Park /24"/895]

vant are the different approaches to health education? [RU-I7N/M, | 1Ju/J]
er
Approach to health education: There are 4 well known approaches to health education —
1) Regulatory approach (Managed prevention):
° ce be defined as any governmental intervention, direct or indirect, designed to alter human
ehavior.

* May seem to be simplest and quickest way to improve health or bring about desired changes in
society.

2) Service approach:
¢ Aimed at providing all the health services needed by the people at their door steps on the
assumption that people would use than to improve their own health,

3) Health education approach:
¢ Since attitudes and behavioral patterns are formed early is life. We must move back in time &
start health education with young population.
© There are many problems e.g. cessation of smoking, use of safe water supply, fertility control
which can be solved only through health education.”

4) Primary health care approach:

* This is a radically new approach starting from the people with full participation and active
involvement in the planning and delivery of health services based on principal of primary health
care.

Q. What are the stages of health education?
Q. Write down the stages of adoption of new idea or practice. [DU-18M, 16J,12Ju]
Q. Discuss stages of health education to adopt a new ideas.
Answer
Stages in health education:
1) Awareness: At this stage, the person comes to know about the new idea or practice.
2) Interest: At this stage, the person seeks more detailed information.
3) Evaluation: During this stage, the person weighs the pros & cons all the practice and evaluates its
usefulness to him or to his family by mental exercise and reach a decision.
4) Trial: At this stage, the positive decision is put into practice.
5) Adoption: At this stage, the person decides that new practice is good and adopts it.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 896]

Q. sale eae ducation can promote public health? [DU-16N]
Q. Mefitionshe components of health education. [RU-17N]
oan re the contents of health education? [SUST-16M]
nsw.
Contents of health education: May be divided into 8 main divisions —

1. Human biology: Much of the teaching pertaining to human biology is done in schools. The need for
exercise, rest & sleep are taught. The effects of alcohol, smoking, resuscitation & first aid are also
taught.

2s Nutrition: To guide people to choose optimum and balanced diets, which contain nutrients necessary
for energy, growth and repair. Education is given on the nutritive value of foods & most expensive
foods are by no means the more nutritious. Health education is also given about storage, preparation,
cooking, serving and eating of food.

3. Hygiene:

a. Personal hygiene: The aim is to promote standard of personal cleanliness within the setting of
the conditions where people live. It includes bathing, clothing, washing hands and toilet, care of
feet, nails & teeth, spitting, coughing, sneezing, personal appearance and inculcation of clean
habits in the young.

ist the principles of health education. [DU-15Ju, SUST-16N, CU-13J]

Q. Discuss any two of them. [SUST-16N]

Answer

Erinciples of health education: It is possible to abstract certain principles of learning & use them in health

education.

1) Credibility: It is the degree to which the massage to be communicated is perceived as trustworthy

by the receiver.

2) Interest: It is a psychological principle that people are unlikely to listen to those things, which are
not to their interest. It is salutary to remind ourselves that health teaching should relate to the
interests of the people.

Participation: It is a key word in health education. Participation is based on the psychological

principle of active learning, which is better than passive learning.

Motivation: In every person, there is a fundamental desire to learn. Awakening this desire is called

- motivation. There are two types of motives - primary & secondary.

5) Comprehension: In health education, we must know the level of understanding education and
literacy of people to whom the teaching is directed.

6) Reinforcement: Few people can learn all that is new in a single contact. Repetition at intervals is
extremely useful. Related information assists comprehension & understanding. Every health
campaign needs reinforcement.

7) Learning by doing: Learning is an action process; not a memorizing one in the narrow sense.

8) Known to unknown: In health education work, we proceed from the known to the unknown i.e.
start where the people are and with what they understand and then proceed to new knowledge.

9) Setting an example: The health educator should set a good example in the things he is teaching.

10) Good human relations: Good human relations are of utmost importance in learning. Studies have
shown that friendliness and good personal qualities of the health educator are more important than
his technical qualifications.

11) Feedback: It is one of the key concepts of the systems approach. The health educator can modify
the elements of the system (e.g. massage, channels) in the light of feedback from his audience.

12) Leaders: Psychologists have shown and established that we learn best from people whom we
respect and regard. In the work of health education, we try to penetrate the community through the
local leaders - the village headman, the school- teacher or the political worker.

In health education, we must proceed “from known to unknown”:

In health education work, we must proceed “from the concrete to the abstract”; “from the particular to
the general”; “from the simple to the more complicated”; “from the easy to more difficult”, and “from the
known to the unknown”. These are the rules in teaching.

Q. Define motivation. [DU-16J, CU-16N/J, RU-17M, 16J]
Q. Classify motivation with example. [RU-17M,16J]
Q. ‘Motivation is important in health profession’-justify. [CU-16N]
Q. Write short note on: Motivation [RU-15Ju]
Answer :
Motivation:
Motivation is an intra-psychic instinct, desire or force of attitude or behavioural change. In every
person, there is a fundamental desire to learn. Awakening this desire is called motivation.

According to William Scot, Motivation means ‘a process of stimulating people to action to accomplish
desired goals’.

It involves a chain reaction as illustrated below:
Felt needs +> Wants or goals > Tension — Satisfaction of wants — Actions for achieving goals.

Motivation of people results in:
a. Improved commitment

b. Improved participation &
c. Improved performance.

There are two types of motives:
1. Primary motives: (e.g. sex, hunger, survival) are driving forces initiating people into action; these
motives are inborn desires.
2. Secondary motives: (e.g. praise, love rivalry, rewards and punishment, recognition) are based on
desires created by outside forces or incentives.

; In health education, motivation is an important factor i.e. the need for incentives is a first step in
learning to change. The incentives may be positive or negative.

Example:

; To tell a lady, faced with the problem of overweight, to reduce her weight because she might develop
Cvs disease or it might reduce her life span, may have little effect, but to tell her that by reducing her weight
she might look more charming and beautiful, she might accept health advice.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 899 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 4/511]

Classification of audio-visual aids (media) used in health education:
(1) Auditory aids: Radio, Tape recorders, Microphones, Amplifiers, Earphones.

(2) Visual aids: :
(a) Not requiring projection: Chalk-board, leaflets, posters, charts, flannel graph, exhibits,
models, specimens etc.
(b) Requiring projection: Sliders, film strips.

(3) Combined A-V aids: Television, sound films (Cinema), slide-tape combination.
[Ref- Park / 24/900]

Advantages of audio-visual aids:

1) They supply a concrete basis for conceptual thinking and hence reduce meaningless word-responses
of students. ,

2) They have a high degree of interest for students.

3) They make learning more permanent.

4) They offer a reality of experience which stimulates self-activity on the part of pupils.

5) They develop a continuity of thought; this is especially true of motion picture.

6) They contribute to growth of meaning and hence vocabulary development.

7) They provide experiences not easily obtained through other materials and contribute to the
efficiency, depth & variety of learning.

Chapter-22: Social science & Meee bth ——————

Q. Define behaviour. [SUST-16N, CU-15,12J]
Q. Classify behaviour, [DU-15J, SUST-16N]
Q. What are the types of behavior with illustration? [DU-16M]

Q. What are compliance behaviour and avoidance behaviour?
Answer

Behaviour:
Human behaviour is the result of physical and mental factors (body & mind) interacting in complicated
ways. Behaviour is “the total reactions (of an individual) accessible to external observation.

[Ref- Park / 24" / 710]
Or,
The various voluntary movements undertaken by the body are in response to motives and decisions.
They are described as a whole as behaviour, Behavior can refer to every activity of the body as an individual.
Similar activities are thus classified as patterns of behaviour.
[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 470]

Classification of behaviour:
1. Health behaviour:
i) Compliance behaviour: It is the result of motives that move towards a desired action. For
examples, accepting immunization, taking nutritious food, exercising, brushing teeth, bath etc.
ii) Avoidance behaviour: This is the result of motives that move away from disliked or feared
ee For examples, stopping the use of cigarette smoking, avoiding fatty food an alcoholic
rinks.

2. Ilness behavior: It refers to how people react with symptoms. In illness behaviour, people will wait to
see whether the symptoms persist or worsen after detecting a symptom and if the symptom continue the
affected person will seek help before seeking medical help.

3. Treatment behavior: It refers to those activities used to cure diseases and restore health.

[Ref- Park /24"/711 + Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5"/ 471]

Q. How behaviour can be considered as a cause of disease?
Q. How behaviour influences on human health?

Answer

Behavior as cause of disease:

The main causes of death in developed countries are no longer infectious diseases caused by specific
organisms, but degenerative conditions of multiple aetiologies, which have their origin in the way they live in
society.

Disease prevalence depends on the interaction of biological and social characteristics in the individuals.
Personal habits related to life style, which are strongly connected with certain diseases such as smoking with
lung cancer, early promiscuity with cervical cancer and diet with coronary heart disease.

Another behavior factor in disease prevalence is the psychological make-up of the individual. In
practice there is an interplay between internal conflicts and external stresses which affect the coping and
defensive adaptations of individuals and so after their vulnerability to organic disease.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" / 470]

Q. What are the causes of behaviour?
Answer
Causes / determinants of behaviour:
1) Environmental stimuli.
2) Emotions and feelings.
3) Needs.
4) Motivation.
5) Intellectual perception.
[Ref- Park /24"/711]

Q. Mention the types of responses,

Answer

Types of responses: All forms of behaviour are responses to stimuli. They are classified as follows —
1) Physical responses; habits, skills.

2) Organic responses: emotions, feelings, tension

3) Intellectual responses: perceptions, thinking, reasoning.
[Ref- Park /24"/744)

For Viva

* Emotion: An emotion is a strong feeling of the whole organism. Emotions motive the human
behaviour. An emotional experience is characterized by both external and internal changes in the
human being.

A) Some major emotions are: Fear, Anger, Love, Hate, Jealousy, Moodiness, Joy, Sorrow,
Sympathy, Pity, Lust, Grief etc,
B) Some specific emotions:
1) Fear: Most common emotion. It can produce excitement or depression. Some of the
common fear of man are — fear of dark, fear of snakes, fear of death etc.
2) Anger: It is a destructive force which may create offensive situation.
3) Anxiety: Can be observed by rapid pulse and breathing, flushing, tremor, sweating and
dry mouth.
4) Love: The emotion by which a man can enjoy a happy and meaningful life in this

world.
[Ref- Park /24"/712]

* Psychosocial illness: There are a group of diseases known as “psychosocial diseases” (mind acting on
body), e.g. essential hypertension, peptic ulcer, asthma, ulcerative colitis which are attributed to

disturbed emotional states.
[Ref- Park / 24/712]

Q. Mention the measures for control of emotion.

Answer

Measures for control of emotion: The following tips may be useful in controlling one’s emotion —
1) Cultivate hobbies, good hobbies of reading and recreation.
2) Adopt a philosophy of life to enable you to avoid mental conflicts.
3) Try to understand your own limitations.

4) Develop a sense of humor.
[Ref- Park / 24" /712]

Q. What are the human needs?
Q. Mention the kinds of human needs.

Answer

Kinds of human needs:

1) Biologic needs: These are ‘survival’ needs, A hungry man needs food, thirsty man water & sick
man need medicine etc. There are other needs such as sleep, rest, recreation and fresh air, The
doctor should be aware of these needs in the day-to-day care of the patients.

2) Social needs: The need for company, love, affection, recognition & education are all social
needs. Some of these needs are met by the family, and some by the community.

3) Economic needs: Economic security, that is security from want, is one which everyone desires.

=conomic needs:
4) Ego-integrative needs: The desire for Prestige, power and self-respect come in this category.

[Ref- Park /24"/712]

For Viva

° Attitudes: An attitude has been defined as a relatively enduring organization of beliefs around an
object, subject or concept which predisposes one to respond in some preferential manner. Attitudes are
not learnt from text-books, they are acquired by social interaction, ¢.g. attitude toward persons, things,
Situations and issues (e.g. government policies, programmes and administrative measures.

Attitudes are acquired characteristics of an individual. They are more or less permanent ways of

behaving.
An attitude includes three components:

Y A cognitive or knowledge element
v Anaffective or feeling element and

YA tendency to action. [Ref- Park /24"/713]
ef- Par!

> Opinions and beliefs: Opinions are views held by people on a point of dispute. They are based on
evidence available at the time. Opinions by definition are temporary, provisional. They can be looked
on as beliefs for the time being. Beliefs, on the other hand are permanent, stable, almost unchanging. It
is thus easier to give up one’s opinions when faced with the facts, attitudes and beliefs do not succumb

So easily.
[Ref- Park /24"/713]

: Perception: The word perception implies observation, recognition and di

Errors in perception:
1) Imperception: That is, inability to recognize. This may be due to damage to the sense

organs, e.g. anesthesia.
2) Ilusion: An illusion is a false perception. Mistaking a rope for a snake, a tree for an animal
are called illusions. Illusions occur in mental diseases. Illusions may be auditory or visual.
3) Hallucination: Hallucination is an imaginary perception. Itis a gross error of perception.
Seeing objects that do not exist, hearing sounds that are false, seeing objects moving in a
room are called hallucinations. Hallucinations occur in mental disorders. ,

[Ref- Park /24"/713]

+ Cognition: Cognition means thinking skills that include language use, calculation, perception, memory,
awareness, reasoning, judgment, learning, intellect, social skills, and imagination.

Conditions affecting learning:
1)

Intelligence: Learning depends upon the intelligence or mental faculty of an individual. It involves
the activity of sensory adjustment and motor mechanisms of the body. The mental faculty is related
to heredity, nutrition and 1Q. Children with low IQ are poor learners. They may not learn at all.

2) Age: The curve of leaning reaches its peak between 22 and 25 years or age. After the age of 30,
there is a sharp decline. It has been appropriately said. You cannot teach an old dog a new trick,

3) Learning situation: Physical facilities for learning, viz, institutions, teachers, textbooks,
audiovisual aids promote learning.

4) Motivation: In order to learn effectively, there must be adequate motivation. The powerful motives
are encouragement. praise, reward and success. These stimulate learning.

5) Physical health; A physically handicapped person. e.g. deaf, dumb, chronically sick cannot leam.

6) Mental health: Worries, anxieties, and fears interfere with learning.

Q. Discuss the theories of learning.
Answer
The theories of learning:

1) Learning by conditioned reflex: It is well known that when dogs see food, they begin to salivate;
this is an inborn reflex. Pavlov, the Russian physiologist discovered that if a bell was rung when the
dogs were fed, eventually, salvation could be induced by the ringing of the bell alone. This is called
conditioned reflex.

2) Trial and error: The lower animals (Apes & cats) learn by trial & error method. We also learn a
good deal by this method. A child ‘tries & tries again’ using a number of approaches until
accidentally the ideal approaches become obvious.

3) Learning by observation & imitation: A child copies or imitates gesture, facial expressions and
movements such as walking. He learns language by observation & imitation. Observation is an
important element in medical examination. .

4) Learning by doing: Here, there is coordination of muscular responses with sensory impulses.
Nursing skills (e.g. bed making, applying bandages, giving bath) are leant by doing.

5) Learning by remembering: We also learn by memorizing - remembering dates, events,
memorizing a poem, remembering faces etc.

6) Learning by insight: When we are faced with a problem, we solve it by insight or mental
exploration. When the doctor makes a diagnosis, some amount of insight is involved. It appears that
human begins learn by a combination of methods.

7) Demonstration: Here a procedure is carried out step by step, slowly and accurately before an
audience, the demonstrator ascertaining that the audience understands how to perform it. The
demonstration involves the audience in discussion, when possible.

8) Field experience: It involves a series of activities for diagnosing problems, planning procedures to
solve them and implementing and evaluating these programmes. It provides opportunities to
acquire with number of skills.

9) Problem solving.

[Ref- Park /24"/714]

Habits, Frustrations & Conflicts

* Habits: Habit is an accustomed way of doing things, Habits and sad to have 3 characteristics —
Y They are acquired through repetition

vY They are automatic, and

v They can be performed only under similar circumstances.

o

<

Habits accumulated through generations emerge as customs, and customs in turn create
habits. Habits once formed persist and influence human behaviour.

“» Frustrations: All people have needs - biological, social, economic, which they try to satisfy. When
they are unable to meet their needs and desires, they feel frustrated.
The sources of frustration may be external, e.g. unemployment, failures and defeats or, internal,
e.g. lack of health, lack of intellectual ability, etc.

“ Conflicts: A conflict is like a tug of war between two or more courses of action or between opposing
ideas. The person is required to act one way or the other, often generating painful emotions as for
example in choosing a life partner or a job. He has to weigh the pros and cons of the situation to be able
to make a correct decision. It is essential for a person's mental health that conflicts should be resolved
as quickly as possible, within a reasonable period of time, before emotional disturbances occur.

Personality

Q. Define personality. [RU-15Ju,12Ju,1 Wu, 10Ju]

Q. Enumerate the component of personality. [SUST-16M]

Q. Write short note on: Personality.

Answer
Personality:

The term personality is a key word in psychology. It implies certain physical and mental traits, which
are characteristics of a given individual. These traits determine to some extent the individuals behaviour or
adjustment to his surroundings.

Components of personality:

1) Physical: Height, weight, colour, facial expression, physical health.

2) Emotional: Fear, anger, love, jealousy, guilt, worries.

3) Intelligence: Intelligent or dull.

4) Behaviour: Gentle, kind, affectionate, balanced, submissive and aggressive.

Types of personality:
1) Extrovert (Type-A): It is a person who is thought to be dashing, practical, active and showing off

and easily mixes with people.
2) Introvert (Type-B): It is a person who is reserved, shy & generally keeps to himself.

3) Mixture of both.
j [Ref- Park /24"/715]

Q. How personality of an individual is developed? [DU-10J]
Q. Illustrate the influencing factors to develop personality. [RU-10J]
Answer

Stages of personality development:

1) Infancy: The first | year of life is called infancy. The infant is hardly a social creature . There is
rapid physical and mental growth. The infant is totally dependent on the mother. By the end of first
year; the infant is able to stand up for a short while and tries to walk with a little support. He enjoys
simple tircks and games.

2) Pre-school child: This stage is marked by considerable growth of brain. The child feeds himself,
speaks, loves his home, fears dark, loves stories and wants to assume responsibility. He begins to
mix with other small children.

3) School age: The school age period ranges from 5 to 15 years. The school going child is active all
the time. By the age of 8, the mental powers are fully developed. The brain of the child at the age of
8 years is almost of the same size as an adult. The child begins to reason. There is gradual
detachment from the family, and greater attachment to his playmates and friends. He begins to form
groups. The period of childhood terminates with the onset of puberty, which is about 11 years in the
case of girls and 13 in the case of boys.

4) Adolescence: Adolescence or "teenage" is turbulent period in one's life. This is a period of rosy

dreams, adventure, love and romance. The teenager strives for independence, He dislikes parental

authority. He becomes fully aware of social values and norms. There is rapid physical growth.

Adults: The person is mature and more balances. The physical and mental characteristics are fully

developed. It is difficult to draw a line when adolescence ceases, and adulthood begins.

6) Old age: It is difficult to say when old age begins, It is a gradual process marked by decline in
physical powers and acuity of sense organs. Old age is marked by certain psychological changes
such as impaired memory, rigidity of outlook, irritability, bitterness. Inner withdrawal and social

maladjustment. '

Defense mechanism

Q. State defense mechanism. [DU-13Ju]
Q. What is defense mechanism? What are the types of defense mechanism?
Answer
Defense mechanism:
When an individual is faced with problems, difficulties or failures, he employs certain ways or devices
to achieve health, happiness or success. These are called defense mechanisms.

Types of defense mechanism:

1) Rationalization: Instead of accepting failure and correcting himself, the individual tries to make
excuses and justifies his behavior. This is called rationalization.

2) Projection: Sometimes the individual blames others for his mistakes or failures.

3) Compensation: Many people make use of compensation to enhance their self-esteem and prestige.

4) Escape mechanism: Some individuals adopt what is known as an “escape mechanism” to .
overcome failure or defeat. Some students pretend illness and do not appear for examinations. This
is an escape phenomenon.

5) Displacement: It is trying to escape from one situation and fixing blame on another situation.

6) Regression: Some people resort to childhood practices (e.g. weeping when something goes wrong)

as a mode of adjustment.
[Ref- Park /24"/ 715]

Family: The family isa primary unit in all societies.
Itis a group of biologically related individuals living together and eating from a common kitchen.
___ The term family differs from household in that all the members of a household may not be blood
relations, e.g. servants.

Types of family:
1, Nuclear / elemental family: It consists of the married couple and their children while they are still
tegarded as dependants. They tend to occupy the same dwelling space. In the nuclear family, the

husband usually plays a dominant role in the household,

2. Joint family:

> It consists of a number of married couples & their children who live together in the same
household. All the men are related by blood and women of the household are their wives,
unmarried girls and widow of the family kinsmen.
All the property is held in common,
All the authority is vested in the senior male member of the family.
The familial relations enjoy primacy over marital relations. Early & arranged marriage is
advocated toward off any threat from marital relationship.

VVvV

3. Three generation family: It is confused with joint family. It is fairly common in the West. This tends
to be a household where there representatives of 3 generations. It occurs usually when young couples
are unable to find separate housing accommodation and continue to live with their parents and have

their own children.

Functions of the family:

1. Residence: Family provides a clean & decent home to its member.

2. Division of labour: The male had the sole duty to earn a living and support the family. The female had
the total responsibility for the day to day care of children and running of the household. In

industrialized & urbanized communities, there is less marked distinction between the functions of men

& women.

Reproduction & bringing up of children.

Socialization.

Economic function.

Social care: Family provides social care by
a) Giving status in a society to its members, i.e. use of family names where it occurs. Some have a

strong feeling of kinship that they belong to a particular family- it denotes some kind of
association with someone distinguished in that particular society.

b) Protecting its members from insult, defamation etc.

c) Regulating marital activities of its members.

d) Regulating to a certain extent political, religious and general social activities.

e) Regulating sex relations through incest-taboos.

Q. Mention the functions of family relevant to health behavior and health.
Q. Discuss the role of family in health and disease [DU-14J,12J] / in social life [RU-16N].
Q. Write down role of family members in maintaining good health and keep the

members of the family free from disease. [CU-10Ju]
Answer

Functions of family relevant to health behavior and health:

1. Child rearing: Physical care (feeding, nutrition, hygiene, sleep, clothing, discipline, habit training) of
the dependent young in order that they may survive to adulthood and perpetuate the family.

2. Socialization: By socialization is meant teaching the young the values of society, and transmitting
information, culture, beliefs, general codes of conduct, by example and precept in order to make them
fit for membership in the wider society of which the family is a part.

3. Personality formation: The family act as a “placenta” excluding various influences, modifying others
that pass through it and contributes some of its own in lying the foundation of physical, mental and
social health of the child.

4. Care of dependent adults:

Y Care of the sick and injured.
Y Care of women during pregnancy and childbirth.
Y Care of the aged and handicapped.

5. Stabilization of adult personality: The family provides an opportunity to release the tension and stress
so that the individual can attain the mental equilibrium. Mental illness, alcoholism, narcotic addiction,
and certain chronic illnesses such as peptic ulcer, colitis, high blood pressure, rheumatism, skin diseases
are accepted as “stress diseases”.

6. Familial susceptibility to disease: Certain diseases such as hemophilia, colour blindness, diabetes, and
mental illness are known to run through families. Schizophrenia, psychoneurosis and some forms of
mental deficiency are also known to have a familial incidence. The family is often the playground also
for such communicable diseases as tuberculosis, common cold, scabies, diphtheria, measles, mumps,
tubella, chicken pox, dysentery, diarrhoea, and enteric fever.

7. Broken family: Children who are victims of broken families have been found to display in later years
psychopathic behavior, immature personality and even retardation of growth, speech and intellect.
Children from these families may drift away to prostitution, crime and vagrancy.

8. Problem families: Problem families are those which lag behind the rest of the community. Children
who are reared in such an environment are victims of prostitution, crime, and vagrancy.

Q. Discuss the doctor-patient relationship. [SUST-18M,16M]

Answer
Doctor-patient relationship:

The doctor-patient relationship is central to the practice of healthcare and is essential for the delivery
of high-quality health care in the diagnosis and treatment of disease. The doctor-patient relationship forms one
of the foundations of contemporary medical ethics. For most physicians, the establishment of good rapport with
a patient is important. Some medical specialties, such as psychiatry and family medicine, emphasize the
physician-patient relationship more than others, such as pathology or radiology.

Role of a doctor in developing doctor-patient relationship: .
1) A doctor must always keep in mind the importance of preserving human life from the day of

conception until death.
2) When some examinations and treatments are beyond his capacity, he should summon another

doctor who has the necessary ability.
3) A doctor should maintain absolute professional secrecy of the patient. ; ;
4) A doctor must give necessary treatment in emergency circumstances, unless he is certain that it can

be given by others.
Role of a patient in developing doctor-patient relationship:
1) A patient must have confidence in the competence of their physician and must feel that they can

confide in him or her. shan:
He should furnish the doctor with complete information about past illness, family history of

diseases and the facts & circumstances of his illness.
3) He should strictly follow the instructions of the doctor as regards diet, medicine, mode of life etc.

4) He should pay a reasonable fee to the doctor.

2)

4) The doctor’s greed for money.

Q. Discuss the principal structural organs of WHO.
Answer
Principal structural organs of WHO/ organization of WHO: The WHO consists of 3 principal organs- .

* The World Health Assembly: This is the “Health Parliament” of Nations and the supreme governing
body of organization. It meets annually, usually in May and generally in Geneva, but from time to time
in other countries. It is composed of delegates representations Member States, each of which has one
vote. The main functions of the Health
Assemblies are:

> To determine the international health policy and programs.
To review the work of the past year.
To approve the budget needed for the following year.
To elect Member States to Disintegrate a serve for 3 years on the Executive Board and to
replace the retiring members.

VVVV

* The Executive Board: The Executive Board is composed of 34 members technically qualified in the
field of health. Members are elected for three-year terms. The main Board meeting, at which the agenda
for the forthcoming Health Assembly is agreed upon and resolutions for forwarding to the Health
Assembly are adopted, is held in January, with a second shorter meeting in May, immediately after the
Health Assembly, for more administrative matters.
Functions:

» To give effort to the decision and politics of the Assembly.

» The Board has also the power to take immediate action itself in an emergency, such as

epidemics, earthquakes and floods where immediate action is needed.

%

“ The Secretariat: The secretariat is headed by the Director General who is the chief technical and
administrative officers of the organization. The DG is appointed by the WHA on the nomination of the
EB for a five year term.

Function: To provide Member States with technical and managerial support for their national health
development programs.

Q. What do you mean by executive body of WHO?
Answer
Executive body of WHO:

It had originally 18 members, each designed by a Member State. Subsequently, the number was raised
to 24 & 30. The Health Assembly increased the membership from 30 to 31, providing that no fewer than 3 are
to be elected from each of the WHO regions. The members of the body are to be “technically qualified in the
field of health", they are designed by, but do not represent their governments. One-third of the membership is
renewed every year. The executive body meets at least twice a year, generally in January and shortly after the
meeting of the World Health Assembly in May.

|Ref- Park /24"/ 961]

ICDDR,B:

The International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (ICDDR,B), established in 1960
is an international health research institution located in Dhaka. It was formerly known as Cholera Research
laboratory that was transformed into ICDDR,B in 1978. With the changing trend in the world scenario in health
and population over the years, ICDDR,B has expanded its activities to address some of the most critical global
health needs. In collaboration with partners from academic and research institutions throughout the world, the
Centre conducts research, training and extension activities as well as programmed-based activities,

Objectives:
1) To undertake and promote research on diarrhoeal diseases and on related subjects and nutrition.
2) To prevent and control diarrhoeal diseases in developing country.
3) To improve health care method and public health programs in developing countries:
4) To train and disseminate knowledge in those fields and to develop improved means.

Divisions of ICDDRB: The centre is divided into 4 divisions —
> Clinical science division
> Community medicine division
» Laboratory science division
> Population science division

Major achievements:

1) Development of Dhaka solution.

2) Development of oral rehydration therapy.

3) Development and evaluation of cholera vaccine.
4) Development of improved ORS.

5) Dissemination of knowledge on diarrhea research.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"/574+ Lecture]

International health regulation (IHR)

‘

Q. What is international health regulation?
Answer

International health regulation (IHR):

The International Health Regulations are an international legal instrument which is legally binding on
all WHO Member States who have not rejected them (or, subject to the procedure foreseen in the IHR, who
have made reservations) and on all Non-Member States of WHO that have agreed to be bound by them.

Purpose: ;
The purpose of the International Health Regulations adopted in 1969 [IHR (1969)] is to ensure

maximum security against the international spread of diseases with a minimum interference with world traffic.
The THR (1969) only apply to three infectious diseases: cholera, plague and yellow fever.

Q. Why were the THR revised?
Answer ‘ ;
Because of their narrow scope of application and other limitations, the IHR (1969) were revised by the
WHO Member States. In May 2005, the World Health Assembly adopted the revised International Health
Regulations [IHR (2005)]. The current IHR (1969) will be replaced by the IHR (2005) when the latter come
into force on 15 June 2007.

The purpose and scope of the IHR (2005) are to prevent, protect against, control and provide a public
health response to the international spread of disease in ways that are commensurate with and restricted to
public health risks, and which avoid unnecessary interference with international traffic and trade. The IHR
(2005) also establish a single code of procedures and practices for routine public health measures at
international airports and ports and some ground crossings.

Q. Name the diseases under surveillance and regulation.
Answer:
Diseases under international surveillance program are:
1) Smallpox. .
2) Influenza (HIN1).
3) Poliomyelitis.
4) Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SIRS).
5) Typhus fever.
6) Relapsing fever.
7) Ebola.
8) Zika virus.

Q. Write short note on: Geneva Convention.
Answer '
Geneva conventions: There are four Geneva Conventions adopted on 12 August 1949, They are:
Geneva conventions I- to protect wounded and sick in armed forces on land as well as medical
personnel.
Geneva conventions II- to protect the same categories of people at sea as well as the shipwrecked.
Geneva conventions III- Concerning treatment to prisoners of war.
Geneva conventions IV- regarding protection of civilians in time of war.

Q. What are the pufposes of research?
Answer

Purposes of research:

1. Fill in gaps in information.

Q. What are objectives of research?
Answer

Objectives of research:
1.General objective: It is a short statement that tells in summary forms what will be done during the

studies.
2. Specific objectives: Every research work involves several task. It is statements that tell about each task
that will be (was) undertaker during the research works are turned as specific objectives.

3.Ultimate objectives: It is short statement that tells about the benefits or indication application of
utilization of study finding.

Q. What is research methodology?

Answer

Research methodology: Research methodology is the internationally acceptable rules and regulations to
conduct a research so that the findings can be disseminated throughout the world.

Q. What do you mean by HPSP? / Discuss HPSP.
Answer
Health & population Sector Programme (HPSP);

In the context of various weaknesses, shortfalls and anomaly observed during the implementation of the
Fourth Socioeconomic Development Plan, a five year Health and Population Sector Programme (HPSP)
covering the period July 1998-June 2003, has been formulated in consultation with the development partners
and stakeholders to reform the health and population sector and provide a package of essential health care
services to the people of Bangladesh. The external support will be provided by the World Bank, multilateral and
bilateral development partners.

Aims:
1) To maximize health benefits relative to per capita expenditure.
2) To meet felt needs of the clients.
3) To strengthen service delivery & improve system management.

Objectives:
1) To decrease IMR.
2) To decrease MMR.
3) To control communicable diseases.
4) To improve reproductive health care.
5) To reduce unwanted pregnancy.
6) To increase life expectancy at birth.
7) To decentralize health care services.

Components of HPSP:
. Essential Services Package (ESP)

reorganization of service delivery

Integrated support services.

Hospital level services.

Sector wide management (SWM) of programme.
Policy and regulatory action.

Other services of public health importance.
Other health and nutrition services.

SAAS Ss

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder / 5" /37]

Q. Explain ESP. What are the components of ESP?
Q. State the components of ESP. [DU-12J]
Answer

Essential Services Package (ESP):
Due to resource constraints it is not possible to provide services needed by all segments of population.
It is, therefore, necessary to prioritize the urgently needed interventions in the health and population sectors,
particularly for the most vulnerable groups of population that will have greatest health impact per Taka spent.
ESP will be delivered to address the most important health needs of the population through different

levels of PHC system.
The elements of ESP: The elements of ESP are grouped into five major areas —
1) Reproductive health care (safe motherhood) including family planning.
2) Child health care (ARI, CDD, EPI, Blindness Prevention).
3) Communicable disease control (TB, Leprosy, Malaria, Kala-azar, Filariasis, STD) including EPI.
4) Limited curative care (common conditions and injuries).
5) Behaviour change communication (BCC): Social change, advocacy, social marketing.

ESP principal: Client centered services focusing on the needs of women & children. At all level of services,

increase the —
> Quality of service.

Q. Explain HNPSP.
Answer
Health, nutrition and population sector programme (HNPSP):

‘As the life of HPSP is to come to an end in June 2003 the Government has decided to launch a new
project - Health, Nutrition and Population Sector programme (HNPSP) of 3 year duration.

But since the Project Concept Paper (PCP) and the Project Implementation Paper (PIP) have not been
completed the launching of HNPSP is likely to be delayed. According to the public health experts the existing
programme has yielded hardly any palpable result and hence the decision to introduce a new programme
without the full implementation of the existing one does not seem to be logical.

[Ref- Rashid, Khabir, Hyder /5"™ 137]

House fly

Q. Identify the model. Mention the points in favour of its identification. What are the diseases

transmitted by it?
Answer
Identification:
House fly.

Identifying points:
The body is divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
Head bears a pair of antennae, a pair of large compound eyes and a retractile proboscis.
The thorax is marked with 2 — 4 dark longitudinal strips.
The thorax bears a pair of wings and three pairs of legs.
The legs and the body are covered with numerous short and stiff hairs, called the tenent hairs.

The abdomen is segmented and shows light and dark markings.

Diseases transmitted by house fly:

1) Diarrhoea
2) Dysentery

3) Cholera

4) Gastro-enteritis

5) Amoebiasis

6) Enteric fever (Typhoid and paratyphoid)
7) Helminthic infestations

8) Poliomyelitis

9) Conjunctivitis
10)Trachoma

11)Anthrax

12)Yaws
